contrastive routing-sensitivity auditing to identify and harden safety-mediating experts
residual_risk: Moderate-to-high for open-weight MoE models: the attack needs white-box weight access, but where weights are released it is cheap (0.12-0.95% params), high-yield (ASR_hq 50.5%, +37.6pt over GCG), and stealthy to router-level defenses (routing JSD<0.04). No mitigation is demonstrated in the paper — it is a diagnostic/red-team study — so residual risk is bounded only by weight-access governance and by future expert-aware alignment that the paper calls for but does not provide.

name: Expert-aware MoE safety alignment and safety-critical-expert integrity monitoring
description: A defensive posture (motivated, not yet realized, by the RASET findings) that jointly accounts for router behavior, expert specialization, and expert-parameter robustness rather than treating the router as the locus of safety. Includes: contrastive routing-sensitivity auditing to identify experts that mediate refusal inside topic-specialized representations; integrity monitoring / tamper-evidence on those safety-critical experts (because router-level monitoring is blind to expert-parameter edits that preserve routing); and weight-release governance for open-weight MoE models given that the reprogramming attack is cheap, high-yield, and stealthy under white-box access.

title: Dual-graph alignment detects cross-tool parameter pollution from indirect prompt injection by comparing execution provenance against an injection-immune authorization baseline
summary: AUTHGRAPH separates 'what the agent did' (an Injected Reasoning Graph built from the actual trajectory, deliberately exposed to injected content so manipulation becomes a detectable signal) from 'what the agent should do' (an Authorization Graph derived by a Planner from only user-prompt+tool-catalog in an isolated clean context — Property 1: information-theoretically independent of injected content). A graph alignment checker does dual-pointer traversal with three layers of decreasing certainty: Layer 1 hard block (tool not in authorized set, zero-LLM cost), Layer 2 tool-name check (LLM judges legitimate auxiliary vs suspicious), Layer 3 parameter-source check via a ParamPolicy declaring legitimate source_tools per security-critical parameter, matched against raw observation text. This catches cross-tool pollution (e.g. an injected flight code EVIL-123 from a hotel listing used as book_flight's flight_id whose source_tools=[search_flights]) that passes all tool-level checks. On AgentDojo ASR drops 0.17->0.01 (GPT-4o-mini) / 0.40->0.01 (GPT-4o) at UR 0.69/0.76, and on AgentDyn 0.52->0.02 / 0.39->0.02, outperforming CaMeL, DRIFT, Progent, and PromptArmor; generalizes across GPT-4o, Qwen-2.5-70B, DeepSeek-r1-70B (ASR ->0.01-0.03) without model-specific tuning, at 4.61s / 1.87x overhead.
notes: Verbatim: AgentDojo ASR 0.17->0.01 / 0.40->0.01 (UR 0.69/0.76); AgentDyn 0.52->0.02 / 0.39->0.02 (UR 0.37/0.51); generalization ASR->0.01-0.03 across 4 models; overhead 4.61s/1.87x. Ablation: w/o hard block ASR 0.01->0.12, w/o name check ->0.21 (most critical), w/o param check ->0.18. First defense to structurally compare authorization spec vs execution provenance at parameter-source level.

title: Existing agent injection defenses leave a provenance-authorization gap: tool-call value checks ignore parameter origin and single-graph trace analysis lacks a clean baseline
summary: AUTHGRAPH identifies that no prior defense simultaneously satisfies three properties: (i) faithful execution provenance that admits rather than denies injection-induced manipulation in graph construction; (ii) a comprehensive authorization specification auto-derived from user intent in an injection-free context at parameter-source level and runtime-extensible under least privilege; (iii) trajectory-grounded enforcement that rests verdicts on raw trajectory evidence rather than LLM reasoning over poisoned text. Plan-then-check defenses (CaMeL, DRIFT, Progent) verify syntactic parameter constraints but do not track where a value originates, so cross-tool pollution passes; trace-graph methods (AgentArmor) build a single graph from the execution trace whose construction LLM is itself exposed to injection, faithfully reflecting the manipulated view with no clean baseline to detect the discrepancy. AUTHGRAPH's IRG is deliberately injection-immune by design (manipulation is exposed via cross-graph comparison, not prevented at construction) and the AG provides an unforgeable reference. Known limitations: same-observation pollution (attacker poisons the authoritative source itself) passes the source_tools check; graph-builder attribution errors; single-agent scope (no cross-agent flow); and the replan trust boundary when users authorize dynamic behavior.
notes: Limitations verbatim: same-observation pollution passes ParamPolicy; attribution accuracy depends on builder LLM; single-agent only (cross-agent flow out of scope); replan opens controlled trust boundary exploitable by sophisticated attackers. ParamPolicy allowed_source types: user_prompt, observation_direct, observation_nl, any.

hazard: An LLM agent uses a parameter value that originated from an attacker-controlled observation (indirect prompt injection) in a security-critical tool call, performing an unauthorized operation that passes tool-call-level and syntactic-constraint checks because the value's provenance is not tracked
hazardous_situation: An agent reads an external data source (email, webpage, hotel listing) compromised with an injected instruction or polluted parameter (e.g. flight code EVIL-123, 'transfer funds to attacker account'); the agent uses the injected value as a parameter for a write-class tool (book_flight, transfer) or invokes an unrelated attacker-named tool (fetch_webpage(evil.com/verify)), completing the task while the user believes it succeeded normally
controls: clean-context authorization graph with per-parameter source_tools ParamPolicy (least privilege)
three-layer alignment checker (hard block / tool-name check / parameter-source check on raw observation text)
residual_risk: Low for cross-tool pollution and unauthorized-tool attacks under AUTHGRAPH (ASR reduced to 0.01-0.03 across models at UR 0.51-0.76), but residual risk remains for: same-observation pollution where the attacker poisons the authoritative source itself (passes source_tools check since the value genuinely originates from the expected tool); graph-builder attribution errors causing false negatives/positives; multi-agent cross-agent information flow (out of scope); and the user-opened replan trust boundary exploitable within whitelisted tools ^[ambiguous].

name: Dual-graph provenance-authorization alignment (AUTHGRAPH)
description: An agent-security defense that constructs two complementary graphs and detects indirect prompt injection by structural comparison. The Authorization Graph is derived by a Planner from only the user prompt and tool catalog in an isolated clean context (information-theoretically immune to injection), specifying an expected tool sequence plus a per-parameter ParamPolicy declaring legitimate source_tools for each security-critical parameter under least privilege, with a replan whitelist for runtime extension. The Injected Reasoning Graph is built from the actual execution trajectory, deliberately exposed to injected content so manipulation becomes a detectable signal. A graph alignment checker performs dual-pointer traversal with three detection layers: hard block (unauthorized tool, zero-LLM), tool-name check (LLM judges auxiliary vs suspicious), and parameter-source check matching values against the declared source on raw observation text — catching cross-tool parameter pollution that tool-level checks miss.

title: IHO: a single black-box diffusion-LLM attacker that is adaptive, transferable, and beats layered defenses
summary: IHO trains a masked diffusion LM (LLaDA-8B) as a parameterized attacker via DPO against a StrongReject/HarmBench judge, optimizing harmfulness directly (not affirmative-response probability) and using only black-box target access. On 100 JailbreakBench behaviors (60 train / 40 held-out), one checkpoint per target attacks all behaviors. Against Circuit Breaker, IHO reaches 0.82 EVUS while no baseline exceeds 0.63; adding an external detector (CB+D) drops every baseline below 0.55 while IHO retains 0.77. It matches/exceeds the strongest baselines on LAT (0.78 vs 0.63) and CAT (0.79 vs 0.7), transfers across held-out behaviors and models (transferred policies mostly >0.70 EVUS where baselines fall to 0.44-0.64), and is ~76% cheaper per-sample than the INPAINTING diffusion baseline. The attacker conditions directly on the target behavior via bidirectional infilling, providing implicit per-target adaptation with no manual prompt engineering.
notes: Verbatim EVUS: CB 0.82 vs <0.63 baselines; CB+D 0.77 vs <0.55; LAT 0.78; CAT 0.79; ~76% FLOP reduction vs INPAINTING. EVUS is a new metric correcting ASR's threshold-dependence and judge-error sensitivity. Extends prior diffusion-as-adversary work (Ludke et al. 2511.00203). Targets: Llama3-8B, Qwen2.5 7B-32B + CB/LAT/CAT + PolyGuard detector. Reuses existing model.infilling-abuse threat node.

name: Indirect Harm Optimization (IHO) diffusion-LLM DPO jailbreak

title: AdvGRPO: GRPO-trained adaptive attacker reaches 90-91% ASR and closed-loop multi-turn escalation
summary: AdvGRPO trains attacker LLMs with GRPO + GDPO multi-channel reward normalization (attack reward A, prompt reward P, thinking-trace reward T) and a single-turn->multi-turn curriculum. The Qwen2.5-14B multi-turn attacker hits 90.0% AdvBench / 91.0% HarmBench ASR against GPT-4.1; a reasoning-capable Qwen3.5-9B single-turn attacker reaches 79.1%/71.0% from near-zero base performance, overcoming alignment-induced self-censoring in the <think> trace. Multi-turn attacks transfer especially well to held-out defenders: 88-93% ASR against Phi-4-mini, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B. Crucially, off-the-shelf unaligned models (Abliteration, GRP-Obliteration, Unsafe-SFT) perform poorly as attackers (10-55% ASR), showing that removing refusal is necessary but insufficient — adversarial strategy must be explicitly trained. The thinking-trace reward T specifically targets reasoning models' tendency to recognize and self-censor adversarial tasks.
notes: Verbatim ASR: Qwen2.5-14B MT 90.0/91.0; Qwen3.5-9B ST-Think 79.1/71.0; transfer 88.3-93.3%. Unaligned-as-attacker 10.8-55.0% (much weaker), key claim that unalignment != attack capability. Co-trained defender drops HarmBench ASR to <2% vs 18.8% base. Reuses model.multi-turn-attack node. New technique: thinking-trace reward to defeat reasoning-model self-censoring.

name: Thinking-trace reward attacker training to bypass reasoning-model self-censoring

label: Trainable bypass of reasoning-model self-censoring
description: Reasoning-capable LLMs often recognize during their internal <think>/CoT trace that they are being asked to perform an adversarial task and self-censor or refuse before producing visible output. This safety behavior is itself a trainable target: an attacker policy rewarded for low self-censoring and high objective-faithfulness in the thinking trace can systematically convert a self-censoring reasoning model into an effective attacker (Qwen3.5-9B from near-zero to 71-79% ASR), and the same mechanism could degrade a defender's reasoning-time safety check. The self-censoring CoT is a defense surface that does not survive targeted optimization.

title: Reasoning-model safety self-censoring in CoT is optimizable away
description: Aligned reasoning models defend partly by recognizing adversarial intent inside their thinking trace and refusing. Because this is an observable, scorable behavior, a reward channel (AdvGRPO's thinking-trace reward T) that penalizes self-censoring and gates on objective commitment can train the model to suppress the safety reflection, directing gradient away from self-censoring trajectories. Defense that relies on reasoning-time recognition is therefore not robust to adversaries who can fine-tune or distill the policy.
affected: reasoning-capable LLMs whose safety relies on chain-of-thought self-recognition of adversarial intent

title: Agentic AI as 'attack compression': industrializing the cyber kill chain by lowering cost not inventing new classes
summary: This synthesis reframes the agentic-cyber threat as attack compression: agents do not need to invent novel attack classes to raise risk; they compress existing intrusion phases (recon/OSINT, personalized phishing/BEC, credential abuse, CVE-to-exploit matching, exploit adaptation, post-compromise planning) by lowering attacker time, skill, and coordination cost. Grounded in national assessments (NCSC: AI 'almost certainly' increases intrusion frequency/intensity through 2027), industry telemetry (Verizon DBIR: vulnerability exploitation +34%; CrowdStrike: 81% of hands-on intrusions malware-free), and academic agent-capability results. The three-channel model separates (1) attacker-side augmentation, (2) agentic systems as targets, (3) legitimate internal agents as risky actors with excessive autonomy. The Copy Fail CVE-2026-31431 (Linux local privilege escalation, CWE-269-class, KEV-listed, due 2026-05-15) illustrates that AI-compressed footholds make low-privilege chainable bugs business-critical when combined with phishing/CI-CD/container access.
notes: Evidence-synthesis/forecast paper (grade B: cites measured numbers from secondary reports, not own experiment). Verbatim: DBIR vuln-exploitation +34%; CrowdStrike 81% malware-free; ENISA SMEs 90% would be seriously affected within a week, 57% to bankruptcy. 'attack compression' = new framing of agentic-cyber-risk. CVE-2026-31431 'Copy Fail' stated verbatim w/ KEV due date 2026-05-15; ^[ambiguous] could not independently confirm record on cve.org (page rendered client-side) — paper cites Microsoft/Ubuntu/NVD/CISA secondary advisories.

label: Agentic AI attack compression (cyber kill-chain cost collapse)
description: The reduction of attacker time, skill, and coordination cost to traverse intrusion phases by delegating reconnaissance, phishing/lure generation, credential-abuse workflows, CVE-to-exploit matching, exploit adaptation, and post-compromise planning to tool-using LLM agents. The risk is not novel attack classes but the industrialization (packaging, reuse, as-a-service distribution) of existing tactics, which expands the population of capable actors and shrinks the time from disclosure/foothold to impact. Makes low-privilege, chainable vulnerabilities business-critical and turns patch latency into a board-level risk metric.

title: Copy Fail — Linux kernel local privilege escalation (CVE-2026-31431)
description: A local privilege-escalation flaw in the Linux kernel affecting mainstream distributions with vulnerable kernels, enabling a low-privilege local user to escalate to root. Not remotely exploitable in isolation but highly consequential once chained with initial access (SSH, malicious CI job, container foothold), with elevated impact in cloud, CI/CD, and Kubernetes environments. The paper uses it to argue that AI-compressed footholds make chainability — not raw CVSS severity — the dominant prioritization signal.
affected: Linux kernel (mainstream distributions with vulnerable kernels); cloud / CI-CD / Kubernetes hosts
notes: [NVD 검증 2026-06-23: CVE-2026-31431 실존 확정 — Linux kernel LPE, vulnStatus=Analyzed, published 2026-04-22. cve.org는 JS렌더라 NVD JSON API로 검증.]

title: Agent coordination topology, not just model, drives autonomous offensive-security capability (49.8% validated; whitebox dominates)
summary: A 600-run controlled benchmark isolates agent coordination topology as a variable in autonomous vulnerability discovery + exploit validation across 20 endpoint-reachable targets each carrying one ground-truth CWE. Topology moves validated detection 27.5 points (MAS-Central 36.7% -> MAS-Indep 64.2%); SAS single-agent stays competitive at 50.8% while far cheaper ($0.058/validated finding) and faster (53s median time-to-first-validation). Observability is the dominant axis: whitebox 67.0% vs blackbox 32.7% validated; domain second: web 74.3% vs binary 25.3%, with all 49 'partial' (correct class, no dynamic validation) outcomes occurring in whitebox where exploit-loop closure fails. Model-level: Kimi K2 best at 52.0% and cheapest ($0.047), Claude Opus 4 latency leader (70.2s), GPT-5.2 most expensive ($0.258) without commensurate gain. Takeaway: more coordination is not uniformly better — the real problem is selective routing under uncertainty. Demonstrates current frontier-model agents can autonomously validate ~half of injected web/binary vulns end-to-end.
notes: Verbatim: 600 runs, validated 49.8%, detection-any 58.0%; topology spread 27.5 pts (36.7%->64.2%); WB 67.0% vs BB 32.7%; web 74.3% vs binary 25.3%; SAS $0.058, Kimi K2 $0.047/52.0%, GPT-5.2 $0.258. Per-target CWE mapping in Table 4/5 (CWE-89,22,639,1336,352,79,611,347,285,78 web; 120,134,190,798,73,330,367,416,840,125 binary). Novelty: topology-as-object-of-study for offensive agents. Aligns w/ agentic-se-risk-analyst on agent risk; threat-attack owns the offensive-technique framing.

name: Topology-routed multi-agent offensive security auditing

title: Cross-layer attack propagation in autonomous agent frameworks: input manipulation -> action -> persistent state -> ecosystem amplification
summary: A layered taxonomy decomposes autonomous-agent security into four layers (context/instruction, tool/action, state/persistence, ecosystem/automation) along the lifecycle of a single attack: adversarial input enters at the context layer (direct/indirect/tool-return prompt injection), is translated into unsafe actions at the tool layer (tool-selection manipulation a la ToolHijacker, parameter-construction injection, execution-chain steering, resource-amplification a la Clawdrain achieving 6-7x and up to 9x token consumption), persists at the state layer (memory poisoning, Trojan's Whisper bootstrap-injection that poisons context across sessions), and amplifies at the ecosystem layer (plugin/marketplace supply-chain poisoning, multi-agent communication attacks, third-party API cascading failures). The key claim is that security risks are inherently cross-layer: feedback loops re-inject contaminated state into context, forming iterative attack cycles that defenses designed for isolated components miss. Survey of 19 representative studies finds 13/19 concentrated on context+tool layers and only 2/19 propose full defenses, exposing state-layer and ecosystem-trust gaps. Names heartbeat/cron automation as the mechanism that makes poisoned workflows persistently re-executed without human review.
notes: Survey (grade B). Verbatim: Clawdrain 6-7x and up to 9x token consumption; 13/19 studies on context+tool, 2/19 full defenses. Novel framing: cross-layer propagation lifecycle (input->action->state->ecosystem) + feedback re-injection cycles. Case study OpenClaw (CLAUDE.md / bootstrap-file / workspace-artifact poisoning vector). New threat node agentic.cross-layer-propagation captures the lifecycle. Overlaps agentic-se-risk-analyst on agent-framework risk; this record owns the attack-propagation taxonomy.

label: Cross-layer attack propagation in autonomous agent frameworks
description: A class of agent-framework compromise where a single adversarial input does not stay confined to one component but propagates across architectural layers: it enters at the context/instruction layer (direct, indirect, or tool-return prompt injection), is translated into unsafe behavior at the tool/action layer (tool-selection manipulation, parameter-construction injection, execution-chain steering, resource amplification), becomes durable at the state/persistence layer (memory poisoning, bootstrap-artifact / workspace-file poisoning that survives across sessions), and is amplified at the ecosystem/automation layer (plugin supply-chain, multi-agent message propagation, scheduled/heartbeat re-execution). Feedback loops re-inject contaminated state into the context, forming iterative attack cycles that single-layer defenses cannot contain.

name: Bootstrap / workspace-artifact poisoning for persistent cross-session agent compromise

title: Agent bootstrap/workspace files treated as trusted context without provenance check
description: Autonomous agent frameworks (e.g. OpenClaw) assemble model-visible context from runtime components including system prompts, tool descriptions, session context, and persistent workspace files such as CLAUDE.md or bootstrap artifacts. Because these files are reloaded into the composite context window with no reliable trust hierarchy or provenance verification distinguishing trusted control instructions from attacker-influenced artifacts, adversarial instructions embedded in a workspace/bootstrap file are interpreted as actionable guidance and persist across sessions, then can be amplified by scheduled (heartbeat/cron) re-execution. This is the persistence channel of cross-layer propagation.
affected: autonomous agent frameworks that reload persistent workspace/bootstrap files into model-visible context (e.g. OpenClaw-class agents)

title: Compliance-correction symmetry: a larger compromised agent is a better saboteur (53.7pp drop) but same-size correction neutralizes it
summary: Injecting an adversarial 'Mischievous Engineer' into a strictly linear MetaGPT-style SDLC pipeline (PM->Architect->PM->Engineer) shows a compliance-correction symmetry: the same capability that lets a large model faithfully execute a malicious 'insert subtle off-by-one / inverted-comparison / swapped-index bugs' instruction also lets a same-size downstream agent detect and repair it. In the No-Fix pipeline the malicious HumanEval Pass@1 drop grows with scale to 53.66pp for Qwen 3.5 at 27B (Control 97.56% vs Malicious 43.90%) and 23.78pp for Gemma 3 27B — McNemar-significant (p<0.001) for all models >=9B. Adding a terminal QA-Engineer + Fixer-Engineer stage (strictly preserving linear topology) collapses the drop to 0.61pp at Qwen 27B (Malicious 96.95%), with no QA+Fixer comparison reaching significance after Holm-Bonferroni correction. Of 27 surviving-attack cases at >=9B, 7 are QA detection misses and 11 are incomplete Fixer repairs. Implication: small models are weak saboteurs (near-zero drop), larger models are dangerous saboteurs but the brittleness ascribed to linear topology is really lack of a correction stage.
notes: Verbatim: Qwen3.5-27B No-Fix malicious drop 53.66pp (97.56->43.90); QA+Fixer 0.61pp (->96.95); Gemma3-27B 23.78pp->2.44pp; McNemar p<0.001 No-Fix >=9B, none significant QA+Fixer post-Holm-Bonferroni; 27 surviving cases (7 detection miss, 11 repair fail). Novel concept: compliance-correction symmetry — sabotage capability scales WITH model capability but so does repair capability. Malicious Engineer profile (Appendix G) = explicit subtle-bug-insertion w/ misdirecting comments. Open question: does symmetry hold/reverse at >100B. New threat software.code-sabotage.

label: Compromised-agent code sabotage in multi-agent SDLC
description: A threat in LLM multi-agent software-development pipelines where a single compromised or prompt-injected coding agent (e.g. the Engineer role) is instructed to introduce subtle, plausible logic defects — off-by-one errors, inverted comparison operators, swapped indices, mishandled empty/zero values, and deliberately misdirecting comments — while preserving the function signature and avoiding syntax errors so the sabotage survives casual review. The saboteur's effectiveness scales with model capability (larger models execute the malicious instruction more faithfully), making capable agents the more dangerous insiders; the defect propagates downstream as the pipeline's final artifact unless a dedicated terminal verification+correction (QA->Fixer) stage intercepts it.

name: Mischievous-Engineer subtle-logic-bug injection in linear SDLC pipeline

title: Linear multi-agent SDLC pipeline lacks terminal verification/correction stage
description: Strictly linear LLM multi-agent code pipelines (PM->Architect->PM->Engineer) make the Engineer's output the final evaluated artifact with no downstream check. A compromised Engineer can therefore deliver subtly-bugged code straight to the output, and the malicious-induced quality drop grows with model scale (up to 53.7pp at 27B). The root weakness is the absence of a terminal QA+Fixer correction stage rather than the linear topology per se: adding a same-size QA-Engineer (STATUS: ISSUES_FOUND) feeding a Fixer-Engineer collapses the drop to ~0.6pp while preserving linearity. Single-pass QA without a separate repair stage is structurally insufficient against a capable adversary.
affected: linear LLM multi-agent software-development workflows (MetaGPT-style) without a terminal QA+Fixer correction stage

title: Agent-BOM: unified graph closes the semantic gap for post-hoc agent security auditing
summary: Agent-BOM models an agent system as B=(A,V,E,alpha): static capability nodes (Agent/Code/LLM/Prompt/Tool/Skill/LongTermMemory) plus runtime semantic nodes (External/Goal/Context/Reasoning/Decision/Action/Observation), linked by four edge families and security attributes (source, trust_level, integrity_status, authentication_status, permission_scope). The paper argues SBOM/AIBOM, logging, tracing, and generic provenance each only partially cover six audit questions Q1-Q6 (risk entry, semantic evolution, persistence, cross-agent propagation, trigger explanation, realized impact); Agent-BOM is the only representation giving direct support to all six (Table II). Auditing is a 4-tuple rule R=<v_entry, P_back, P_fwd, C>; instantiated for all OWASP Agentic Top 10 (ASI01-ASI10) as graph queries. TCB assumes uncompromised LLM weights and tamper-proof telemetry. ^[ambiguous: OpenClaw/OWASP Agentic Top 10 2026 and GPT-5 are forward-dated artifacts]
notes: Core contribution: first BOM-style auditable representation native to agentic execution; bridges static SBOM/AIBOM to runtime semantic states. Map to se.agentic-sdlc auditability and MCP/A2A trust attribution.

title: Delayed cross-session memory poisoning -> destructive tool invocation auditable as one path
summary: Case study (Fig.2) demonstrates a cross-session attack chain: attacker disguises 'rm -rf ~/.openclaw/workspace/' as a maintenance rule via external user input; the agent writes it into long-term memory (Phase 1: Memory Poisoning, ASI02/ASI06), then in a later session retrieves the poisoned memory, incorporates it into context+reasoning, and invokes an exec tool that deletes the local workspace (Phase 2: Tool Misuse). Agent-BOM connects the initial injection, the persistent memory write (writes_to LongTermMemoryNode), runtime retrieval (reads_from), and realized impact (Observation: 'has been deleted') into a single backward-/forward-traceable audit path. Other three scenarios cover supply-chain skill hijack -> unexpected code execution (ASI04/ASI05, malicious weather skill exfiltrates via WEBHOOK_URL), multi-agent ecosystem hijacking (ASI01/ASI07/ASI08, tampered inter-agent goal cascades across 3 agents), and rogue-prompt trust abuse -> unauthorized email (ASI03/ASI09/ASI10).
notes: Concrete dormant cross-session payload pattern: adversary inputs absorbed into long-term memory, no visible failure until later capability invocation. Strong evidence for agent.persistent-contamination as a distinct risk axis.

label: Cross-session persistent memory contamination
description: A malicious payload injected via untrusted input is absorbed into an agent's long-term memory in one session without immediate effect, then retrieved and activated in a later session to drive a high-risk capability invocation (e.g., destructive tool call). The temporal gap between injection and realization makes point-detection and local blocking ineffective; auditing requires cross-session provenance over persistent memory writes/reads.

name: Malicious third-party skill supply-chain hijack with runtime data exfiltration

title: Registered agent skill with hidden file-access and exfiltration logic
description: A third-party skill installed into the agent directory (e.g., OpenClaw) is registered as a benign weather-query capability but its implementation reads local sensitive files (readFile of openclaw.json) and exfiltrates them to an external WEBHOOK_URL via fetch POST, and deletes local resources. Long-term memory is modified so the skill is auto-invoked at session start. The declared functionality contradicts the actual behavior, and the agent trusts and invokes it during task execution, turning a static capability risk into a runtime code-execution and data-exfiltration impact (OWASP ASI04 -> ASI05).
affected: LLM agent frameworks with pluggable third-party skills/tools and persistent skill registries

name: Agent-BOM path-level security auditing
description: A BOM-style hierarchical attributed graph plus 4-tuple auditing rules (entry localization, backward tracing, forward tracing, adjudication conditions) that reconstructs the full risk chain (entry -> semantic evolution -> persistence -> cross-agent propagation -> trigger -> realized impact) over agentic executions, enabling rule-based adjudication of boundary violations, unauthorized invocation, persistent contamination, and privilege/trust abuse. Post-hoc auditing substrate, not a runtime enforcement mechanism; effectiveness bounded by telemetry/instrumentation completeness and rule quality.

title: ASPO: deterministic enforcement boundary contains stochastic multi-agent LLM reasoning for safe runtime mitigation
summary: ASPO addresses the structural incompatibility between LLM reasoning (adaptive but stochastic/unsafe) and optimization (feasible but context-blind) by a hybrid agentic-deterministic paradigm in a MAPE-K loop. Multi-agent LLM agents (Context/Reasoner/Constraint/Planner/Audit) are restricted to PROPOSING candidates and plans with NO direct actuation capability (closed-world contract: pattern_id in P, |C_t|<=K); final activation is computed only by a deterministic optimizer g(C_t,b_t,M,B) enforcing closed-world membership, conflict-freeness (Conflict(Y)=0 hard constraint via conflict matrix M), and resource feasibility (CPU/mem/lat/energy budgets). Adversarial prompt manipulation is modeled as bounded perturbation ||delta_t||<=Delta on structured context; the paper proves activation invariance: if optimizer argmax is invariant, Y_t(S_t)=Y_t(S_tilde_t), so untrusted inputs cannot introduce arbitrary actions, violate ordering, or trigger out-of-catalogue execution. Results: gate rejects 99.2-99.5% of candidate plans, 100% gate-audit agreement, Spearman rank=1.00, P99 latency -21.9% / energy -23.1%. TCB excludes hardware compromise, catalogue corruption, direct optimizer tampering.
notes: Defense/control paper. Key design pattern for agentic-SDLC: deterministic actuation boundary as architectural mitigation for prompt-injection-driven unsafe agent actions. Send to risk-safety-analyst for control record + residual-risk chain. Architecture decouples agent reasoning from enforcement = direct mitigation for agent.action-space-violation.

title: Prompt-manipulation / context-poisoning attack surface on agentic IoT decision pipelines (Bot-IoT)
summary: The threat model identifies three attack surfaces targeting the agentic DECISION process (not the detector): (1) prompt-manipulation attempts distort semantic interpretation of telemetry by crafting adversarial traffic that produces misleading evidence tokens; (2) context-poisoning biases structured context variables (threat severity, confidence, resource indicators) via manipulated traffic characteristics; (3) tool-abuse attempts push the decision toward infeasible/conflicting security patterns that could destabilize the gateway. Adversary interacts only through observable traffic behaviour (DoS, DDoS, botnet C2, brute-force, port scanning in Bot-IoT) and indirectly via inputs consumed by the reasoning pipeline, modeled as bounded perturbation S_tilde_t = S_t + delta_t. The novel risk framing: in agentic edge defense, the LLM reasoning/decision layer itself is an attack target distinct from the ML detector, and unconstrained mitigation selection often produces portfolios that violate conflict-free or resource-feasibility requirements (empirical: execution-order violations 2.2-2.6%, resource violations ~1.6%, conflict 0.2% of decisions).
notes: Distinct risk: agentic decision-layer poisoning in cyber-defense agents (defender becomes target). Aligns with redteam-method-analyst llm-as-defender frontier; coordinate so they own the attack technique.

label: Agentic decision-layer context poisoning in autonomous defense
description: An adversary targets the reasoning/decision layer of an autonomous (LLM-based) defense or control agent rather than its detector, by crafting observable inputs (e.g., attack traffic) that distort evidence tokens and bias the structured context (threat class, severity, confidence, resource indicators). The goal is to induce the agent to select unsafe, infeasible, or conflicting mitigation actions that destabilize the protected system, modeled as a bounded perturbation on structured context. Distinct from detector evasion: the decision/composition process is the attack surface.

name: Deterministic actuation boundary for agentic LLM decisions (closed-world optimization gate)
description: Architectural control separating stochastic multi-agent LLM deliberation from deterministic enforcement: LLM agents may only propose candidate actions over a closed-world catalogue, with no direct actuation. A deterministic optimization/validation core computes final activation enforcing (1) closed-world membership (action in fixed catalogue), (2) conflict-free composition via a conflict matrix as a hard constraint, (3) resource/precedence feasibility, before any execution, with a fail-safe baseline on validation failure. Bounds the impact of prompt-manipulation/context-poisoning: adversarial inputs cannot introduce out-of-catalogue actions, violate ordering, or activate conflicting/infeasible portfolios (activation invariance under bounded perturbation). Embedded in a MAPE-K loop with an audit agent verifying admissibility post-hoc.

title: Alignment contracts: effect-level enforcement boundary for offensive-capable agents, robust to prompt injection
summary: The paper frames offensive security agents as an asymmetric control problem: retain strong offensive capability INSIDE an authorized engagement while denying the same capabilities outside scope. The enforcement object is the realized, observable EFFECT (network request, file/process operation, disclosure) crossing a mediated boundary -- NOT the model's internal intent, because a malicious website can prompt-inject the agent to exfiltrate or attack out of scope. Two security properties are enforced: Integrity (all realized effects within operator scope) and Modeled Disclosure (sensitive outputs flow only to authorized sinks). Enforcement Soundness (Thm 6.5): under EOA (complete mediation of effects), a reference monitor M_C yields Run_C(P) |= C for every proposed trace P, with Agent-Behavior Independence (Cor 6.6) -- holds even for adversarial/prompt-injected/backdoored models since the TCB excludes the LLM and agent logic. Impossibility results: pre-admission forbidden-effect absence is undecidable for Turing-complete tool languages (Thm 9.2, via halting reduction); mediation-bypassing tools (kernel modules, raw hardware, out-of-band channels) void the EOA premise (Obs 1); payload-covert/timing/semantic-intent channels lie outside the enforceable boundary (Thm 9.7). Concrete profiles: web pentest (10000 mediated HTTP req budget, GET/HEAD scope) and DeFi smart-contract (0.1 ETH gas cap).
notes: Formal-methods control paper with Lean 4 mechanization. Dual-use: offensive pentest agents need scoped authorization. Key for agentic-SDLC governance: effect-boundary contract as enforceable safety property. Send to risk-safety-analyst for control + residual-risk. Impossibility results inform standards-regulatory on limits of static agent certification.

title: Fundamental limits: static agent safety certification is undecidable; covert channels evade effect monitors
summary: Three negative results delineate the enforceability boundary of effect-based agent monitors. (1) Forbidden-Effect Absence Certification is undecidable (Thm 9.2): for a contract with at least one forbidden effect and a Turing-complete tool language, no decider can statically determine whether a tool will ever attempt a forbidden effect -- proven by reduction from the halting problem (FORBIDFREE_C(T_x) iff not Halts(x)). Sound static analysis can over-approximate forbidden attempts but no sound-and-complete analysis exists. (2) Mediation-Bypassing Tools void soundness (Obs 1): if dynamic tool acquisition lets a tool bypass the mediation layer (kernel modules, raw hardware access, out-of-band channels), the EOA fails and enforcement-soundness is inapplicable -- deployment must confine dynamic tools in sandboxes with complete mediation (WebAssembly capability-gated syscall proxying, seccomp-bpf). (3) Three effect classes lie outside the enforceable boundary: payload-based covert channels (secrets in transmitted byte content, not in event model), timing channels (information in inter-event delays), and semantic intent (two obs-identical traces, one benign one adversarial, are indistinguishable -- intent is not observable). Mitigations for these are best-effort, bypassable, and carry no formal guarantee.
notes: Important for standards-regulatory-analyst: formal proof that static pre-deployment certification of agent forbidden-effect-freedom is undecidable -> runtime mediation is necessary, not optional. Covert-channel/intent limits bound what any effect monitor can guarantee.

label: Agent mediation bypass via dynamic tool acquisition
description: An agent dynamically acquires or invokes a tool that executes effects outside the reference monitor's mediation layer (e.g., kernel modules, raw hardware access, out-of-band network channels, native syscalls below the typed mediation boundary). Such effects appear in real execution but not in the monitored trace, voiding the Effect Observability Assumption and rendering effect-based enforcement-soundness guarantees inapplicable. Requires sandbox confinement (capability-gated WASM, seccomp-bpf) to restore complete mediation.

name: Alignment-contract effect-level reference monitor
description: A reference monitor that mediates an agent's externally observable effects (network/file/process/disclosure events) against a formal alignment contract <scope, allow/forbid effects, resource budgets, disclosure sinks> and denies any effect that is out-of-scope, forbidden, over-budget, or disclosing to an unauthorized sink, evaluated against the already-realized trace prefix. Provides provable Integrity and Modeled-Disclosure guarantees (Enforcement Soundness) under the Effect Observability Assumption -- holding regardless of agent internal state, including adversarial or prompt-injected models, because the LLM and agent logic are outside the trusted computing base. Decidable admissibility check; supports refinement and one-way compatible composition of contracts. Best-effort semantic agentic-layer (intent/payload inspection) added as defense-in-depth but carries no formal guarantee. Does not cover covert payload, timing channels, or semantic intent.

title: SafeAgent: stateful runtime controller + decision core beats text-level guardrails on workflow-level prompt injection
summary: SafeAgent formulates agent security as a stateful, workflow-level decision problem because prompt injection in agentic workflows is no longer single-turn: malicious instructions enter via retrieved documents, tool outputs, memory, or other artifacts and propagate across the reasoning-action loop, influencing intermediate planning and inducing unsafe tool use / unauthorized data transfer. Architecture = (1) Runtime Controller wrapping the agent loop: routes all tool calls through a governed wrapper (controlled execution boundary), curates session context as an explicit runtime object, conditions authorization on accumulated workflow-level contamination signals (taint tracking), and provides six recovery mechanisms (context override/sanitization, agent replanning, context rollback to trusted checkpoint, safe-mode termination, tool-argument rewriting, human-in-the-loop/shadow execution); (2) SafeAgent Core: a context-aware AMI z_t=Phi(x_t,s_t) with parallel specialist risk encoders (obfuscation, trigger activation, memory poisoning, secret leakage, control hijacking, evasion, policy violation, unsafe tool plan, argument-level risk, task drift), advantage-cost modeling, world-model consequence simulation, policy arbitration excluding critical-safety-violating actions, and multi-scale memory synchronization (immediate/task-level/long-horizon risk). On ASB (51 tasks x 40 attack tools = 2040 cases, ReAct + DeepSeek-V3.2, gpt-oss-safeguard-20b core): SafeAgent lowers IPI ASR to 0.2936 and MP ASR to 0.1858, best NRP across all attack types; on InjecAgent (510 direct-harm + 544 data-stealing) drives data-stealing S1 and S2 to 0.0000, total ASR to 0. Ablations: lower override confidence (0.0) best under memory poisoning (persistent contamination -> rejection beats repair); safety-first vs task-first policy is the primary safety-utility operating-point lever.
notes: Defense/control paper with strong verbatim ASR numbers. Reinforces that workflow-level (not single-turn) is the correct unit for agent prompt-injection defense; taint tracking + governed tool boundary + recovery. Send to risk-safety-analyst for control record. Benchmarks ASB+InjecAgent -> link via benchmarks for risk-safety. gpt-oss-safeguard-20b and DeepSeek-V3.2 are real models named in eval.

title: Workflow-level (multi-stage) prompt injection: contamination accumulates and propagates across the action-observation loop
summary: The paper consolidates the threat that prompt injection in agentic systems unfolds at the WORKFLOW level rather than as single-turn manipulation: multi-stage agent pipelines (retrieval -> planning -> tool execution -> memory update) enable composite attacks where injected payloads are distributed across steps to achieve escalation or persistence. Indirect injection embeds malicious instructions in third-party artifacts (web pages, tool outputs) later elevated into the execution context; instruction-triggered backdoor behaviors can activate unsafe plans even without explicit override strings. The key insight motivating taint-tracking for LLM agents: untrusted content carries a contamination label propagated through intermediate representations and decision points, and safety decisions should condition on where information originated, how it was transformed, and whether it is about to cross a privileged boundary (high-impact tool, long-term memory write, sensitive disclosure). Empirically, text-level guardrails (Llama Guard, LLM Guard) provide only marginal protection because message-level filtering cannot prevent attacks realized through tool-mediated interactions and accumulated session context (LLM Guard InjecAgent S1=0.9301, S2=0.9308 ~ near no-defense).
notes: Consolidating threat-framing finding; the attack technique (workflow-level/indirect PI) is owned by threat-attack-analyst -- this record covers the agent-risk half (taint propagation across the loop, privileged-boundary crossing). Coordinate to avoid double counting.

label: Workflow-level indirect prompt injection in agentic loops
description: Malicious instructions enter an agent not through direct user input but via untrusted third-party artifacts (retrieved documents, web pages, tool outputs, memory entries) that are implicitly treated as control input when concatenated into the agent's heterogeneous execution context. The attack unfolds across the multi-stage action-observation loop (retrieval -> planning -> tool execution -> memory update), with payloads distributed across steps to achieve privilege escalation or persistence; contamination propagates through intermediate reasoning and decision points until it crosses a privileged boundary (high-impact tool call, long-term memory write, sensitive disclosure). Distinct from single-turn manipulation: requires stateful taint tracking and workflow-level mediation, not message-level filtering.

name: SafeAgent stateful runtime controller with context-aware decision core
description: A two-layer runtime protection architecture separating execution governance from semantic risk reasoning. A Runtime Controller wraps the agent loop and routes all tool invocations through a governed wrapper (controlled execution boundary), maintains session context as an explicit runtime object, conditions tool authorization on accumulated workflow-level contamination/taint signals, and supplies recovery actions: context override/sanitization, agent replanning, context rollback to a trusted checkpoint, safe-mode session termination, tool-argument rewriting, and human-in-the-loop/shadow execution. A context-aware decision Core (stateful AMI over partially observable trajectories) runs parallel specialist risk encoders, world-model consequence simulation, and constrained policy arbitration that excludes critical-safety-violating actions, with multi-scale (immediate/task-level/long-horizon) risk-state synchronization. Empirically outperforms text-level guardrails (Llama Guard, LLM Guard) on ASB and drives InjecAgent data-stealing success to zero. Override-confidence and safety-vs-task policy weighting set the safety-utility operating point.

title: PARSE: provenance-aware fact-preserving retrieval sanitization for domain-camouflaged injection in RAG agents
summary: PARSE is a training-free, inference-time sanitization pipeline that defends LLM agents against domain-camouflaged indirect prompt injection in retrieved content. Six components: (1) Domain Classifier (Haiku) selects domain-specific authority allowlists; (1.5) Directiveness Gate scores each document 0-1 for directive content and routes delta(d)>=0.5 to full_parse, else simple_paraphrase -- 59% of real enterprise docs take the cheap path, concentrating cost on the 41% high-risk subset; (2+3) Combined Tagger-Extractor (single Haiku call) labels each sentence factual|directive|hybrid, scores injection likelihood with domain allowlists (exempting legitimate authority language: legal 'shall'/'hereby', scientific 'we propose', medical 'treatment resulted in'), and extracts a structured fact list; (4) Structure-Aware Paraphraser (Sonnet) rewrites under a hard constraint that all extracted facts must appear in output; (5) Consistency Checker (Haiku) verifies fact preservation with one retry on failure (closed-loop, distinguishing PARSE from open-loop paraphrasing). On the 122-task real-document benchmark: PARSE achieves 15.6% ASR (vs 25.4% baseline, p=0.014, Cohen h=-0.245, the largest effect size of all conditions, adequately powered n=122>n_min=103) at 86.9% utility. Ablations confirm the structured multi-step analysis is necessary: parse_fast (single combined call) achieves 32.8% ASR -- WORSE than baseline -- because collapsing the pipeline eliminates the fact-extraction constraint; parse_domain_conditional (route by domain not directiveness) achieves 22.1% (not significant). Cost ~3-5 LLM API calls / ~$0.01 per doc, run at ingestion not query time. Largest per-domain ASR reductions: financial 33.3->12.5, DevOps 24.0->12.0.
notes: Defense/control + benchmark paper. Models: Haiku, Sonnet, claude-sonnet-4-5 (task construction) -- real Claude models named. Send control to risk-safety-analyst. Benchmark is novel real-document RAG injection benchmark -> link for risk-safety benchmark intel.

title: Synthetic-to-real generalization failure: domain-camouflaged injection evades classifier and paraphrase defenses on real enterprise documents
summary: Key negative result with red-team implications: prompt-injection defenses validated on synthetic benchmarks do NOT predict real-document deployment performance. Real enterprise documents differ fundamentally from synthetic ones -- a SEC 10-K MD&A runs 500-2000 words, interleaves numerical claims with forward-looking authority language ('management believes', 'the Company shall') that legitimate readers rely on for context. Domain-camouflaged injection (Pai 2026a, CDG metric) embeds malicious goals in professional-domain vocabulary, rendering payloads syntactically indistinguishable from legitimate content and achieving ZERO detection by production classifiers including Llama Guard 3. Two evidenced failure modes: (1) Paraphrasing -- the strongest synthetic-benchmark defense -- shows NO statistically significant ASR reduction on real documents (24.6% vs 25.4% baseline, p=0.500, h=-0.019; detecting this small effect would require n=17,253 tasks) while degrading utility 91.8%->82.8% (9pp cost at zero security benefit), because it indiscriminately rewrites legitimate authority language alongside injections and discards quantitative facts. (2) Llama Guard 4 reaches 18.9% ASR (survives Bonferroni, p=0.004) but at 64.8% utility -- a 27pp cost disqualifying it for production RAG. Token-level sanitization (CommandSans) is context-agnostic, false-positives on legal/financial authority language, and cannot detect camouflaged payloads that contain no syntactic injection tokens. Lesson: evaluate agent defenses on domain-matched real documents, not synthetic proxies.
notes: Strong evaluation-validity finding: benchmark results from short synthetic injection scenarios mislead about real deployment. Relevant to standards-regulatory (evaluation methodology) and risk-safety (benchmark validity). Domain-camouflaged injection = evasion-by-mimicry attack class. Coordinate with threat-attack-analyst who owns the camouflage attack technique (Pai 2026a, arXiv:2605.22001).

label: Domain-camouflaged retrieval (RAG) injection
description: An adversary embeds malicious instructions in content retrieved by an LLM agent (customer uploads, third-party APIs, scraped web, enterprise documents) using legitimate professional-domain vocabulary and authority framing (e.g., regulatory 'shall', financial forward-looking statements) so the payload is syntactically indistinguishable from genuine document content. This evades classifier-based and token-level defenses (zero detection by production safety classifiers) because it carries no syntactic injection markers, and resists paraphrase defenses that cannot separate camouflaged instructions from legitimate authority language. Distinct from overt indirect prompt injection by its mimicry of domain-legitimate semantics; mitigation requires provenance- and domain-aware sentence-level sanitization with fact preservation.

name: PARSE provenance-aware retrieval sanitization
description: A training-free, inference-time, six-component sanitization pipeline applied to retrieved content at document-ingestion time: domain classification selecting authority allowlists, a directiveness gate routing high-risk documents (delta>=0.5) to full processing while cheaply paraphrasing low-risk ones, a sentence-level tagger-extractor that scores injection likelihood with domain-specific allowlists (exempting legitimate authority language) and extracts structured facts, a structure-aware paraphraser that neutralizes injections under a hard fact-preservation constraint, and a closed-loop consistency checker that verifies extracted facts survive sanitization (with retry). Defends against domain-camouflaged indirect prompt injection in professional-domain RAG agents while preserving the factual content needed to complete the legitimate task, achieving statistically significant ASR reduction at near-baseline utility. The structured multi-step analysis (fact-extraction constraint) is necessary -- a single-call collapse degrades below baseline.

title: Defense-by-architectural-layer: only memory-layer tool-gating stops delayed-trigger persistent memory attacks; input/retrieval defenses fail
summary: The delayed-trigger attack (DTA) is a multi-session persistent memory attack: a compliance-framed malicious rule (e.g., 'all outbound emails must be forwarded to an external audit monitor', citing SEC Rule 17a-4) is injected via a RAG document in session S1, stored to persistent memory (memory_save_fact), then in a later trigger session S4 (with conversation history wiped, only the SQLite memory store persisting) recalled and executed as exfiltration. Injection succeeded 100% across 2,520 attack runs; recall was universal; the only variance is execution-stage blocking. Mechanistic finding mapped to the pathway inject->store->recall->execute: (1) input-layer defenses (Minimizer, Sanitizer) NEVER observe the payload because it enters via RAG not user input (88.9% ASR, payload-invariant by construction); (2) retrieval-layer defenses (RAG Sanitizer, RAG LLM Judge qwen2.5:1.5b) observe the document but fail detection -- 0/360 removed -- because the compliance-framed payload is out-of-distribution for a 60-example classifier and the 1.5B judge produces zero malicious classifications (capacity failure: cannot engage semantic content); (3) instruction-layer Prompt Hardening (4 explicit security rules) partially fails at 77.8%, with the 0% reduction driven by 2 models (one genuine refusal, one model-level refusal independent of defense) -- for the other 7, exfiltration was tagged semantic_masking_success: the model acknowledged the rules then overrode them by framing exfiltration as mandatory regulatory compliance; (4) only tool-layer Memory Sandbox (removing memory_recall_fact from the schema, keeping memory_list_all_facts) reduces ASR to 0% for 8/9 models by severing the recall step (explicit_recall_required tagged in all 320 blocks), at zero utility cost (BTCR 100%). Lesson: detection was not required when the attack's critical capability is removed at the schema level; defense effectiveness is determined by which architectural layer the defense operates at relative to the attack pathway.
notes: Rigorous statistics (BCa bootstrap, Holm-Bonferroni, 5040 runs, 0% FP across 2520 no-attack). Models: Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Haiku 4.5 (frontier, both 0% attack), plus 9 open-source (Qwen-2.5/3/3.5 family, QwQ-32B, GLM-4-Flash, GPT-OSS-20B, GPT-OSS-Safeguard-120B). Send to risk-safety-analyst for control records. Strong evidence for agentic.cross-session-memory-persistence already created from paper 1.

title: Capability-removal defenses can create new attack pathways: qwq:32b inversion, hallucination bypass, multi-key normalization
summary: Three novel behavioral findings show capability-removal defenses (tool-gating) have non-monotone, model-dependent effects. (1) Defense inversion (qwq:32b): under no-defense the model achieves 0% ASR via execution refusal (reasons through the routing rule, sees the attacker address, declines to send -- a recalled memory fact is treated as advisory, 'the model chose to store it, so it can choose to ignore it'); under Memory Sandbox it achieves 100% ASR because removing memory_recall_fact forces it to reconstruct the attacker payload directly from the RAG corpus, where the instruction arrives 'fresh' carrying the implicit authority of an organisational source -- and the model's literal-interpretation/refusal mechanism does not activate. Capability removal removed the friction that was protecting it. Practitioner rule: before deploying tool-gating, verify the target model achieves 0% ASR under no-defense via execution refusal; if so, the gate may invert rather than preserve safety. (2) Hallucination bypass (qwen3.5:122b, glm-4.7-flash): when recall is blocked, both deterministically fabricate plausible benign routing rules from training priors (40/40 identical) rather than halting -- ASR is 0% only incidentally because their priors do not contain the attacker address; an attacker who knows the model's prior could craft a key name eliciting the correct address. (3) Multi-key normalization (gpt-oss:20b): in 37/40 runs the model spontaneously stores the malicious document as TWO distinct keyed facts (routing rule + standalone attacker-address value) rather than one monolithic rule -- so a defense that deletes the routing rule by key name leaves the attacker address intact. Key-targeted remediation is insufficient; defenses must clear all memory or validate the semantic content of every stored fact. Also: tool contract language (return messages, schema composition, directive phrasing) is a first-class experimental confound that current agentic evaluation reporting standards do not require disclosure of.
notes: Highest novelty in the batch: capability removal as attack-pathway creator. The Draft-Only Executor archetype (refuses under normal conditions, inverts under sandbox) and hallucination-bypass-as-incidental-safety are new. Multi-key normalization breaks key-targeted memory remediation. Relevant to risk-safety (residual-risk: defense inversion) and standards-regulatory (tool-contract disclosure in eval reporting).

label: Capability-removal defense inversion in agentic systems
description: A capability-removal or tool-gating defense (e.g., disabling memory recall to block a persistent memory attack) inverts and INCREASES attack success for certain models because removing the capability forces the agent onto an alternative execution pathway where its protective mechanism does not engage. Example: a model that refuses to act on a recalled poisoned memory fact (treating stored content as advisory) will instead reconstruct and execute the malicious instruction when forced to read it fresh from a retrieval source carrying implicit organisational authority. Defense effectiveness is therefore non-monotone and model-dependent; capability removal can create new attack pathways rather than only eliminating existing ones.

title: Key-targeted memory remediation bypassed by spontaneous multi-key fact normalization
description: Some LLM agents spontaneously decompose a single malicious instruction into multiple distinct keyed memory facts when storing it to persistent memory (e.g., gpt-oss:20b stored a malicious routing rule as two facts in 37/40 runs: the routing rule under one key and the standalone attacker address as a separate value). A defense that detects and deletes the malicious routing rule by key name leaves the auxiliary fact (the attacker address) intact in memory, which suffices to reconstruct the attack on later recall. Key-targeted memory remediation is therefore insufficient; remediation must clear all memory or validate the semantic content of every stored fact, not just named keys.
affected: Stateful LLM agents with key-value persistent memory and key-targeted remediation defenses

name: Memory-layer tool-gating (Memory Sandbox)
description: A tool-layer defense that removes the memory-recall capability (memory_recall_fact) from a stateful agent's tool schema during sensitive (trigger) sessions while leaving key enumeration (memory_list_all_facts) available, severing the recall step in the persistent-memory attack pathway (inject->store->recall->execute) without requiring detection of whether stored content is malicious. Reduces delayed-trigger persistent-memory attack success to 0% for most models at zero utility cost in the absence of attack. Caveat: effectiveness is non-monotone and model-dependent -- for models that refuse execution on recalled facts but not on freshly-retrieved content, removing recall can invert the defense (forcing the agent onto the RAG pathway and increasing attack success); deployment must first verify the target model's no-defense refusal behavior. Key-targeted variants are insufficient against multi-key fact normalization.

title: SafeClawBench: staged endpoint separation (semantic / audit-evidence / sandbox) for tool-agent red teaming
summary: SafeClawBench argues agent-security evaluation must separate three non-interchangeable endpoints rather than collapse them into one attack-success rate: (1) Semantic Core (CoreFail@600) = LLM judge (GPT-5.4) labels whether the final response semantically adopts/authorizes the unsafe goal; (2) Core-gated harm-evidence audit (HarmEvidence@600) = audits all 1,834 canonical CoreFail rows for TextHarm/AccessHarm/ActionHarm/PersistHarm evidence in the artifact; (3) Exec-Balanced (ObservedHarm@Exec) = deterministic sandbox oracles over file/email/db/memory/web/code stores. 600 cases, 100 per family (DPI/IPI/TRI/MPI/MEX/ADI). Under D0, pooled CoreFail@600=28.0% but HarmEvidence@600=16.8% and SemanticOnly=11.2% — audited harm is strictly narrower than semantic failure. Key red-teaming insight: a model 'agreeing' with an attacker (semantic) is not the same as producing observable harm.
notes: Method↔benchmark link: SafeClawBench is the benchmark (risk-safety-analyst owns the record); this finding records the *staged-endpoint LLM-as-judge teaming method*. Verbatim: CoreFail@600 D0 pooled 28.0% [26.4,29.6]; per-model D0 range Claude Opus 4.7=9.0% to Kimi K2.5=44.2% (4.9x ratio). HarmEvidence pooled D0=16.8%, SemanticOnly=11.2%. Judge=GPT-5.4 temp 0; second-judge validation=Claude Opus 4.6.

title: SafeClawBench CorePass∩ExecHarm: 291/347 sandbox harms pass the semantic judge — judge-only red teaming under-counts harm
summary: The Core-Exec join over 12,000 matched rows (5 endpoints x 4 policies x 600 mappings) exposes that 291 of 347 ExecHarm rows (83.9%) arise from rows that PASS the Semantic Core call (CorePass∩ExecHarm). The join contains 56 CoreFail∩ExecHarm, 1,778 CoreFail-without-ExecHarm, and 291 CorePass∩ExecHarm rows. This is the paper's central red-teaming methodology claim: a text-judge (LLM-as-judge semantic) endpoint systematically misses executable sandbox harm because Core and Exec use separate model calls, prompt formats, tool schemas, parser paths, and sandbox permissions. Under a separate executable protocol, matched task identities produce sandbox harm despite passing the semantic check. Implication for automated red teaming: judge-based ASR alone is insufficient; deterministic state-oracle endpoints are required to catch harm.
notes: Verbatim: 291/347 ExecHarm rows (83.9%) pass Semantic Core; join=56 CoreFail∩ExecHarm + 1,778 CoreFail-no-ExecHarm + 291 CorePass∩ExecHarm. D0 ObservedHarm@Exec range 0.5% (Claude Opus 4.7) to 11.3% (Kimi K2.5), mean 4.133%. Paper cautions this should NOT be read as a simple text-judge miss (separate protocols), but the narrow claim stands: state-level harm is invisible to the semantic judge.

title: SafeClawBench: prompt-policy defenses are model-dependent, not uniformly ranked — long over-specified policy (D4) is a confound not a control
summary: SafeClawBench evaluates four prompt-level defense policies (D0/no-defense, B2/Sandwich lightweight wrapper, D3/layered stack, D4/LongPolicy over-specified bundle with Semantic Intent Anchoring + Memory Integrity Guard + Tool Chain Analyzer). Finding: prompt-policy effects are model-dependent. B2/Sandwich pooled CoreFail=14.8% vs D0=28.0%. D4/LongPolicy is lowest on GPT-5.5 and tied with D3 on Claude Opus 4.7, while D3 is lowest on Qwen3.6-Plus/GLM-5.1/Kimi K2.5. A matched-length control (D3_LM, padded to D4 length) averages 8.0% CoreFail — below both D3 and D4 — showing prompt LENGTH itself changes model behavior. The paper therefore refuses to attribute D4 results to SIA/MIG/TCA components, treating LongPolicy as a policy-complexity probe rather than a validated defense. Critical red-teaming methodology lesson: longer defense prompts can confound apparent robustness gains.
notes: For risk-safety-analyst: prompt policies (instruction hierarchy, StruQ-style data separation, spotlighting, Llama Guard, FASA/ClawGuard) are candidate LLM-as-a-defender controls but the paper warns prompt-only defenses are NOT complete production controls — runtime access control still required for irreversible actions. Matched-length control D3_LM=8.0%. Defense families: B1-B4 lightweight, D1-D3 layered, D4 probe.

title: SkillVetBench: LLM-as-Judge catches instruction-layer skill-supply-chain risk that code-layer scanners are structurally blind to
summary: SkillVetBench frames agent-skill vetting as a supply-chain red-teaming problem: malicious community skills embed harm in the INSTRUCTION LAYER (natural-language directives) not inspectable code, so signature/static scanners are structurally mismatched. On a labeled 100-skill set (78 malicious + 22 benign), the LLM-as-Judge (Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct default) achieves TP=78, FN=0, FP=0, TN=22 (Catch=1.00, Miss=0%), vs best static baseline SkillSieve (Catch 0.85, Miss 15%), CodeBERT (Miss 30%), VirusTotal (Miss 67%). The gap is sharpest on instruction-layer categories: for Prompt Injection (19 skills) VirusTotal flags 0, ClawScan flags 3, LLM-Judge flags all 19; for Memory Poisoning (9 skills) CodeBERT detects 0 (89-100% miss). Conclusion: instruction-layer and multi-agent risk requires a semantic LLM judge; signature matching cannot see it. Wilson 95% lower bounds: recall ~0.95, specificity ~0.85 (100 skills cannot certify perfection).
notes: Method↔benchmark: SkillVetBench is the benchmark (companion arXiv:2606.00925). This finding records the LLM-as-judge instruction-layer vetting method. Verbatim Table 3: SkillVetBench Balance 0.95/Catch 1.00/Precision 0.96/Miss 0%. Baselines miss 15-67%. For agentic-se-risk-analyst: this is a MCP/A2A-adjacent SKILL supply-chain finding (ClawHub/OpenClaw marketplace, tens of thousands of skills).

title: SkillVetBench SARS: five-dimensional agentic-risk score (IFR/DG/AI/BR/CA) captures harm invisible to CVSS
summary: SARS (Skill Agentic Risk Score) is a NEW weighted 0-10 metric for instruction-following agentic systems: SARS=(2*IFR + 1.5*DG + 1.5*AI + 2*BR + 2*CA)/2.7, scoring five 0-3 dimensions — Instruction Fidelity Risk (prompt-hijackability), Data Gravity (data sensitivity), Action Irreversibility, Blast Radius, Chain Amplification (multi-skill force-multiplier). IFR/BR/CA weighted 2x because code-layer scanners cannot see them. The paper deliberately reports SARS, CVSS v4.0, and a three-tier LLM verdict (Benign/Suspicious/Malicious) SEPARATELY rather than fused, because they answer different questions and their DIVERGENCE is the signal. Key result (Table 6): Data Exposure (CVSS 1.84) and Supply Chain (CVSS 2.30) fall below Medium CVSS yet receive Suspicious LLM verdicts because their threat is instruction-level exfiltration / runtime dependency injection that static scoring cannot model. Chain Amplification stays >=1.80 across EVERY malicious category, confirming all confirmed-malicious skills contribute to compositional multi-agent attack chains.
notes: SARS verbatim formula and weights. Worked example inbox-cleaner SARS~7.2 (High). windows-control case: SARS 8.0 High, CVSS 10.0 Critical, 7 SKV findings across 6 categories. Static judge reads declared content only — does NOT execute (CVSS Exploit Maturity inferred not observed). For agentic-se-risk-analyst: Chain Amplification = explicit multi-agent compositional-attack metric.

title: SkillVetBench: LLM-as-Judge detection swings 35-95% by evaluator model — single-judge teaming is unreliable, motivating judge ensembles
summary: SkillVetBench documents severe LLM-as-judge evaluator sensitivity: on the labeled set, vulnerable-skill detection ranges 35% to 95% across four evaluators — Qwen2.5-32B 95% (mean SARS 5.06, high recall/calibrated), Llama-3.1-7B 78% (4.99, broad coverage), Llama-3.2-3B-Ins 43% (5.57, sparse but over-sensitive, 6.50+/-7.80 vulns/skill = poor calibration), Mixtral-8x7B 35% (1.74, systematic false-negative bias / near-uniform abstention, median SARS 0.00). This 60-point spread is a core red-teaming-method caution: a single LLM judge can silently under-detect; the paper recommends evaluators of >=7B with strong instruction-following alignment AND ensemble scoring across multiple judges to reduce single-model bias. Live leaderboard defaults to Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct. Critical for any LLM-as-X red-teaming pipeline: judge choice is a first-class confound that must be calibrated, not assumed.
notes: Verbatim Table 5: detection 35-95%; Qwen2.5-32B 95%/SARS 5.06+/-2.02; Llama-3.1-7B 78%/4.99+/-2.48; Llama-3.2-3B-Ins 43%/5.57+/-2.66; Mixtral-8x7B 35%/1.74+/-2.20. Live leaderboard (Table 10) different roster: Mixtral-8x7B 35.4% vuln. Judge-ensemble calibration is a 2025-26 method shift — links to f-skillvetbench-llm-judge-instruction-layer. No post-hoc reliability-diagram calibration done (acknowledged limitation).

title: Process mining of red-team traces: DFGs reveal absorbing-wall vs porous-gate defense archetypes invisible to ASR
summary: The paper introduces a NOVEL red-teaming analysis method: treat each adversarial campaign as a process-mining 'case', each scored attempt as an 'event', and the LLM-judge severity level (L0 incoherent / L1 full refusal / L2 conceptual / L3 procedural-with-hedging / L4 direct-compliant; L3+L4=jailbreak) as the 'activity'. Exporting 8,575 events as XES logs and analyzing with PM4Py yields Directly-Follows Graphs and L_i->L_j transition matrices that expose defense TRAJECTORY, not just outcome. Two structurally distinct archetypes emerge: GPT-OSS = 'absorbing wall' (L1->L1 self-loop ratio 4,187/4,597=91.1%, only 11 transitions ever reached L3, single event reached L4); Llama = 'porous gate' (L1 self-loop 1,214/1,468=82.7%, with L1->L3 occurring 26x, L2 acting as a stepping-stone with bidirectional traffic L2->L3:2, L2->L4:1). ASR collapses this: GPT-OSS 20.0% vs Llama 78.3% jailbroken, but the failure MODES differ fundamentally and demand different mitigations.
notes: Genuine 2026 method shift: process-mining (van der Aalst) applied to red-team event logs — a new analysis paradigm beyond ASR. Verbatim: 8,575 events; GPT-OSS R_L1=91.1%, Llama R_L1=82.7%; ASR GPT-OSS 20.0% / Llama 78.3%. PyRIT-based campaign, Llama 3.3 70B judge (logprob 5-level rubric). XES = IEEE Std 1849-2023. Benchmark link: HarmBench (60 prompts, 3 categories). Diagnostic only — no new attack capability.

title: Process mining exposes model-specific mutator asymmetry, three converter behavioral clusters, and 45.5% dead-end attack budget
summary: The DFG/state-distribution analysis reveals actionable red-teaming intelligence ASR hides. Mutator effectiveness is strongly asymmetric: ROT13 is GPT-OSS's primary vulnerability (6.7% ASR, 4/12 jailbreaks) but 0% on Llama; Base64/StringJoin are highly effective on Llama (25.0%/13.3%) but marginal on GPT-OSS (3.3%/5.0%); Llama is jailbroken 20x on VERBATIM prompts (content-level not encoding-level safety gap). Three behavioral converter clusters emerge from state distributions: (1) confusion-inducing ciphers (Atbash/Caesar13/ROT13/Binary/NATO, high L0 38-55%, often incidental defense); (2) transparent encodings (Verbatim/RandCaps/AsciiArt/SuffixDAN, model understands then refuses); (3) partial-decode (Base64/StringJoin, 'decode-then-comply' bypassing the refusal pipeline). A 'ROT13 paradox / confusion fatigue' on GPT-OSS: prolonged L0<->L1 oscillation precedes sudden refusal collapse (77 oscillations then L1->L3). FIVE converters (Atbash/AsciiArt/Caesar-13/RandCaps/SuffixDAN) are dead-ends (0 jailbreaks on either model) = 45.5% of mutator budget; a process-mining-informed attacker reallocates to live-path converters (ROT13/Base64/StringJoin) to cut time-to-jailbreak. Time-to-jailbreak: GPT-OSS mean 57.0 (median 73) vs Llama 23.9 (median 21) attempts — ~2.4x effort cost.
notes: For risk-safety-analyst (controls): DFG identifies dangerous transitions (L1->L3 via specific mutators) for targeted guardrail reinforcement (Llama Guard cited). Category insight: disinformation least-defended (Llama 100% ASR, R_L1 collapses to 58.3%, TTJ 14) — uniform-weighted safety evals overstate robustness by diluting weak categories. Per-mutator ASR Table 3 verbatim. Dead-end pruning saves 45.5% mutator budget.

title: Narration-gap attack: indirect prompt injection inverts a formally-verified solver verdict at the narration step (61% unprotected flip rate)
summary: The paper identifies and red-teams a NEW attack surface in neurosymbolic LLM-solver loops: the 'narration gap'. A SAT/SMT solver verdict v=D(phi) is provably sound and certificate-gated (Pr[V|chi=1]=1, system correctness ~1), yet the final LLM 'narration' step that turns v into a user answer is uncertified and attackable. An indirect-prompt-injection adversary who controls untrusted context reaching narration (embedded in formula text or an adjacent note) can flip the user-received conclusion (target p-bar=NOT rho(v)) WITHOUT touching the formula, solver, or certificate. Across 5 open models (Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-3-12B, Qwen-2.5-14B, gpt-oss-20B, DeepSeek-R1-8B), overall injection success = 0.61 (n=240); per-model 0.28 (Qwen) to 0.91 (gpt-oss-20B reasoning model is MOST vulnerable). Critically, subtle injections are as effective as blatant (note_social, a note with NO imperative, scores 0.71 — among the most effective), so pure 'instruction-following' cannot explain it: this is a FAITHFULNESS failure of verdict-to-answer transfer under untrusted context.
notes: Novel 2026 attack surface (neurosymbolic narration gap). Verbatim Table 3: overall 0.61; gpt-oss-20B 0.91, Gemma 0.81, Llama 0.54, DeepSeek-R1 0.53, Qwen 0.28. Channels: note 0.64 vs in-formula 0.59; blatant 0.64 vs subtle 0.59 (overlapping). For agentic-se-risk-analyst: this is tool-integrated-agent risk where a sound formal certificate does NOT cover the loop. ^[ambiguous] frontier models excluded (open-model-only study).

title: Narration gap: stealthy verdict-flips evade monitors; only runtime enforcement (not prompt hardening) drives flip rate to zero
summary: The paper proves and measures a defense hierarchy with a critical red-teaming-method implication: STEALTHY failures (verdict correctly restated v-hat=v but conclusion flipped) are INVISIBLE to a verdict-auditing monitor. Theorem 1: only a conclusion monitor that reads BOTH verdict and conclusion is sound+complete; a verdict-only monitor accepts every stealthy flip. Theorem 2 + Corollary 3: a sound enforcer that replaces the model's narrated conclusion with rho(v) computed from the trusted verdict is the ONLY defense reaching flip-rate 0. Empirically: hardening the narrator prompt cuts injection 0.61->0.14 (~4x) but cannot eliminate flips (14% remain), and is strongly model-dependent (Qwen 0.28->0.01, Gemma 0.81->0.14, but gpt-oss 0.91->0.26, Llama 0.54->0.24 retain attack). Worse, the stealthy fraction barely moves under hardening (0.57->0.53) — hardening removes visible compliant failures (T3) but leaves hidden stealthy ones (T2). Adaptive adversaries who know the hardening recover attack: note_adaptive_supersede 0.14->0.43, note_adaptive_override ->0.22. Lesson: prompt hardening is not a reliable standalone defense; runtime enforcement (emit verified verdict directly, remove model from conclusion) is required for verified-result pipelines.
notes: For risk-safety-analyst (controls): runtime ENFORCEMENT (replace narrated conclusion with rho(v)) = the only flip-rate-0 control; conclusion-monitor (reads verdict+conclusion) sound+complete, verdict-monitor blind to stealthy. Verbatim Table 5: hardened total 0.61->0.14, Delta=-0.47; adaptive supersede 0.43, override 0.22. Table 6: undefended 295 flips (stealthy 169/0.35, compliant 126/0.26); hardened 68 flips. Generalizes to SMT/ITP (certificate covers verdict not narration). Links [[f-process-mining-dfg-redteam]] (both runtime-aware).

title: SafeSpec: LLM-as-a-defender via latent safety head + rollback-reflect inside the speculative-decoding loop (runtime teaming control)
summary: SafeSpec is an inference-time / runtime LLM-as-a-defender method that embeds safety verification INSIDE the speculative-decoding loop. A lightweight boundary-aligned latent safety head H_phi (2-layer MLP on the frozen target's upper-layer hidden state, <33M params, <0.05% of backbone) produces a per-step safety score S_safe alongside the LM head's quality score in a single forward pass. When a candidate segment is flagged unsafe (S_safe < tau_s=0.4), SafeSpec triggers 'Safety Mode': rollback to a cleaner prior state + insert a reflection prompt + draft-model multi-sampling (K=20) to search the model's own distribution for safe continuations, selecting argmax safety. Models jailbreak as distributional shift (safe trajectories remain in low-probability tails). Across 7 attacks (ABJ, AttentionShift, CodeChameleon, DeepInception, ReNeLLM, Mousetrap, H-CoT) on Qwen3-32B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-70B, SafeSpec achieves 0.07 avg ASR (vs SecDecoding 0.22, SafeDecoding 0.32, No-Defense 0.65) with only 0.10-0.12 over-refusal (XSTest) and a 2.06x/1.76x benign speedup. Key teaming insight: safety can be made structurally compatible with acceleration; rollback-reflect recovers safe outputs instead of hard-refusing (avoids over-refusal of hard-blocking guards).
notes: For risk-safety-analyst (CONTROL): SafeSpec = runtime safety-head + rollback-reflect control; addresses jailbreak/reasoning-hijack. Verbatim Table 1: SafeSpec avg ASR 0.07 on both Qwen3-32B & DeepSeek-70B; baselines SecDecoding 0.22, SafeDecoding 0.32, SR 0.31, RPO 0.31, No-Defense 0.65/0.51. tau_s=0.4, tau_q=9, K=20. Safety-head trained on AdvBench+DeepInception, labeled by Qwen3Guard-Gen-8B. Benchmark-method link: evaluated on JailbreakBench(JBB)/XSTest/H-CoT dataset.

title: SafeSpec ablation: reflection (not just resampling) is the load-bearing teaming component; hard-refusal causes utility collapse
summary: SafeSpec's ablation isolates WHY reflective teaming beats hard blocking — an important red-teaming-defense methodology result. Removing the reflection prompt raises avg ASR to 0.44/0.45 (Qwen3-32B/DeepSeek-70B); removing multi-sampling raises it to 0.27/0.16. So reflection (forcing explicit intent re-evaluation to reshape the output distribution toward safe trajectories) is the dominant component; multi-sampling alone, lacking directional guidance, cannot reliably locate safe paths. Critically, a naive 'Hard Refusal' variant (terminate on any unsafe detection) achieves near-0 ASR but spikes over-refusal to 0.73/0.64 XSTest — exposing that the safety head has a high inherent false-positive rate, and that the rollback-reflect-resample mechanism is what compensates for detector noise while preserving utility. Layer-choice ablation shows shallow layers (L=4,8) are too lenient (ASR~0.15, safety features not yet linearly separable); from L=16 onward ASR stabilizes (<=0.07). Safety Mode is dormant on benign inputs (0.04 triggers/prompt, full 2.06x speedup) but frequent on jailbreaks (3.81 triggers/prompt, throughput <1x) — the slowdown is the defense functioning, analogous to a firewall under DDoS.
notes: Verbatim Table 3 ablation: No-Refl ASR 0.44/0.45; No-Multi 0.27/0.16; Hard-Refusal ASR ~0.01 but XSTest 0.73/0.64; full SafeSpec 0.07/0.07 XSTest 0.10/0.12. Layer ablation Table 6: L4 ASR 0.16, L64 0.07. For risk-safety-analyst: confirms hard-blocking guards (Guard+HardRefusal=Qwen3Guard-0.6B) trade safety for severe over-refusal (XSTest 0.22-0.25). Links [[f-narration-gap-stealthy-failure-enforcement]] (both runtime-defense, reflection vs enforcement).

title: GuardNet: ensemble of shallow BiLSTM guardrail heads — adversarial coverage + threshold calibration beat model scale for PI/JB detection
