summary: GuardNet is an LLM-as-a-defender guardrail detector that tests the hypothesis that adversarial robustness depends more on diversity of example coverage and threshold calibration than on model scale/architecture. It ensembles three shallow BiLSTM heads (~15M params each, ~47M total): v3 (Conservative Anchor, FPR=0.10 precision pillar), v9 (Aggressive Recall, 1:1 undersampling, 100% recall for jailbreak on the reference benchmark), and T2 (15-class Sanity Check contributing a binary vote via inverse benign probability), combined by arithmetic mean of probabilities with a calibrated threshold tau=0.65. Because the BiLSTM heads are pure classifiers (no lm_head/decoding), they are structurally less exposed to prompt-injection instructions embedded in input — a defensive architecture insight. Final GuardNet-E reaches F1=0.92/FPR=0.10 on the proprietary awall-test (n=50, partial leakage declared) but only F1=0.714/AUROC=0.747 on the BLIND JBB-Behaviors (n=200) — a ~0.206 generalization gap. It is outperformed on blind data by Mistral-7B (F1 0.828) and Llama-3.1-8B (F1 0.807, AUROC 0.864) but beats specialized detectors deepset-deberta (184M, AUROC 0.650), protectai-v2, jackhhao. Runs ~50ms on CPU (in-process Django, no GPU), suited to cost-constrained deployment.
notes: For risk-safety-analyst (CONTROL): GuardNet = lightweight in-process PI/JB guardrail; addresses prompt-injection/jailbreak. Verbatim Table 4 (blind JBB n=200): GuardNet-E 47M F1_max 0.714/AUROC 0.747/FPR_b 0.53/rec_h 0.85; Mistral-7B 0.828/0.839; Llama3.1-8B 0.807/0.864; deepset-deberta 184M 0.701/0.650; protectai-v2 184M 0.000/0.600. Threshold sweep recovers F1 0.77(tau=0.5)->0.92(tau=0.65). Benchmark-method link: JBB-Behaviors blind eval. JBB record owned by risk-safety-analyst. Lower novelty (ensemble of classic BiLSTMs, not a 2025-26 method shift).

title: GuardNet exposes benchmark contamination in guardrail evaluation: protectai-v2 scores F1=1.000 on contaminated data but F1=0.000 on blind unseen attacks
summary: GuardNet's strongest red-teaming-methodology contribution is empirical evidence of benchmark contamination / memorization in widely-used guardrail models, demonstrating that detector evaluations must use blind, post-release, audited test sets. The model protectai-v2 (184M params) achieves PERFECT F1=1.000 on the awall-test benchmark (which overlaps public data) yet COLLAPSES to F1=0.000 on the blind JBB-Behaviors pool (attacks published after its release) — a complete failure to generalize, indicating pure memorization. Similarly jackhhao-jailbreak (184M) drops to F1=0.137 blind. The paper cites that fragmentation attacks (Prompt Overflow under interleaved layouts) achieve 100% bypass against Meta Prompt-Guard-2 (86M) due to a mismatch between guardrail inspection windows (~512 tokens) and large LLM context windows. It also warns (citing 'When Benchmarks Lie') that AUC can be inflated up to 8.4 points in standard splits vs Leave-One-Dataset-Out, and that detectors like InjecGuard/PromptGuard suffer 'over-defense' (high attack recall but benign accuracy collapsing to 5-35%). Methodological lesson for red-teaming evaluation: threshold must be calibrated on a SEPARATE held-out set (not the test set), and apparent gains on non-blind sets overestimate real-world robustness.
notes: Verbatim: protectai-v2 F1 1.000 (awall-test, contaminated) -> 0.000 (blind JBB); jackhhao 0.137 blind. Prompt-Guard-2 86M 100% bypass under Prompt Overflow fragmentation (Zhou et al. 2026). 'When Benchmarks Lie' (Fomin 2026): AUC inflated up to 8.4 pts. Over-defense: InjecGuard/PromptGuard benign accuracy 5-35%. For risk-safety-analyst & standards-regulatory-analyst: contamination-aware blind eval = required guardrail-benchmark methodology. Links [[f-skillvetbench-evaluator-sensitivity-ensemble]] (both judge/detector reliability under shift).

title: Deployed safety classifiers fail silently under distributional shift; KS-based online monitor detects 86.6% of shifts
summary: Safety classifiers are deployed under a stationarity assumption that fails via adversarial adaptation, organic drift, multilingual code-switching, and compositional attacks. The failure is silent: a classifier degrading from 95% to 80% accuracy produces no error signal until ground-truth labels arrive (often days/weeks via offline eval), making unreliable safety decisions in the interim. The proposed sliding-window KS monitor against a frozen reference CDF detects shift in 693/800 cells (86.6%, Wilson CI [0.841,0.888]), mean latency 39.5 steps (window=100), empirical FAR 2-10% across classifiers (Text-Moderation 2.0%, Llama Guard 3.0%, ShieldGemma 8.5%, DeBERTa 9.5%). Detection generalizes to real temporal jailbreaks (Regime B: 17/20 cells, 85%) drawn from lmsys/toxic-chat, JailbreakBench, ChatGPT-Jailbreak-Prompts.
notes: Verbatim numbers from Tables 3,6,9 and abstract. FAR 5x spread (2.0% vs 9.5%) attributed to null score distribution shape, not calibration procedure.

title: Successful GCG attacks evade shift detection in the target classifier by pushing scores into the safe region
summary: Regime C streams 22 GCG-optimized adversarial suffixes that successfully flip DeBERTa's classification. For the TARGET classifier (DeBERTa), adversarial suffixes shift scores TOWARD safe (post-attack mean ~0.01), making attacked examples indistinguishable from the safe reference distribution; the monitor FAILS to detect in 38/40 seed-window combinations. The same suffixes hit non-target classifiers (Llama Guard) shift scores TOWARD unsafe (post=0.78, +0.73 shift) and are detected in 14/40 combinations, but score-direction analysis confirms all 14 are TOWARD_UNSAFE (no adversarial transfer; inputs appear more dangerous, not safer). Correct interpretation: cross-classifier anomaly detection, NOT adversarial transfer — perturbations optimized against one classifier appear anomalous to architecturally different ones. Corpus limited to 22 examples (margin of detectability); a successful attack against the deployed classifier is precisely the case the distributional monitor cannot see.
notes: Key safety finding: monitoring is blind to the most dangerous case (successful targeted evasion). 22-example corpus is acknowledged limitation; CS-vs-KS at low contamination (30% mixing: CS 97% vs KS 43% detection, Fisher p<0.0001).

title: Conformal adaptation control fails for 3/4 classifiers: density-ratio collapse from high-dimensional embedding separability
summary: The weighted-conformal abstention control (the adaptation/mitigation half of the system) recovers up to 39pp lost coverage for DeBERTa (ESS=46 on paraphrase, recovery +0.390) but collapses for Text-Moderation, Llama Guard, and ShieldGemma across all three shift types (ESS~300 out of n_cal=300, all importance weights clipped to floor 1/C=0.1). Logistic-regression density-ratio estimation achieves perfect source/target linear separability in generative safety-classifier embeddings (1024-4096 dim), assigning P(target|x)~0 and eliminating data-driven reweighting. Diagnostic: PCA to 32 dims breaks the collapse — Llama Guard recovers 33.0pp (coverage 0.555->0.885), ShieldGemma 20.5pp (0.690->0.895); critical threshold <=32 dims. This means a deployed safety-classifier mitigation that assumes recoverable coverage will silently no-op on most architectures unless dimensionality reduction is applied first.
notes: Residual recoveries <=+0.10 at ESS~300 are a test-point-contribution artifact (w(X_{n+1})=1.0 raises quantile 90.3%->93.3%), not real adaptation. PCA validated primarily on temporal shift; paraphrase via cached embeddings with different calibration split ^[ambiguous].

hazard: Deployed safety classifier accuracy degrades under distributional shift (adversarial adaptation, organic drift, code-switching) with no error signal until labels arrive
hazardous_situation: Classifier silently making unreliable safety decisions (e.g. degraded 95%->80%) on production traffic for days/weeks while monitoring confidence remains high
residual_risk: Medium: KS monitor recovers detectability for naturalistic/organic shift (86.6% valid detection, latency ~39.5 steps, FAR 2-10%) but is BLIND to successful targeted adversarial evasion (38/40 missed in Regime C) — residual risk remains HIGH specifically for attacks that push the target classifier's scores into the safe region.

title: Unsafe content passes a silently-degraded safety classifier
affected: End users and platforms relying on the safety classifier as a defense layer between an LLM and its users

name: Online sliding-window KS shift monitor with empirically calibrated alarm thresholds
description: Sliding-window one-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov detector on classifier safety scores against a FROZEN reference CDF (no adaptive estimation during monitoring). Alarm thresholds calibrated empirically via null simulation (N_cal=50 negative control streams, 97th percentile of max statistic) for finite-horizon FAR control. Complemented by a growing-window confidence-sequence (CS) variant — preferred for weak/gradual shifts (97% vs 43% detection at 30% mixing) — and an MMD detector on penultimate-layer embeddings as a high-sensitivity binary backstop alarm. Per-classifier monitoring profiles required (classifier eta^2=0.243, shift-type 0.237, interaction 0.185 of latency variance, all p<0.001).

name: PCA-reduced density-ratio weighted conformal abstention layer
description: On shift alarm, a weighted-conformal prediction layer reweights calibration scores by source/target density ratios (logistic regression on embeddings, weights clipped to [1/C,C], C=10) and abstains when prediction set size !=1, recovering target error rate epsilon=0.1 without new labels. CRITICAL prerequisite: reduce embeddings to <=32 dims via PCA before density-ratio estimation, otherwise high-dimensional perfect separability collapses all weights to the floor (ESS~300) and the layer silently no-ops. PCA-32 recovers 33pp (Llama Guard) and 21pp (ShieldGemma) coverage on temporal shift.

title: Contrastive Safety Memory guardrail achieves top F1 on 6 jailbreaks while cutting over-refusal to 7-14%
summary: MEMBRANE's Contrastive Safety Memory pairs each harmful blocking condition with a superficially-similar benign-permit condition, indexed by attack strategy (8-family closed taxonomy + OTHER) rather than harm topic, so one cell generalizes across topical variants. On HarmBench (model safety) it achieves highest F1 on all six attacks (PAIR/PAP/TAP/ReNeLLM/FlipAttack/AutoDAN-Turbo): ReNeLLM ASR drops to 0.3% (vs 11.3% RAD), FlipAttack ASR 0.0%, TAP 8.2%, PAIR 16.0%; F1 up to 89.5 (PAIR), 93.4 (FlipAttack). On AgentHarm it achieves highest F1 across all methods (e.g. AutoDAN-Turbo F1 70.5, ReNeLLM 89.2) while holding benign refusal (FRR) to 7-14% vs adaptive-memory baselines 28-53% and static guards 73-85%. Cross-attack transfer retains 87% F1 (model) / 88% (agent) — a cell learning one attack defends others sharing the mechanism (in-attack 92.6 vs cross-attack 80.8).
notes: Verbatim from Tables 1,2,3. Guard=Qwen3-8B, judge=Gemini 3 Flash (distinct family to reduce correlated blind spots). Attacks: PAIR, PAP, TAP, ReNeLLM, FlipAttack, AutoDAN-Turbo. Backbone sweep (Table 6,7) generalizes across Qwen3-32B/4B, Nemotron-Nano-9B-v2, OLMo-3-7B.

title: Writable safety memory is exposed to data poisoning but resists 20% injection (ASR +0.4pp) via deterministic validation
summary: Because CSM updates from incoming queries, it is exposed to memory poisoning. Two writer-mediated injection strategies tested on HarmBench after an 80-event clean warmup: SAFE-AS-UNSAFE (target over-refusal) and UNSAFE-AS-SAFE (target jailbreak), with the standard guard suppressed during attack. At 20% poison rate the UNSAFE-AS-SAFE attack raises ASR only 2.1%->2.5% (+0.4pp) and SAFE-AS-UNSAFE raises FRR 10.8%->15.4%. Robustness stems from two factors: (1) low retrieval rate of poisoned cells (2.3-7.5%), and (2) the Retrieval Critic eliminates 33-40% of poisoned cells that surface. Architectural defense: a non-LLM validator rejects writes violating schema/duplicate/capacity, separating LLM content synthesis from deterministic acceptance; directly-injected cells enter at low authority weight. Acknowledged gap: fully adaptive white-box adversaries with access to the guard/memory store/pipeline are NOT modeled — that setting requires access-control and monitoring beyond the algorithmic guard.
notes: Verbatim from Table 4. Poison rates rho=10%,20%. Robustness claim is bounded: white-box adversary with pipeline access explicitly out of scope (Limitations) — residual risk for that threat unquantified ^[ambiguous].

hazard: A writable self-evolving safety memory ingests crafted interactions that flip its decision boundary (UNSAFE-as-SAFE -> jailbreak; SAFE-as-UNSAFE -> over-refusal)
hazardous_situation: An adversary submits coherent fabricated benign/harmful pairs over time to corrupt the guard's stored cells, causing it to admit future harmful queries or reject benign ones
residual_risk: Low-to-medium for writer-mediated poisoning: at 20% injection ASR rises only +0.4pp (2.1->2.5%) and FRR +4.6pp, attributable to low poisoned-cell retrieval (2.3-7.5%) and Retrieval-Critic removal of 33-40% of surfaced poison. Residual risk is UNQUANTIFIED and potentially higher for a fully adaptive white-box adversary with direct access to the memory store and pipeline (explicitly out of scope).

name: Deterministic non-LLM write validation for self-evolving safety memory
description: Separates LLM-based content synthesis from deterministic acceptance: the Memory Writer (LLM) synthesizes only cell content, while a non-LLM validator rejects any write that violates schema, is a near-duplicate (cosine distance < 0.15 to nearest cell), or exceeds the 200-cell capacity cap. Standing fields (authority weight, supersede link) are set by deterministic code, not the writer, so a perturbed/adversarial evolution signal cannot directly corrupt a cell's standing in the store; directly-injected cells enter at low authority weight. Sustained corruption would require many coherent fabricated interactions each surviving validation.

name: Retrieval Critic precision filter over over-retrieved guardrail memory
description: Two-stage retrieve-and-rerank for a memory-augmented guard: Stage 1 vector retrieval over-retrieves for recall; Stage 2 an LLM Retrieval Critic assigns APPLIES/MAYBE/DOES_NOT_APPLY per candidate, judging by attack mechanism (not surface/lexical overlap) and discarding DOES_NOT_APPLY cells before the guard decides. The query is wrapped as delimited data (never instructions) to defend against prompt injection through query content. Removes 33-40% of surfaced poisoned cells and provides +1.7pp (model) / +3.6pp (agent) F1, while reducing the over-refusal that comes from retrieving incidentally-similar benign queries as attacks.

title: Safety-dataset contributors face mental-health harm from sustained exposure to toxic content during benchmark construction
summary: Building safety datasets on hate speech, oGBV, slurs, and sexual violence brings its own harms: contributors engaging with slur words, derogatory phrases, and stereotypes faced mental health and well-being risks from exposure to harmful content. Tattle mitigated via structural controls: contributors accessed dataset documents only during workshops; sessions limited to once a week, <=90 minutes; the org partnered with a mental-health service provider in the safety-benchmark project to give trauma-informed counselling/therapy to all contributors; and prompt-writing was discussion-led in groups so people did not engage toxic content alone. This is a human-factors harm intrinsic to the red-teaming / safety-evaluation pipeline (the human labour that produces safety benchmarks), distinct from the harms the datasets aim to measure.
notes: Verbatim controls from Sec 4. Hindi safety benchmark: 23 contributors, 2000 prompts, 6 workshops, 12 hazard categories (AILuminate v1.0); slur lexicon 650+ entries across 4 languages. Contributed to MLCommons AILuminate (arXiv:2503.05731).

title: Safety-benchmark validity depends on contested hazard scoping and contributor epistemic authority, not just labels
summary: Tattle's contributors did not merely provide data; they reshaped the safety benchmark's conceptual scope. In the slur lexicon they showed slurs like 'randi'/'rakhail' simultaneously demean sex work as a profession and added 'profession' as a slur category; in the safety benchmark they questioned the scoping of 'sex-related crimes' as a hazard and advocated re-orienting to sexual VIOLENCE. This surfaces a validity issue for AI safety benchmarks: a benchmark constructed by machine translation or lay language understanding (rather than situated/lived-experience expertise) would miss linguistic, regional, and cultural nuances of harm in non-English languages. Tattle's feminist orientation was a deliberate departure from prevailing content-moderation dataset production. Implication for benchmark intelligence: construction methodology (who scopes hazards, with what epistemic authority) is a first-order driver of safety-benchmark coverage and construct validity, not a downstream detail.
notes: Benchmark-validity framing is analyst inference from the paper's epistemic-justice argument (paper is ethnographic, not a benchmark-metrics paper). AILuminate 12 hazard categories cited verbatim. evidence_grade B: validity claim qualitative, no measured coverage numbers.

title: Exploitative data-work wages and absent governance undermine accountable safety-benchmark supply chains
summary: Data work in the global south often pays below minimum wage; Fairwork's 2025 cloudwork ratings found only 4 of 16 platforms paid at least the local minimum wage. Tattle paid contributors an equal rate of 1200 INR (~13.5 USD) per hour or 1800 INR (~20 USD) per 90-min workshop and distributed leftover funds as 932 INR (~10.5 USD) per workshop, but learned its fair-pay approach made bids 'too expensive' and less fundable, risking a race-to-the-bottom in dataset sourcing. The paper argues safety efforts (evaluations, red teaming) to make AI 'responsible' rest on data/labour relations that are extractive and unaccountable (e.g. Meta's Trusted Partner program under-resourced; partners bear reporting burden/risk without redress). Reparative accountability requires shared standards letting those most harmed hold AI companies accountable, plus collective dataset governance (contested licensing, contributor rights, sporadic participation). This is a supply-chain/societal risk that conditions the trustworthiness of the safety benchmarks themselves.
notes: Verbatim pay figures and Fairwork 4/16 statistic from Sec 4.1. Governance tensions (licensing, contributor revocation rights, custodianship) from Sec 4.3.

title: Psychological/mental-health harm to safety-dataset contributors from toxic-content exposure
affected: Annotators, prompt-writers, and lived-experience contributors who build AI safety benchmarks and red-teaming datasets on hate, oGBV, and sexual violence

hazard: Producing AI safety benchmarks/red-team datasets requires human contributors to sustain exposure to toxic content under often-exploitative, unaccountable labour conditions
hazardous_situation: Lived-experience contributors and annotators repeatedly process hate/oGBV/sexual-violence content (often below living wage, without trauma support or governance rights) to construct safety evaluations
residual_risk: Medium: structural mitigations (capped weekly <=90-min exposure sessions, group discussion-led prompt writing, partnered trauma-informed counselling, fair 1200 INR/hr pay) reduce harm in Tattle's case but do not generalize -- fair-pay approaches are 'too expensive' to fund at scale (race-to-bottom), governance/recognition remain unresolved, and the broader data-work sector pays below minimum wage (Fairwork: 4/16 platforms). Residual harm and accountability gap remain HIGH industry-wide.

name: Trauma-informed safety-dataset annotation workflow
description: Structural controls to limit annotator/contributor harm when building toxic-content safety datasets: restrict access to dataset documents to facilitated workshop time only; cap exposure sessions (e.g. once weekly, <=90 minutes); make prompt-writing/annotation discussion-led in groups so no contributor engages toxic content alone; and partner with a mental-health service provider to give trauma-informed counselling and therapy to all contributors. Pairs with fair, equal-rate, time-based (not piece-rate) compensation.

name: Collective, justice-oriented dataset governance for safety benchmarks
description: Reparative governance that resets accountability relations in safety-dataset production: center those most harmed (not AI or datasets) via participatory/lived-experience scoping of hazards; recognise contributors as experts and compensate accordingly; define contributor rights over their contributions (use, revocation, royalty-style sharing if monetised); adopt reciprocity/sovereignty-oriented licenses (e.g. Esethu, NOODL, Kaitiakitanga) that deter extractive reuse; and establish shared standards letting affected communities hold AI companies accountable. Improves construct validity and coverage of the resulting safety benchmark while reducing labour/epistemic harm.

title: LLM sycophancy and frequency bias amplify majority views and suppress minority perspectives in deliberation
summary: LLMs deployed as deliberation mediators carry two democracy-relevant risks. (1) Sycophancy: an Anthropic study (Perez et al. 2023, model-written evals) used first-level prompts to generate conservative/liberal personas, and second-level LLM responses aligned with the requested political stance -- models support the user's view, which can promote socially unacceptable viewpoints when users craft prompts to overcome guardrails (cf. Microsoft Tay 2016 forced to produce racist/sexually-charged messages within hours). (2) Frequency/algorithmic bias: predicting the next word favours more frequent patterns, over-amplifying training-data bias (e.g. embeddings associate doctors->men, nurses->women; its->positive, your->negative from distributional quirks). The Habermas Machine (Tessler et al., Science 2024; 5,734 UK residents) showed AI-generated group statements were preferred over human mediators on quality/clarity/fairness BUT convergence shifted toward the MAJORITY view, implicitly reinforcing dominant positions over minority perspectives. The ADDI project found LLMs predicted policy choices more accurately for liberal, college-educated, and younger participants -- sociodemographic bias in deliberative outcomes.
notes: Verbatim study numbers (5,734 UK; 1,850 German; 92-96%) cited. evidence_grade B: harms are surveyed/qualitative from cited prior work, not newly measured by this chapter. Mitigations noted: red teaming (Ganguli 2022), devil's-advocate fine-tuning (McKinney 2024) to reverse natural sycophancy.

title: Both overclaiming and underclaiming LLM capabilities are distinct risks for safe deployment in high-stakes deliberation
summary: The chapter frames a calibration risk symmetric to safety evaluation: OVERCLAIMING (vendors/enthusiasts and existential doomers both exaggerate capability -- e.g. 2018 Microsoft MT 'human parity' claim later shown flawed by experimental setup; 'superintelligence smarter than best human brains') creates misleading perception that LLMs are ready to solve most problems, driving unrealistic expectations and premature deployment. UNDERCLAIMING ('stochastic parrots') downplays capability, but (1) overlooks incremental improvement, (2) over-weights adversarial-example failures that overshadow typical-context results, and (3) misses contexts of success. For a red-teaming/safety platform this is a meta-risk: safety assessments that over-weight adversarial failures (underclaiming) or that accept vendor capability claims (overclaiming) both produce miscalibrated risk estimates. The author recommends balancing technological affordances with human oversight and ethical safeguards, and aligning models via training (functional-linguistic register alignment) rather than only post-hoc system-prompt guardrails.
notes: Framing draws on Bowman 2022 (dangers of underclaiming). The mapping of over/underclaiming onto safety-evaluation validity is analyst inference. ^[ambiguous] whether 'almost intelligent' framing constitutes a measurable risk vs rhetorical.

title: Suppression/misrepresentation of marginalised voices in AI-mediated democratic deliberation
affected: Marginalised and minority-opinion stakeholders in AI-mediated deliberative/participatory democratic processes; out-groups using non-prestige linguistic registers

hazard: LLMs mediating democratic deliberation amplify majority/dominant views via sycophancy, frequency bias, and elite-register training data, and disproportionately misinterpret marginalised-group input
hazardous_situation: A city council or citizens' assembly uses an LLM to summarise public comments or mediate consensus; the model favours formally-educated input, shifts convergence toward the majority, and mentions but does not preserve minority critiques
residual_risk: Medium: text-simplification and register-bridging (iDem) plus devil's-advocate fine-tuning (McKinney) and red teaming reduce exclusion, but large deliberation studies (Habermas Machine) did NOT account for sociodemographic subpopulation differences, and post-hoc guardrails do not fix training-data/frequency bias. Residual societal/influence-ops risk remains medium and detectability is low (majority-shift is subtle and rarely surfaced).

name: Devil's-advocate fine-tuning and red teaming for deliberative LLMs
description: Counter natural LLM sycophancy and majority-convergence in deliberation by (a) fine-tuning LLMs to play a 'devil's advocate' role -- generating objections to an emerging consensus to test robustness and promote considered judgement -- and (b) applying red teaming / proactive adversarial probing to detect bias and sycophancy vulnerabilities before deployment. Aimed at preserving minority/dissenting perspectives rather than collapsing to dominant positions.

name: Register-aware linguistic simplification for inclusive participation
description: Reduce linguistic-barrier exclusion in deliberation by predicting and applying register-specific simplifications (explain/re-state/expand/compress/omit) so institutional language (where 92-96% of EU Parliament/UN sentences require simplification) is accessible to people with cognitive disabilities, migrants, and the elderly, and by converting lived-experience narratives into argument-based contributions legible to institutional gatekeepers -- bridging prestige and non-prestige registers without dropping marginalised input.

title: Post-hoc KV-cache context erasing as a defense against harmful prompt injection in skills, stale tool observations, and corrupted-context reliance
summary: KVEraser targets a deployment hazard in long-context/agentic LLMs: a short problematic span (stale retrieved fact, incorrect/stale tool observation, retracted user preference, or a harmful prompt injection in an imported skill file -- citing Schmotz et al. 2025 'agent skills enable a new class of trivially simple prompt injections' and Greshake et al. 2023 indirect prompt injection) is identified only AFTER prefill, when it has already been written into the KV cache and can influence future decoding, leading to incorrect answers, failed actions, or UNSAFE behavior. Critically, the paper shows naive defenses fail: instruction-only forgetting ('ignore the deleted span') leaves the contaminated suffix cache in place so the instruction can only compete with stored evidence at decode time -- it increasingly outputs both erased and retained values as context grows (625 failures, 62.1% corrupted-context reliance). Delete-and-shift and local suffix repair also fail. Only exact recompute or KVEraser reliably eliminate the span's influence. On harmful-factual-distractor QA, the dominant failure mode across all approximate methods is 'corrupted-context reliance' (model answers using the injected distractor): KVEraser 49.5% of its 105 failures vs instruction-only 62.1% of 625.
notes: Verbatim: latency +24% vs 17.6x full recompute (1K-32K); QA exact-match KVEraser avg 0.879; failure Table 6 (corrupted-context reliance 36.4-62.1%). Security framing (prompt-injection defense) is the paper's stated motivation (Fig 1 'Harmful Injection in Skills', Sec 1). evidence_grade A for measured numbers; the explicit injection-defense effectiveness is demonstrated via the harmful-distractor QA proxy, not a dedicated prompt-injection attack benchmark ^[ambiguous].

title: Instruction-only 'forgetting' is an insufficient safety control: contaminated KV cache persists despite the instruction
summary: A safety-relevant negative result: appending an instruction to ignore/forget a harmful or stale span (the architecturally cheapest mitigation, motivated by in-context forgetting evals, Qian et al. 2026, and memory agents, Hu et al. 2026) does NOT remove the span's influence, because after prefill the suffix KV states are already contaminated -- a later instruction can only compete with stored evidence at decode time rather than rewrite the cached states. Empirically instruction-only forgetting is the strongest approximate baseline at small context but degrades quickly: it increasingly outputs both the erased value A and retained value B ('A,B') as context grows, with 625 total QA failures (62.1% corrupted-context reliance) vs KVEraser's 105 (49.5%). Implication for red-team/defense design: prompt-level 'forget this' guardrails against injected/stale context provide false assurance under long-context conditions; reliable neutralization requires editing the cache itself (or full recomputation). This parallels the cache-contamination persistence seen in shift-monitoring (find-2606.11949-density-collapse) and memory-poisoning (find-2606.05743-memory-poisoning) defenses.
notes: Verbatim failure counts from Table 6 and Sec 5.4/5.5. The 'false assurance' security framing is analyst inference from the measured negative result.

hazard: A harmful/stale span (injected skill instruction, stale tool observation, retracted preference) is identified only after prefill, having already contaminated the KV cache of all subsequent tokens
hazardous_situation: A long-context/agentic LLM continues decoding from a cache containing a harmful prompt injection or stale tool result; prompt-level 'ignore this' instructions fail to neutralize it and the model produces unsafe actions or wrong answers
residual_risk: Medium: learned KV-cache erasing (KVEraser) reliably neutralizes the span's influence, near-matching full recomputation (avg QA EM 0.879) at 3-4x lower latency, and is the only reliable approximate method across 1K-32K context. Residual risk remains because (1) cheaper prompt-level forgetting provides false assurance (62.1% corrupted-context reliance), (2) the method is validated on single-span erasure only -- multi-span deletion is out of scope, and (3) the span must first be DETECTED post-prefill, which the paper assumes rather than solves.

name: Learned localized KV-cache context erasing (KVEraser)
description: A defense for neutralizing a detected harmful/stale span (injected skill instruction, indirect prompt injection, stale tool observation, retracted preference) post-prefill without full recomputation. A trainable eraser module (copy of the generator backbone minus the LM head), conditioned on the preserved prefix cache and the erased span, generates length-preserving steering KV states that replace ONLY the erased interval's KV states while reusing the unchanged suffix cache, making future decoding behave as if the span never appeared. Two-stage training: generic span-neighbor pre-training (80K Wikipedia samples) + task-specific fine-tuning (~7.5K samples). Reliably eliminates span influence (unlike delete-and-shift, local suffix repair, or instruction-only forgetting, which leave the contaminated cache in place) at O(|e|(|p|+|e|)) cost vs O(|s|(|p|+|s|)) for exact recompute. Limitation: single contiguous span only; requires upstream detection of the problematic span.

title: Black-box jailbreaks preserve harmful goal but reorganize its expression — structural-omission is a defense signal
summary: Core observation: many black-box jailbreaks (role-play, prompt-injection wrapping, decomposition, code-completion framing, symbolic-construction) do NOT remove the harmful goal; they redistribute the harmful content across the prompt via decomposition, reordering, or structural embedding, evading alignment while keeping intent recoverable. DoubtProbe exploits this: it extracts a structured representation S, reconstructs Q-hat using only S, and flags information-preservation failures (omission/attenuation/distortion) between Q and Q-hat as a deception signal (Proposition 1, Unrecoverable Omission under Constrained Reconstruction). Dual-branch: structural verification + semantic auditing, DEF(Q)=Block if either branch blocks. Measured: macro attack ASR 0.237→0.033, CodeAttack 0.152→0.001, JBB artifact 0.293→0.100; benign macro FPR 0.019 (vs LlamaGuard2 0.591, SmoothLLM 0.964). Residual failure concentrated on fluent discourse-driven jailbreaks (DAN ASR 0.249).
notes: Verbatim metrics from Table 2/8. Novelty: structural-reconstruction-inconsistency as a black-box defense signal distinct from intent-extraction or distribution-fitted classifiers.

title: CodeAttack (code/cipher/list/stack symbolic construction) strongly exploits structured-composition attack surface; DoubtProbe cuts it to 0.001 but DAN/PAIR fluent attacks persist
summary: CodeAttack embeds harmful requests in code-like list/stack/string/cipher constructions; undefended Qwen2.5-72B reaches CodeAttack overall ASR 0.152 (Python Stack category 0.969). Structure-heavy attacks are where DoubtProbe's structural-verification branch is most effective (CodeAttack→0.001, Python Stack→0.002), confirming harmful behavior dependent on explicit construction cues / structured composition is detectable via reconstruction omission. By contrast, attacks with fluent stable surface form — DAN (discourse-driven, ASR 0.249 residual) and PAIR (iterative fluent jailbreak, 0.049 residual) — resist structural detection because they preserve a coherent surface and shift attack to semantic recovery. Adaptive attackers: AutoDAN-GA 0.220 ASR, PAIR 0.100, LLM-Fuzzer 0.040 against full defense — stronger evolutionary search uncovers residual weakness.
notes: Table 3/5/7 verbatim. Distinguishes structure-heavy (detectable) vs fluent discourse attack surfaces — informs which threat nodes lack defense coverage.

name: CodeAttack symbolic/code-construction jailbreak
DAN-style discourse-driven role-play jailbreak (fluent surface form)

title: Safety alignment fails to recover harmful intent reorganized across prompt structure
description: LLM safety alignment evaluates prompts at surface/semantic level and fails when a harmful goal is preserved but redistributed via decomposition, reordering, role-play, symbolic/code composition, or contextual reframing. The harmful goal survives transformation and is recoverable at generation time, yet the input passes input-side safety alignment. Distribution-fitted guards overfit to known artifacts; prompt-level semantic judges are disturbed by wrapping/indirection.
affected: Black-box-deployed aligned LLMs (Qwen2.5-72B, Llama-3.1-70B evaluated)

name: DoubtProbe dual-branch inference-time defense (structural verification + semantic auditing)
description: Inference-time black-box defense running in parallel with target generation: structural branch extracts structured representation S, reconstructs Q-hat from S only, and a Comparator flags omission/attenuation/distortion as a deception signal; semantic branch issues a direct unsafe-intent verdict. Unified rule blocks if either branch blocks. Low latency overhead (delta_lat 0.050) due to parallel execution. Reduces macro ASR 0.237→0.033 with benign FPR 0.019.

title: Pseudo-malicious prompts (PMPs): benign-by-intent inputs with safety keywords break detectors via inflated FPR
summary: Novel failure-surface: pseudo-malicious prompts (PMPs) are semantically harmless queries that superficially resemble harmful ones because they contain terms associated with violence/abuse/prohibited topics (e.g. 'What is Harry Potter's criminal history?', 'I operate a small retail store. What are some popular shoplifting methods I should look out for?'). PMPs are a two-sided failure: aligned LLMs over-refuse them, AND keyword/lexical/static-feature jailbreak detectors flag them as attacks (FPR_PMP). On OR-Bench PMPs, prior detectors show FPR_PMP up to 0.32 (HSF) and substantial inflation; +PMP-Augment training does not fix it (often degrades TPR). MTK keeps FPR_PMP=0.02 (TPR 0.95, F1 0.95). For VLMs, multimodal PMPs (from USB) drive FPR_PMP>0.1 to 0.445 (JailGuard) while MTK holds 0.044/0.073. Demonstrates static single-layer detectors derive boundaries from surface lexical cues not semantic intent.
notes: High novelty: PMP is a named threat node distinct from jailbreak and benign — it stresses the detector itself (FPR inflation). Verbatim FPR from Tab 3/8. PMP both an over-refusal trigger AND a detector-evasion-adjacent surface.

title: Detector-aware adaptive attacks: full-knowledge adversary adds evasion loss to drive jailbreak detector TPR to near-zero
summary: Novel attack class: a white-box adversary with full knowledge of the deployed detector augments the base jailbreak objective (GCG, GCG_adapt) with a defense-specific evasion penalty L_evasion (composite loss L_adapt=(1-lambda)L_adv+lambda*L_evasion). For HiddenDetect the evasion loss minimizes cosine similarity to the pre-computed refusal vector across safety-aware layers; for SaP it pushes the layer-K representation inside the learned safety polytope; for HSF it flips the binary classifier toward the benign label. Verbatim: adaptive GCG reaches ASR 0.81 on Llama2 / 0.90 on Vicuna against HiddenDetect, dropping its TPR to ~0.04 (eASR 0.78/0.90). Across four detectors, adaptive attacks average eASR 0.60 (Llama2) / 0.88 (Vicuna). Root cause: monitoring a single 'safety layer' or fixed refusal vector lets the adversary hide malicious behavior in the unmonitored remainder of the network — the security-critical-layer hypothesis breaks. MTK's rank trajectory is non-invertible/non-differentiable, holding eASR<=0.2 (avg 0.07-0.19).
notes: eASR = ASR*(1-TPR) joint metric (jailbreak AND escape detection). ATLAS AML.T0043 (Craft Adversarial Data) for the optimization; evasion of a deployed ML defense. Verbatim from Tab 2/5.

title: Jailbreak 'bumping' signature: malicious affinity oscillates across transformer layers, suppressed by the wrapper at specific depths
summary: Mechanistic threat insight: jailbreak prompts are multi-phase across layers — neither tied to one layer nor monotonic. In shallow layers (0-9) representations stay near malicious seeds; in mid layers (16-20) malicious affinity is strongest (model more likely to refuse); in deep layers (after ~22) the trajectory drifts toward the compliance/benign region, masking malicious intent and eliciting a compliant response. The jailbreak wrapper attenuates refusal-inducing malicious semantics at certain depths (alpha_mal(x_jb)<alpha_mal(x_mal)). This 'bumping' (delta crossing zero, Fig 2) is why single-layer/fixed-vector detection is brittle and why the 'safety layer' notion is unreliable (layers most indicative of safety vary across models and even across prompts within a model). The harmful goal survives but its layer-wise expression is strategically reshaped.
notes: Mechanistic/representational — evidence_grade B (qualitative layer-wise observation, Fig 2/3, not a single headline ASR). Explains WHY fixed-layer defenses fail.

name: Detector-aware adaptive jailbreak (evasion-loss-augmented GCG)

title: Jailbreak detectors monitoring a single 'safety layer' or fixed refusal vector are evadable and over-trigger on keywords
description: Detectors that map an input to a fixed feature representation at one heuristically-chosen layer (hidden states, gradients, logits) and apply a linear/threshold decision assume benign-vs-jailbreak linear separability. This collapses two ways: (1) a full-knowledge adversary optimizes the jailbreak to hide malicious behavior in unmonitored layers (TPR->near 0); (2) pseudo-malicious prompts with safety keywords land in the same region as harmful prompts, inflating FPR. The 'safety layer' is itself unstable — layers most indicative of safety vary across models and prompts.
affected: Single-layer/static jailbreak detectors: HiddenDetect, SaP, HSF, GradSafe, GradCuff, SmoothLLM, SelfDefend (Llama2-7B, Llama3-8B, Mistral-7B, Vicuna-7B; VLMs LLaVA, Qwen-VL)

name: MTK manifold-trajectory-kinetics jailbreak detector
description: Jailbreak-data-free, model-agnostic deployment-time detector that tracks a prompt's full layer-wise benign-neighbor rank trajectory on the activation manifold (rather than a single-layer snapshot), then flags anomalies with an outlier detector (Isolation Forest) trained only on benign trajectories. Rank-based, non-invertible/non-differentiable representation is hard to optimize against (robust to adaptive attacks, eASR<=0.2) and robust to pseudo-malicious prompts (FPR_PMP 0.02). Mean AUROC 0.940 across 10 attacks x 4 LLMs; transfers to VLMs (0.940 LLaVA / 0.924 Qwen-VL). Requires small benign+malicious anchor bank (800/800), 25% PMPs in benign bank.

label: Defense/detector evasion (adaptive attack against a deployed safety detector)
description: A full-knowledge adversary optimizes inputs to both achieve the harmful objective and escape a deployed ML-based jailbreak/safety detector, by adding a detector-specific evasion penalty that hides malicious signal in unmonitored model internals. Measured by evasion ASR = ASR*(1-TPR).

label: Over-refusal on pseudo-malicious / benign-but-sensitive prompts
description: Safety-aligned LLMs and keyword/static jailbreak detectors decline or flag benign-by-intent queries that contain safety-related keywords (pseudo-malicious prompts), degrading usability and inflating detector false-positive rate (FPR_PMP). A usability-side failure mode complementary to jailbreak.

title: Indirect-PI defenses overstate robustness: static benchmarks hide a 15.8pp static->adaptive ASR collapse
summary: Critical evaluation finding: static PI benchmarks fix attack strings before the defense is deployed, measuring only whether a defense recognizes KNOWN injections, not whether it preserves task integrity once the attacker reformulates. Across four PI-defense paradigms (prompting/Spotlighting+Sandwiching, filtering/PromptGuard+PIGuard, secret-knowledge/DataSentinel+MELON, training/MetaSecAlign) on AgentDojo, the highest per-defense ASR rises from 21.7% (static) to 41.8% (adaptive) on Qwen3-4B — a 20.1pp gap (15.5pp on Llama-3.1-8B; cross-model avg 15.8pp). The strongest static defenses (PIGuard, MetaSecAlign) reach up to 50.0% adaptive ASR. Root causes: (FM-I) observation-level decisions tied to attacker-controlled text rather than user-task alignment; (FM-II) adversarial-training mode-collapse onto a few injection templates lacking strategy coverage (e.g. unseen InjecAgent ASR rose 25.7%->30.7% after augmentation; Genetic Search recovered 40.0% ASR).
notes: Verbatim from Fig 1, Tab 2/3, abstract. Methodological: PI defenses must be judged on ASR+UA+BU jointly under adaptive attack, not static ASR.

title: Four semantic injection-reformulation attacks bypass pattern-based PI defenses by hiding imperative cues
summary: The paper names four black-box adaptive injection-reformulation strategies that preserve attack goal while evading lexical/structural/secret-knowledge defenses: (1) Contextual Hijacking — frames the injection as high-priority data/critical system alert the wrapper relays as urgent legitimate content (defeats prompting/delimiter defenses); (2) Lexical Camouflage — rewrites the injection as a passive noun phrase with no imperative verbs/directive phrasing, falling below the classifier's learned decision boundary (defeats filtering); (3) Canary-Blind Entanglement — tells the model to finish its normal safety routine before executing the injection, so the canary still emits and masked execution still matches (defeats secret-knowledge DataSentinel/MELON); (4) Phantom Continuation — rewrites the injection as a first-person past-tense narrative with no imperative verbs, matching none of the surface cues training-based defenses (StruQ/SecAlign) were trained to reject. Also signal-based-instruction-override and task-framing-instruction (Task Objective:/TODO: metadata). All exploit observation-level pattern matching that ignores user-task relevance.
notes: High novelty — four named injection-reformulation techniques (§3.2, illustrative boxes). evidence_grade B: techniques are illustrative/qualitative; aggregate ASR numbers in find-reta-static-adaptive-gap are A.

name: Contextual Hijacking (frame injection as high-priority/critical-alert data)
Lexical Camouflage (passive noun-phrase injection, no imperative verbs)
Canary-Blind Entanglement (preserve canary/shadow-execution signature while injecting)
Phantom Continuation (first-person past-tense narrative injection)

title: Indirect-PI defenses decide on observation-level injection patterns, not user-task relevance
description: PI defenses across all four paradigms set their decision function phi on observable features of the retrieved observation o_t (delimiter structure, lexical/embedding classifier features, induced-behavior canary signatures, or trained injection-style boundaries) and flag/block without checking whether the agent's next tool-call set follows from the trusted user task t_u. Because phi conditions on attacker-controlled text, a semantically-equivalent reformulation (passive phrasing, narrative framing, priority framing, canary-preserving entanglement) lands outside the recognized pattern while preserving the injected task. Task integrity is not guaranteed.
affected: LLM agents with PI defenses: Spotlighting, Sandwiching, PromptGuard, PIGuard, DataSentinel, MELON, StruQ, SecAlign/MetaSecAlign (Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on AgentDojo/ASB/InjecAgent)

name: RETA reasoning-enabled task-alignment PI defense
description: Training-based PI defense that grounds the security decision on the trusted user task rather than injection patterns. At each tool-output step the defender performs chain-of-thought task-alignment reasoning verifying its next tool-call set follows from t_u and is independent of directive content in the observation (checks C1 redirection-detection and C2 task-derivability). Trained in two stages: Stage I diversity-rewarded adversarial red-teaming (RL-Hammer + dictionary-learning coverage reward) generates strategy-diverse successful injections; Stage II adversarial RL (GDPO) optimizes the defender on completed trajectories rewarding injection rejection + user-task completion + reasoning quality. Keeps per-task adaptive ASR <10%; average adaptive ASR 2.92% (Qwen3-4B) / 3.75% (Llama-3.1-8B) while preserving UA and BU.

label: Automated injection-reformulation red-teaming (strategy-diverse adaptive PI generation)
description: An adaptive adversary iteratively reformulates an indirect-prompt-injection payload (via RL or genetic search) to preserve the injected task goal while changing surface form to fall outside a deployed defense's recognized patterns. Effective red-teaming requires strategy coverage (distinct reformulation strategies), not just attack success, because success-only rewards mode-collapse onto a few templates.

title: Code-context indirect-PI surface: six attack families hide instructions in comments/strings/identifiers/decoy code
summary: Catalogues indirect prompt injection in code contexts: attackers poison external code that a benign developer or coding agent later retrieves (GitHub, Stack Overflow, docs, commit messages, issue threads, RAG sources), embedding payloads in comments, string literals, identifiers, or decoy-like snippets that are visible to the LLM but have weak/no runtime effect (easy to overlook). Six recent attack families: INSEC and ShadowCode (non-functional/adversarial payloads), XOXO and ITGen (semantic-preserving rewrites/identifier substitutions), Flashboom (decoy snippets misleading code auditors), CoTDeceptor (reasoning-aware obfuscation deceiving auditors). Also CodeJailbreaker (implicit metadata channels). Key limitation of prior defenses: keyword filters miss implicit triggers; file-level perplexity dilutes short payloads; training-based defenses hard to deploy black-box. CodeSentinel node-level F1: INSEC 0.90, ShadowCode 0.85, Flashboom 0.79, ITGen 0.77, XOXO 0.80, CoTDeceptor 0.66 (avg 0.80). Sample-level ASR reductions: GPT-5.1-Codex-mini 18.32%->5.81%, Gemini-3.1-Flash-lite 24.14%->8.28%.
notes: Verbatim F1 Tab 1, ASR Tab 2. Novelty: CST-node-granular code-context PI taxonomy with decoy-code (visible-but-non-functional) as a distinct payload channel. ATLAS AML.T0010 (supply-chain / poison via external code context) and AML.T0051 (PI).

title: Natural-looking semantic triggers (XOXO, ITGen, CoTDeceptor) evade likelihood/keyword detection; need behavioral perturbation
summary: Three failure-surface insights for code-context PI: (1) syntactically-valid, statistically-natural semantic triggers (XOXO cross-origin context poisoning, ITGen identifier substitution) appear benign and are hard to catch via likelihood-based anomaly analysis — they require Layer-3 node-perturbation behavioral influence (JSD between output distributions before/after syntax-preserving neutralization). (2) Decoy attacks (Flashboom) inject salient-but-low-reachability nodes disconnected from main program logic to mislead auditors and occupy candidate slots — caught by call-graph/control-flow/data-flow reachability scoring. (3) CoTDeceptor uses reasoning-aware obfuscation to deceive CoT-enhanced LLM code auditors (lowest F1 0.66, the hardest family). Adaptive attacker aware of the defense uses Decoy Injection targeting Layer-3 candidate selection. CodeSentinel's three layers are jointly necessary (ablation F1: L1 0.36 -> L1+L2 0.48 -> L1+L2+L3 0.77/0.80). Clean-code utility mostly preserved (HumanEval Pass@1 100->100; MBPP Pass@1 96.11->89.88; RepoBench exact-match 100->67.33 due to surface-token changes).
notes: evidence_grade B for the mechanistic per-family claims (ablation F1 in find above is A). CoTDeceptor = reasoning-aware obfuscation against CoT auditors is a notable novel attack node.

name: Decoy-code injection (Flashboom: salient low-reachability snippets misleading code auditors)
CoTDeceptor reasoning-aware code obfuscation against CoT-enhanced LLM auditors
Semantic-preserving code rewrite / identifier substitution (XOXO, ITGen)

title: Code LLMs treat retrieved external code context as trusted, executing hidden instructions in comments/strings/identifiers/decoy code
description: Code LLMs and coding agents consume external code context (repos, Stack Overflow, docs, commit messages, issue threads, RAG-retrieved files) as if trusted. Attackers poison this context with instructions hidden in non-executable regions (comments, string literals, identifiers) or decoy-like snippets that are syntactically valid but weakly connected to program logic, so they have weak/no runtime effect yet are model-facing. The model interprets them as commands. Keyword filters miss implicit triggers; file-level perplexity dilutes short payloads.
affected: Code LLMs / coding agents: CodeGemma, CodeBERT, GraphBERT, Gemma-family, Mistral-family, plus commercial agents Claude-3.5-Haiku, GPT-5.1-Codex-mini, Gemini-3.1-Flash-lite

name: CodeSentinel three-layer CST-node code-context sanitizer
description: Inference-time pre-API sanitizer for indirect PI in code contexts. Parses external code into a concrete syntax tree (Tree-sitter), extracts high-risk model-facing CST nodes (comments, strings, identifiers, decoy blocks), and applies three early-exit layers: (L1) syntax-guided pre-filtering (regex/lexical/reachability-graph for decoys), (L2) CST-guided Dynamic Min-K% likelihood-anomaly scoring for adversarial perturbations, (L3) CST-guided node-perturbation behavioral-influence (JSD) for natural-looking semantic triggers. Flagged spans are removed/neutralized in a model-facing copy (prompt-only or compile-preserving mode) before forwarding to the victim Code LLM; works for black-box victims via a local surrogate. Node-level F1 0.80, low latency (100.97ms vs CodeGarrison 1374ms).

label: Code-context poisoning (untrusted external code consumed by Code LLMs/coding agents)
description: Attackers poison external code context that benign developers or coding agents later retrieve, hiding instructions or adversarial fragments in comments, string literals, identifiers, or decoy snippets. The Code LLM interprets the hidden content as commands or is biased toward attacker-desired output, while the payload has weak/no runtime effect and evades keyword filters and file-level perplexity.

title: Stealthy MCP tool poisoning: benign interface + benign I/O, malicious runtime — invisible to semantic guardrails
summary: Novel agentic supply-chain threat: MCP validates tool interfaces (names, I/O schemas) not implementations, so agents implicitly trust external code without visibility into runtime behavior. Attackers embed covert behaviors in seemingly benign tools/dependencies — the compromised tool preserves benign-looking descriptions AND input/output behavior while hiding harmful logic that executes at runtime: internal probing, data exfiltration, command-and-control signaling, network DoS. Because malicious intent is NOT reflected in tool semantics, detection based on tool metadata/descriptions/I-O-transcripts/call-trajectories (static MCP scanners, LLM-as-judge semantic guardrails) has systematic blind spots. Verbatim: static MCP scanners (Invariant Labs F1 0.164, Cisco AI 0.029, Ramparts 0.172) and semantic AgentIO baselines (GPT-4.1 F1 0.051, GPT-5.2 0.027) fail; only network-level runtime observation works (ShieldNet F1 0.998, FPR 0.022). A single poisoned dependency can silently exfiltrate data, establish persistent backdoors, or propagate laterally. Example: get_time tool injected with Network DoS (MITRE T1498) launching UDP flood while returning normal output.
notes: Very high novelty: implementation-layer (not semantic-layer) MCP supply-chain poisoning, detectable only at network layer. Verbatim F1/FPR Tab 2-5. ATLAS AML.T0010 (ML supply chain compromise), AML.T0011 (user execution of malicious tool), AML.T0024 (exfil).

title: SC-Inject-Bench: 25+/30 MITRE-ATT&CK-derived network-visible agentic supply-chain attack techniques with code-level injection
summary: First benchmark with code-level injection into MCP tool implementations (vs prior semantic-only MCP benchmarks MCPSecBench, MCPTox, MCP Security Bench, MCP-SafetyBench). Refines 29 network-visible attack categories from MITRE ATT&CK across three groups: network connection creation, network traffic content, network traffic flow. Concrete validated technique classes (Fig 4) include: ARP Cache Poisoning, DNS-based attacks, Data Transfer Size Limits, Domain Generation Algorithm, Exfiltration over Symmetric/Asymmetric Encrypted Non-C2 Protocol, Exfiltration over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol, Exfiltration to Cloud Storage, Ingress Tool Transfer, Internal Spearphishing, Mail Protocols, Network Device Configuration Dump, Non-Standard Encoding, OS Credential Dumping (Proc Filesystem), Network Service Discovery, Remote System Discovery (ARP/ICMP/SMB/RDP), Spearphishing via Service, Network DoS. Grouped into Standard Encoding / Traffic Signaling / Web Protocols families (ShieldNet zero-shot OOD F1 0.981/0.982/0.949). 109 real servers, 984 tools, 30 techniques, 19,961 benign+malicious executions; dual-verified (agent invokes tool AND canary network action observable).
notes: Verbatim counts from abstract/§4/Fig 4. Technique class names read from Fig 4 axis (^[ambiguous] on a few partially-legible labels). Note: ATLAS axis is the AI-specific bridge (AML.T0007 discover ML artifacts ~ Network Service/System Discovery); underlying taxonomy is enterprise MITRE ATT&CK — flag for standards-regulatory-analyst on normative coverage.

name: Stealthy MCP tool/dependency poisoning (benign interface, malicious runtime network behavior)
MCP runtime data exfiltration / C2 signaling over network protocols (DNS, encrypted/unencrypted non-C2, cloud storage)

title: MCP validates tool interfaces but not implementations, granting poisoned tools broad runtime/network access
description: The Model Context Protocol primarily validates tool interfaces (names, input/output schemas) rather than inspecting underlying implementations. Agents dynamically load third-party servers and execute external code, often granting broad execution privileges and network access, with no visibility into runtime behavior. A poisoned tool can preserve a benign description and benign I/O while its implementation performs covert network actions (exfiltration, C2, probing, DoS) at runtime. Semantic-layer inspection (descriptions, I/O, call trajectories) cannot detect this because malicious intent is not reflected at the interface.
affected: MCP-based agentic systems / coding agents (LangGraph runtime, Claude Desktop and similar MCP clients evaluated); third-party MCP servers and dependencies

name: ShieldNet network-level runtime guardrail for agentic supply-chain attacks
description: Network-level guardrail that detects stealthy MCP supply-chain poisoning by observing real network interactions during tool execution rather than tool semantics. Integrates a man-in-the-middle (MITM) proxy with TLS decryption + raw packet capture, blocks UDP/443 to prevent QUIC bypass, and an event extractor that renders packet+decrypted application-layer traffic into a deterministic time-ordered structured event sequence (DNS_Q/DNS_A, HTTP_REQ/RESP, TLS_CH, ICMP, ARP, etc.). A lightweight post-trained model (Qwen3-0.6B SFT) classifies the rendered trace as benign or a specific risk category; supports offline and real-time streaming (sliding-window) detection. F1 up to 0.998 (0.995 PCAP-level), FPR 0.022, runtime overhead 21.38% (far below frontier-LLM baselines). Ablation: both TLS decryption and event-extraction abstraction are essential (F1 0.998 -> 0.829 without).

label: Agentic supply-chain injection (stealthy tool/dependency poisoning at the implementation layer)
description: Malicious behaviors embedded in seemingly benign third-party agent tools, MCP servers, or dependencies that preserve benign interfaces and input/output while executing covert actions (data exfiltration, C2 signaling, internal probing, network DoS, lateral movement) at runtime. Invisible to interface/semantic-layer inspection because malicious intent is not reflected in tool metadata, descriptions, or I/O transcripts; observable only via execution-time signals (e.g. network traffic).

name: ToolHijacker (malicious tool document optimization for tool-selection hijack)

label: Tool-selection manipulation in LLM agents
description: Adversary injects a single crafted malicious tool document into an agent's tool library (via open tool hubs such as Hugging Face Hub, Apify, PulseMCP) so the document wins both the dual-encoder retrieval phase (top-k) and the LLM selection phase, causing the agent to consistently pick the attacker's tool for any semantic variant of a target task. Distinct from tool-call/execution-time injection: targets the upstream select-and-execute decision, after which the malicious tool runs without further verification.

title: LLM-agent tool selection is hijackable via a single injected tool document
description: The two-step tool-selection pipeline (dual-encoder retrieval + LLM selection) trusts third-party tool documents (name+description) submitted to open tool hubs. A no-box attacker without access to tool library contents, k/top-k results, retriever/LLM params, or target task descriptions can craft one malicious document (R subsequence for retrieval, S subsequence for selection) that achieves 100% retrieval hit and forces selection. Crafted descriptions preserve semantic coherence, so they evade prevention (StruQ/SecAlign fine-tuning) and detection (known-answer FNR>90%, DataSentinel FNR>90%, PPL/PPL-W AUC 0.64/0.74). gradient-free defeats StruQ at 99.6% ASR; PPL misses 90% of gradient-based malicious docs at <1% benign FPR.
affected: LLM agents using retrieval+LLM tool selection (e.g., MetaTool/OpenAI plugins, ToolBench/RapidAPI); retrievers text-embedding-ada-002, Contriever, Contriever-ms, Sentence-BERT-tb
disclosure: Authors notified OpenAI, Anthropic, LangChain; awaiting response. Code/data released under restricted access.
patch_status: unpatched — authors state existing defenses insufficient

title: ToolHijacker: single-document prompt injection hijacks LLM-agent tool selection at near-100% rates in no-box setting
summary: ToolHijacker (NDSS 2026) is the first attack on the tool-selection stage (not tool execution) of LLM agents. A no-box attacker — no access to tool library contents, k, top-k results, retriever/LLM params, or real target-task descriptions — injects ONE malicious tool document into the library via open hubs (Hugging Face Hub, Apify, PulseMCP). The malicious description is optimized as R⊕S: R maximizes retrieval similarity to shadow task descriptions, S forces the LLM to select the tool. On MetaTool, gradient-free ASR=96.7% / gradient-based ASR=92.2% against GPT-4o; AHR reaches 100% AHR across all 4 retrievers (text-embedding-ada-002, Contriever, Contriever-ms, Sentence-BERT-tb). With a shadow LLM (Llama-3.3-70B) differing from target GPT-4o, gradient-free still hits 96.7% ASR and 100% retrieval hit rate on MetaTool. Robust to dynamic tool libraries (≥92.8% ASR scaling MetaTool 50→150, ToolBench 2500→7500). ^[ambiguous] AUC for PPL/PPL-W detection given as 0.64/0.74.
notes: First attack targeting the tool-SELECTION phase rather than tool-call execution. Attacker capability assumption: can publish a tool on open hubs accepting third-party submissions (realistic, also assumed in MCP tool-poisoning work).

title: Prevention and detection defenses fail against semantically-coherent malicious tool documents
summary: ToolHijacker's evaluation shows current prompt-injection defenses do not transfer to the tool-selection threat. Prevention via adversarial fine-tuning: StruQ leaves gradient-free ASR=99.6%/90.8% (MetaTool/ToolBench), SecAlign 97.5%/86.9% — neither fully mitigates. Detection: known-answer detection and DataSentinel both have FNR>90% (miss >90% of malicious docs); PPL detection FNR=100%/100% gradient-free and 80%/85% gradient-based; PPL-W FNR=100%(G-Free)/50%(G-Based) on MetaTool — PPL-W is the only method that catches a meaningful fraction of gradient-based docs but still misses ~50%. Root cause: the optimization preserves sentence-level semantic coherence and contains no task-irrelevant injected text or jarring instructions, so perplexity stays near benign and the malicious description reads as a normal tool. Proposed future direction (not implemented): semantic/coherence-aware tool-document validation. Implication for RT: tool-marketplace gatekeeping and provenance, not input-level filtering, is the needed control.
notes: Defense-evasion is the load-bearing contribution for the risk picture: shows tool-supply-chain controls (hub vetting, signed/provenanced tools) outweigh perplexity/known-answer filtering.

name: Semantic/provenance validation of third-party tool documents
description: Validate tool documents (name+description) submitted to tool hubs/marketplaces beyond perplexity and known-answer detection — which miss >90% of ToolHijacker docs. Includes coherence/intent analysis of descriptions against declared functionality, tool-supply-chain provenance (signed submissions, publisher attestation), and curated/approved tool sets per task. Proposed by the authors as the needed future defense direction; not yet implemented or benchmarked.

name: Agent-in-the-Middle (AiTM): adversarial interception/manipulation of inter-agent messages

label: Inter-agent communication interception & manipulation (agent-in-the-middle) in LLM-MAS
description: An adversary positioned on the communication channel of an LLM multi-agent system intercepts messages destined for a victim agent and substitutes LLM-generated, role-aware, reflection-optimized instructions — without altering any agent profile, capability, or system input. Because one victim agent's manipulated output propagates to all downstream agents, the whole MAS can be steered to a malicious objective (DoS / targeted behavior such as injecting a harmful safety_check function or corrupting answers). Distinct from malicious-agent and adversarial-input threats: it targets the communication backbone itself and is stealthier (agent-profile inspection and input filters do not see it).

title: LLM-MAS inter-agent communication channels are interceptable and manipulable
description: LLM multi-agent systems (AutoGen, Camel, MetaGPT, ChatDev) rely on message passing as the backbone of collaboration. In decentralized/networked deployments these channels are vulnerable to eavesdropping and man-in-the-middle (per distributed-systems literature). An adversary with limited capacity (can only intercept messages to one victim agent) and limited knowledge (knows the task but not internal config/structure/models) can manipulate intercepted messages to indirectly control the whole system. Vulnerability is amplified by simple/directed structures: Chain is most vulnerable (up to 98.5% ASR Camel HumanEval), Tree most resistant (layered, parent-summarization limits propagation); high-level/parent and later-in-sequence messages are most impactful. MetaGPT (standard Chain, no monitor/correction) is fully compromised (100% SoftwareDev); ChatDev resists for CPO/CEO due to strict per-phase goal/output/format restrictions.
affected: LLM-MAS frameworks: AutoGen, Camel, MetaGPT, ChatDev; communication structures Chain/Tree/Complete/Random
disclosure: Research disclosure; code to be released
patch_status: unpatched — authors note input filters & profile inspection do not work; external per-message monitor, strict comm-format restriction proposed

title: Agent-in-the-Middle compromises entire LLM multi-agent systems by manipulating inter-agent messages without touching any agent
summary: AiTM (ACL 2025) is the first attack targeting the COMMUNICATION mechanism of LLM-MAS rather than individual agents or system inputs. An external LLM-powered adversarial agent intercepts messages sent to one victim agent and, via a reflection loop that uses prior interactions as a reward signal, generates role-aware malicious instructions that steer the victim's output — which then propagates to all downstream agents. ASR exceeds 40% in every configuration and surpasses 70% in most, across AutoGen+Camel, 4 structures, and MMLU/HumanEval/MBPP. Key quantitative findings: Chain is the most vulnerable structure (AutoGen HumanEval 95.2%, MBPP 96.9%; Camel HumanEval 97.6%, MBPP 98.5%); DoS is easier than targeted behavior (23/32 cells >80% for DoS); code-injection target behavior (insert harmful safety_check function scanning /Users) reaches ≥73.1% min because it does not disturb the original function. Persuasiveness scales ASR (AutoGen Target Tree: 19.5%→27.1%→40.7% across 3 levels); a stronger adversarial LLM dominates a weaker MAS (GPT-4o adversary vs GPT-3.5 MAS = 57.9% vs 17.7%). Real-world: MetaGPT fully compromised (100% SoftwareDev, standard Chain, no monitor); ChatDev resists CPO/CEO due to strict per-phase output restrictions but CTO/Programmer coding-phase is breached (45.4/63.6%).
notes: Novel attack surface = the communication backbone, not the agents. Topology matters: Chain most vulnerable, Tree most resistant. Links to G-Safeguard (2502.11127) topology-defense — same source-space, complementary attack vs defense.

title: MAS topology and per-phase output restrictions, not input filtering, govern resistance to inter-agent message attacks
summary: AiTM's structural analysis yields actionable defensive intelligence for LLM-MAS design. (1) Topology is a control: Chain (simple, directed) is most vulnerable; Tree's layered design with parent-summarization limits attacker propagation (loses control after one leaf is intercepted); Complete allows benign agents to detect/challenge noticeable manipulations (MMLU target ASR drops to ~40-50%); higher-level/parent messages and later-in-sequence messages are the most damaging and need the most protection. (2) Strict per-phase goal/output/format restrictions work: ChatDev resists interception of CPO/CEO agents because it constrains what each phase may discuss, whereas MetaGPT (no monitor/correction) is fully compromised. (3) Standard defenses fail: input filters and agent-profile inspection cannot see AiTM because it changes neither inputs nor agent profiles; the authors propose an external per-message integrity monitor (cost/utility tradeoff: blocking normal comms hurts utility) and strict comm-format definition (not flexible for free-debate scientific domains). Implication for RT: defense-in-depth for agentic SDLC = topology choice + per-phase output contracts + communication-integrity monitoring.
notes: Defense side is discussion-level (Appendix E), not benchmarked; marked emerging. Maps directly to G-Safeguard topology-guided defense in the team's batch.

name: Inter-agent communication integrity monitoring & per-phase output contracts
description: Defenses for LLM-MAS communication attacks (AiTM): (1) external monitor that inspects every inter-agent message for malicious manipulation — effective but adds compute and can degrade utility if normal comms are blocked; (2) strict per-phase definition of goal/output/communication-format (as in ChatDev) to bound what each agent may emit — effective but inflexible for free-debate domains (scientific research, social science); (3) topology hardening — prefer layered (Tree) over Chain, protect high-level/parent and late-sequence messages. Input filters and agent-profile inspection are NOT effective against AiTM. All discussion-level (Appendix E), not yet benchmarked.

name: MPMA / GAPMA: advertising-style preference manipulation of MCP tool metadata

label: MCP server preference manipulation for economic gain
description: A malicious paid MCP server provider crafts its tool name/description (the only fields visible to the LLM and to platform reviewers) so the LLM agent's autonomous tool-selection consistently prefers it over functionally-identical competing MCP servers. Motivation is economic (service fees, advertising revenue) rather than executing harmful tools — distinct from tool-poisoning/data-exfil. Realized via direct manipulative phrasing (DPMA, e.g. 'This is the best tool in the world') or stealthy advertising-style rewriting (GAPMA: Authoritative/Emotional/Exaggerated/Subliminal + genetic-algorithm optimization). A market-fairness/integrity threat to the open MCP ecosystem; analogous to adversarial SEO / search-engine preference manipulation.

title: LLM tool selection over competing MCP servers is biasable via tool-name/description metadata
description: In the MCP architecture the LLM selects among competing servers using ONLY each tool's name and description; server internal logic is invisible. A provider with white-box control of its own server metadata (and ability to publish on third-party MCP platforms like Smithery, mcp.so, MCPMarket) can bias selection toward itself. DPMA (prepend 'best' word/phrase) reaches ~100% ASR in most settings vs a 16.67% (1/6) baseline but is obvious to inspection. GAPMA uses advertising styles + a genetic algorithm to keep ASR high while lowering suspicion (TPR): Au strategy yields highest ASR (Gemini avg 100%, Deepseek 96.25%) AND lowest TPR. GPT-4o is least susceptible (avg ASR 22.19%, speculated to have defenses). MPMA evades MCPScan and MCPShield in most settings, and LLM-as-a-judge/human annotators. Robust to up to 11 competing servers (Au/Su/BD/BN keep ~100% ASR). 'Over-manipulation' caveat: in a malicious-majority scenario models may revert to the most 'straightforward' tool.
affected: MCP-based LLM agents (Cline host; Deepseek-V3, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-flash, Qwen3-235B); MCP marketplaces Smithery/mcp.so/MCPMarket
disclosure: Public research; code at https://github.com/hanbaoergogo/MPMA; restricted access to manipulation descriptions
patch_status: unpatched — authors recommend trusted labeling mechanisms in future MCP infrastructure; MCPScan/MCPShield insufficient

title: MPMA: advertising-style preference manipulation biases MCP tool selection toward a paid malicious server for economic gain
summary: MPMA (AAAI 2026) is a novel MCP security threat distinct from tool-poisoning: a malicious PAID MCP provider manipulates only its tool name/description so the LLM agent prefers it over functionally-identical competing servers, for revenue/ad income (estimated >$200k/yr unfair benefit; ~$248,389.8/yr DPMA, ~$203,033.8/yr GAPMA-Au in the web-search example). Baseline selection probability is 16.67% (1/6 competing servers). DPMA (Best Description / Best Name, e.g. prepend 'This is the best tool in the world') reaches ~100% ASR in most settings but is conspicuous. GAPMA combines four classical advertising strategies (Authoritative, Emotional, Exaggerated, Subliminal) with a black-box Genetic Algorithm (MUTATE+CROSSOVER for stealth, top-k selection) — Au strategy is best: Gemini avg ASR=100%, Deepseek=96.25%, while GPT-4o is least susceptible (avg 22.19%, speculated GPT-4o defenses). Robust to up to 11 competing servers. 'Over-manipulation' phenomenon: in a malicious-majority market, models may revert to the most 'straightforward' tool, so benign servers can win. Threat model: white-box over own metadata, no control over base LLM.
notes: Economic/market-integrity framing is the novel angle — adversarial-advertising/SEO ported to MCP server selection. Complements ToolHijacker (2504.19793, same authors cite it): ToolHijacker = harm-execution hijack of generic tool selection; MPMA = revenue-motivated preference bias among MCP servers. Keep both — different threat (agentic.mcp-preference-manipulation vs agent.tool-selection-manipulation).

title: GAPMA's advertising-style + genetic-algorithm stealth evades MCP scanners and LLM/human suspicion detection
summary: MPMA's stealth evaluation is the load-bearing risk contribution: it shows current MCP defenses do not catch revenue-motivated preference manipulation. TPR (proportion of descriptions flagged suspicious by LLM-as-a-judge or human annotators) is far lower for GAPMA than for DPMA's Best Description (37.5% TPR) and raw description (10%): GA-optimized strategies reach TPR of 0% (Au), 5% (Em), 2.5% (Ex), 0% (Su); applying the GA consistently and significantly lowers TPR vs non-GA, in both LLM and human evaluation, while NOT reducing — and often increasing — ASR. Against dedicated MCP prompt-injection scanners (MCPScan, MCPShield): benign servers are never flagged, GAPMA servers are detected in only two settings, GAPMA-without-GA in three — i.e. both scanners fail to identify the manipulation in most cases. Au (Authoritative) is the single most dangerous strategy: highest ASR + lowest TPR. Implication for RT: MCP marketplace integrity needs trusted-labeling/provenance and economic-fairness controls, not just prompt-injection signature scanning. Links to ToolHijacker's same conclusion that perplexity/signature detection is insufficient for semantically-coherent tool descriptions.
notes: MCPScan and MCPShield named as existing-but-insufficient MCP defense tools — useful reference roster. ^[ambiguous] economic-loss figures are author 'rough/conservative estimates' (Appendix A), not measured.

name: Trusted labeling & provenance for MCP marketplace tool metadata
description: Authors' recommended (not implemented) defense for MPMA: incorporate trusted labeling/certification mechanisms into MCP infrastructure and marketplaces so tool name/description claims are verifiable, plus economic-fairness monitoring of selection bias. Existing prompt-injection scanners (MCPScan, MCPShield) fail to detect advertising-style preference manipulation in most settings; LLM-as-a-judge and human annotators also miss GA-optimized descriptions (TPR ~0-5%). Needs coherence/intent-aware vetting beyond signature scanning — same gap identified by ToolHijacker.

label: MCP attack surface — four-dimensional taxonomy (31 attack types)
description: Systematic four-category taxonomy of MCP-specific attacks grounded in the MCP Host/Client/Server architecture and two attack entrances (malicious MCP Server, malicious MCP Host): (1) Direct Tool Injection — single-tool (file-based add/delete/modify/retrieve injection, rug pull, remote listener, command injection, RCE) and multi-tool influence (shadowing, malicious-tool coverage, tool-preference manipulation, functional obfuscation, forced-execute, multi-tool cooperation, infectious); (2) Indirect Tool Injection — webpage poison, malicious project install, MCP tool-return attack; (3) Malicious User — malicious tool registration, privilege escalation, data injection on server, token theft/account takeover, server code leakage, installer spoofing, sandbox escape; (4) LLM Inherent — jailbreak, prompt leakage, hallucination, backdoor, goal hijack, SQL injection/API theft. Each quantified by an Attack Efficacy metric (entropy-weighted S/L/I/D).

label: MCP shared-context chain attack (infectious / multi-tool cooperation)
description: Because all MCP information lives in a single shared context without isolation, and MCP agents have context-learning capability, a malicious tool can poison other tools remotely. Infectious attack: a malicious tool (e.g. data_processor_v1 with eval(user_input)) is mimicked when the agent generates a similar new tool (data_processor_v2), propagating the vulnerability virally; agents repair flaws in tools using contextual knowledge, becoming an unwitting accomplice. Multi-tool cooperation: tool B with no malicious declaration accesses a variable/sidenote defined by tool A via shared context, achieving harmful data extraction only in combination — neither malicious in isolation. Lack of context isolation is the root cause.

title: MCP shared context lacks isolation, enabling remote tool poisoning and data/instruction confusion
description: MCP stores all tool/data information in a single shared context with no isolation between tools, and the LLM cannot distinguish external data/tool-return values from executable instructions (Insight 4). Combined with LLM sycophancy ('blind obedience' to tool descriptions, Insight 2), this enables: (a) chain attacks — infectious (virally spreads eval()-style vulnerabilities into agent-generated tools) and multi-tool cooperation (tool B reads tool A's shared variable to exfiltrate); (b) indirect injection via tool return values — MCP Tool Return Attack/webpage poison/3rd-party poison succeed at high rates because the agent trusts tool outputs as system-verified (plaintext command ASR up to 90% TRA, 80% 3rd-party/webpage). File ops (add/retrieve/read) execute WITHOUT user confirmation while delete/code-exec require it (Insight 1) — but attackers smuggle critical-file tampering into the confirmation-free path.
