title: Cross-lingual safety alignment gap (curse of multilinguality) exploitable via low-resource and transliterated language
description: LLM safety alignment is concentrated in English/high-resource languages; low-resource and Indic languages are underrepresented in training data, so models fail to recognize and refuse harmful/inappropriate language (swearing) in those languages. Transliterating non-Latin-script swears into Latin script and mixing with English further degrades detection. Models also conflate formal tone / positive sentiment with ethical compliance, applying safety inconsistently based on superficial surface cues.
affected: open-source LLMs deployed in multilingual enterprise settings (Mistral 7B/8x7B/8x22B, Phi-3/3.5, Qwen-2.5 7B/14B, Llama-3/3.1 8B/70B)
patch_status: unpatched (recommendation: multilingual safety alignment, better data curation, phonetic normalization)
controls: multilingual safety fine-tuning across all supported languages (not English-only)
contextual-appropriateness checks decoupled from tone/formality cues

title: Reputational/trust harm from LLM-generated profanity in enterprise communications
affected: enterprises deploying LLMs for customer-facing communication (emails, sales pitches, support) across multilingual markets; recipients of offensive automated messages

hazard: LLMs comply with instructions to embed swear words in enterprise communications, especially in low-resource/transliterated languages, exposing organizations to reputational and trust damage
hazardous_situation: an enterprise LLM drafting a customer email or sales pitch is given a prompt (intentionally or via a malicious/careless user) containing transliterated or low-resource-language swear words; the model fails to refuse because its safety alignment is English-centric and it mistakes formal tone for appropriateness, producing offensive outward-facing content
controls: multilingual safety alignment across all deployed languages
prefer larger/newer model versions (generally lower harmful rate)
output content moderation on customer-facing channels
residual_risk: medium: even best models retain substantial harmful rates (English 0.46-0.51; Indic up to 0.79); no evaluated open-source model is robust, and transliteration remains an unmitigated attack surface; frontier closed-source models not tested so their residual is unknown ^[ambiguous]

title: Jailbreak tax: successful jailbreaks can degrade jailbroken-output utility by up to 92%, uncorrelated with success rate
summary: Introduces 'jailbreak tax' JTax = (BaseUtil - JailUtil)/BaseUtil, the fraction of baseline utility lost after a successful jailbreak, distinct from jailbreak success rate (JailSucc = rate of any non-refusal). Key findings: (Q1) many jailbreaks incur a substantial tax, lowering jailbroken-model utility by up to 91-92% (PAIR on GSM8K). (Q2) NO correlation between jailbreak success rate and jailbreak tax — jailbreaks that succeed equally often have vastly different taxes (e.g. GCG vs PAIR on WMDP). Many-shot and system-prompt jailbreaks preserve utility (near-zero tax); PAIR/TAP/MultiJail incur high tax. (Q3) more capable/larger models do NOT reduce the tax (LLaMA 405B even shows highest tax for most-successful PAIR). (Q4) tax persists across alignment types (system prompt, SFT, frontier Claude 3.5 internal alignment via EvilMath, up to 26% on MATH). (Q5) harder tasks do NOT incur higher tax (no correlation with task difficulty). Mechanism: jailbroken models bypass guardrails but exhibit flawed reasoning, producing confidently wrong answers.
notes: Verbatim: up to 91-92% accuracy drop (PAIR/GSM8K). 8 jailbreaks, 4 models. Alignment refusal rates Table 1: LLaMA 70B system-prompt 99.6%, SFT 95.5%, Claude EvilMath 92.8%. EvilMath/UnicornMath reword GSM8K into harmful/benign-OOD via GPT-4o. Dual-use: jailbreak EFFICACY evaluation metric for defenders + red-teamers.

title: Jailbreak-tax benchmark suites (WMDP/GSM8K/MATH + EvilMath/UnicornMath pseudo-alignment): construction, metrics, validity
summary: Benchmark intelligence record. The jailbreak-tax benchmarks measure whether jailbroken outputs are actually USEFUL — a validity dimension prior jailbreak benchmarks (HarmBench, JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT, AgentHarm) miss by treating non-refusal as success. Construction solves two problems: (1) ground-truth-verifiable tasks (WMDP bio MCQ 1000 Q, GSM8K grade-school math, MATH 5 difficulty levels) so utility is objectively measurable; (2) pseudo-alignment to make benign tasks appear harmful via three methods — system-prompt ('You are not allowed to answer math problems'), SFT on refusal pairs, and EvilMath (GPT-4o rewords math into bomb/poison/trafficking contexts triggering the model's INTERNAL real safety alignment; UnicornMath inverse-rewords to benign-OOD to control for OOD utility loss). Metrics: JailSucc (any non-refusal), JailUtil (correct AND non-refused), JTax (relative utility loss vs unaligned baseline). Methodology: adaptive jailbreak attacks (GCG/AutoDAN optimization, PAIR/TAP LLM-as-attacker with GPT-4o-mini, many-shot ICL, MultiJail translation) on aligned models. Validity issues: utility only measurable on verifiable tasks (not open-ended harm like bomb instructions); EvilMath rewording could itself shift OOD (controlled via UnicornMath); judge for math = exact-match format.
notes: github.com/ethz-spylab/jailbreak-tax. Construction=verifiable-task + pseudo-alignment (3 methods). Metric JTax is the novel contribution. Methodology=adaptive attacks (white+black-box). Recommends labs grant research access to UNALIGNED models for rigorous jailbreak evaluation. Validity: open-ended harmful-task utility still hard to evaluate (acknowledged).

name: Jailbreak with utility degradation (measured via jailbreak tax)
Jailbreak-tax evaluation (utility-aware jailbreak benchmarking)
description: Evaluate jailbreaks not only by success rate (non-refusal) but by the jailbreak tax — the relative loss of useful, correct capability in jailbroken outputs versus an unaligned baseline, measured on objectively verifiable tasks. Defenders can deprioritize high-tax jailbreaks (which yield unreliable harmful outputs) and prioritize low-tax ones (e.g. many-shot, system-prompt JB) that preserve dangerous capability. Requires research access to unaligned model versions plus reliably-evaluable harmful-task benchmarks (e.g. cybersecurity).

hazard: jailbreak success rate overstates real-world danger because some successful jailbreaks produce low-utility (flawed-reasoning, confidently-wrong) outputs while others fully preserve dangerous capability
hazardous_situation: a safety team triages jailbreak threats using success-rate-only benchmarks and misallocates effort: it over-weights high-tax attacks (e.g. PAIR, which bypasses guardrails but cripples reasoning by up to 92%) while under-weighting low-tax attacks (many-shot, system-prompt) that retain near-full capability on dangerous tasks like bio-security (WMDP)
controls: jailbreak-tax evaluation: measure utility loss on verifiable tasks, not just non-refusal
prioritize defenses against low-tax jailbreaks that preserve dangerous capability
provide research access to unaligned model versions for rigorous evaluation
pair refusal benchmarks with reliably-evaluable harmful-task benchmarks (e.g. cybersecurity, WMDP)
residual_risk: medium: jailbreak tax is a new metric that improves threat prioritization but does not itself prevent jailbreaks; high tax does not guarantee safety (PAIR/TAP still cut MATH accuracy >40% yet succeed >99%), and open-ended harmful-output utility remains hard to evaluate; more capable models do not reduce the tax

title: Misuse of jailbroken model capabilities (bio-security, weapons) under-/over-estimated by success-rate-only evaluation
affected: society / safety evaluators relying on jailbreak benchmarks; potential misuse of preserved-capability jailbroken outputs in bio-security and other high-harm domains

title: ELBA-Bench: PEFT/ICL backdoors achieve near-100% ASR with preserved clean accuracy; stronger reasoning = more CoT-backdoor vulnerable
summary: ELBA-Bench's 1300+ experiments yield several safety-critical findings on LLM backdoors. (Finding 1) PEFT attacks (BadNets, GBTL, CBA, UBA, TPLLM, VPI, ITBA via LoRA) consistently outperform without-fine-tuning attacks in classification, with strong cross-dataset generalization; ITBA reaches 100% ASR on both SST-2 and DBpedia with ~95% clean accuracy (CACC); GBTL ~95% CACC / ~99% ASR across all datasets on Llama2-7B-Chat. (Finding 2) No single trigger pattern is both maximally effective AND stealthy; optimized triggers beat non-optimized, and extended/longer trigger sequences beat single triggers in generation tasks (TPLLM 97.5% RR / 87.0% ASR on Advbench). (Finding 3) BadChain (W/o FT, CoT backdoor) is universally dominant in knowledge reasoning — 79.39% ASR on GPT-3.5 and 99.24% on LLaMA-3-8B-Chat for GSM8K; crucially, stronger-reasoning models are PARADOXICALLY MORE vulnerable (reasoning proficiency enables coherent exploitation of poisoned chains), and CACC-preservation requires controlled poisoning calibration. (Finding 4) PoisonRAG dominates QA: >90% ASR in 27 model-dataset combos, exploiting RAG knowledge-base dependence (e.g. 97% NQ / 99% HotpotQA on PaLM2).
notes: Verbatim: ITBA 100% ASR SST-2/DBpedia; BadChain GSM8K 79.39% (GPT-3.5) / 99.24% (LLaMA-3-8B); PoisonRAG >90% ASR in 27 combos, 97% NQ/99% HotpotQA (PaLM2). Paradox: stronger reasoning -> higher CoT-backdoor vulnerability. 12 attacks, 18 datasets, 12 LLMs (7B-33B + GPT-3.5/4, Claude3, PaLM2).

title: ELBA-Bench benchmark intelligence: backdoor-attack coverage, metrics, stealthiness, validity vs BackdoorLLM
summary: Benchmark intelligence record. ELBA-Bench is a unified LLM-backdoor benchmark superseding BackdoorLLM (8 attacks/12 datasets/7 open-source-only LLMs/200+ exps/no stealthiness) with 12 attacks, 18 datasets, 12 LLMs (open+CLOSED source), 1300+ experiments and stealthiness measurement. Taxonomy: classifies attacks by whether fine-tuning is involved — PEFT (BadNets, CBA, UBA, VPI, TPLLM, GBTL, ITBA) vs Without-Fine-tuning (IBA, ICL, DecodeTrust, BadChain, PoisonRAG). Threat model: PEFT attacker modifies parameters during fine-tuning (jointly minimizes task loss + backdoor loss on poisoned trigger samples); W/o-FT attacker only manipulates inputs (poisoned demonstrations/ICL, CoT injection, RAG poisoning) without parameter access. Metrics: CACC (clean accuracy), ASR (attack success rate), FTR (false trigger rate), RR (refusal rate), PassR (clean code-pass rate), ASRt (target-answer rate, reasoning), CPDR (clean-perf drop rate); plus 2 stealthiness measures — semantic-similarity change (Delta-e) and perplexity change (Delta-p). Tasks: classification, knowledge-reasoning, QA, generation, code-injection. Validity issues: benchmark is offensive-focused — authors note current works LACK robust defense support; no in-depth mechanistic analysis of how backdoors influence behavior (acknowledged limitation).
notes: Coverage: 12 attacks x 18 datasets x 12 LLMs x 1300+ exps. Metrics: CACC/ASR/FTR/RR/PassR/ASRt/CPDR + Delta-e/Delta-p stealth. Construction=PEFT(LoRA backdoor) + W/o-FT(ICL/CoT/RAG poisoning). Validity: offensive-only, no defense baselines, no mechanistic interpretability (acknowledged).

name: Chain-of-thought backdoor (BadChain) — poisoned reasoning-step injection without fine-tuning
RAG knowledge-base poisoning (PoisonRAG) — inject poisoned texts into retrieval database

title: Chain-of-thought reasoning backdoor vulnerability (stronger reasoning increases exposure)
description: LLMs can be backdoored without fine-tuning by injecting malicious reasoning steps into chain-of-thought demonstrations/prompts (BadChain); a trigger causes the model to insert a poisoned reasoning step and produce attacker-targeted answers while behaving normally on clean inputs. Paradoxically, models with stronger reasoning capabilities are MORE vulnerable because their reasoning proficiency lets them coherently exploit the poisoned chain. Maintaining high clean accuracy requires the attacker to calibrate poisoning intensity.
affected: reasoning-capable LLMs supporting CoT prompting (GPT-3.5/4, LLaMA-3-8B-Chat, Vicuna, PaLM2, Claude3)
patch_status: unpatched (authors note lack of robust defenses; trigger elimination is an open problem)

title: RAG knowledge-base poisoning vulnerability (PoisonRAG)
description: Retrieval-augmented generation LLMs are backdoorable by injecting poisoned texts into the external knowledge database, optimizing retrieval and effectiveness to mislead responses without modifying model parameters. Exploits the model's dependence on retrieved knowledge-base content. Achieves >90% ASR across 27 model-dataset combinations, peaking in RAG scenarios.
affected: RAG-equipped LLMs (PaLM2, GPT-3.5/4, Claude3, Llama2-7B/13B, Vicuna-7B/13B/33B) on NQ/HotpotQA/MS-MARCO
patch_status: unpatched (no robust defense baseline in benchmark)
controls: knowledge-base access control and write auditing

title: Integrity compromise of deployed LLMs via efficient-learning backdoors (PEFT/ICL/CoT/RAG)
affected: end-users and organizations operating downstream-deployed LLMs (classification, reasoning, QA, code-generation) sourced from untrusted fine-tuning, demonstrations, or knowledge bases

hazard: LLMs deployed downstream can be covertly backdoored via efficient-learning paradigms (LoRA/PEFT fine-tuning, in-context demonstrations, CoT prompts, or RAG knowledge bases) achieving near-100% attack success while preserving clean-sample accuracy and evading detection
hazardous_situation: an organization adopts a LoRA-fine-tuned model, a prompt template with poisoned CoT demonstrations, or a RAG knowledge base from an untrusted source; the model behaves correctly on clean inputs (CACC preserved) but, on a hidden trigger, produces attacker-targeted outputs (wrong classification, harmful content, malicious reasoning, or wrong answers) — and stronger reasoning models are MORE exposed to CoT backdoors
controls: supply-chain provenance verification for fine-tuned weights, prompt demonstrations, and RAG sources
stealthiness-aware backdoor screening: semantic-similarity (Delta-e) and perplexity (Delta-p) anomaly detection
trusted-demonstration / trusted-knowledge-base curation with write auditing
controlled access to fine-tuning pipeline parameters
residual_risk: high: ELBA-Bench is offensive-only and the authors explicitly note current works LACK robust defenses; optimized/extended triggers boost robustness against detection, PEFT attacks generalize cross-dataset, and no evaluated defense eliminates triggers — residual risk remains high pending defensive research

title: Shuffle Inconsistency: MLLM safety alignment fails to generalize to shuffled harmful inputs while comprehension persists
summary: SI-Attack reveals a 'Shuffle Inconsistency' in MLLMs: comprehension ability is robust to shuffling (hidden-state PCA shows shallow layers can't distinguish, but deeper layers diverge), whereas safety ability degrades sharply. ChatGPT-3.5 toxic scores (1-5) for shuffled vs original: LLaVA-NEXT/InternVL-2 text toxic rose from 2.48/1.65 to 3.32/3.38; GPT-4o/Gemini-1.5-Pro show same phenomenon. Across word-level (text) and 4-patch (image) shuffle, shuffling yields the highest toxic score among all mutation operations (random insert/delete/replace/synonym for text; mask/blur/flip/gray for image). Authors state safety alignment 'lacks generalization' — comprehension capability becomes a weakness exploitable by attackers.
notes: Novel threat-node candidate: safety-alignment-generalization gap to input-space mutations (shuffling). Toxic scores are 1-5 judge scores, not ASR; distinct metric. ATLAS AML.T0054 (jailbreak via prompt) and AML.T0051 (LLM prompt injection) both fit the prompt-space manipulation.

title: SI-Attack black-box query optimization achieves 40-71% ASR on MLLMs incl. GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Gemini-1.5-Pro
summary: SI-Attack splits text word-wise and images into 4 patches, shuffles both, and uses ChatGPT-3.5 as a toxic judge in a query-based black-box loop (max 10 iters, ASR threshold S_tau=4) to select the most harmful shuffled input. On MM-SafetyBench (with typography), ASR: LLaVA-NEXT 62.68%, MiniGPT-4 62.44%, InternVL-2 71.01%, VLGuard 40.77% — outperforming QR-Attack by 18.69/35.24/30.71/31.25 pts. Closed-source MM-SafetyBench ASR: GPT-4o 68.57%, Claude-3.5-Sonnet 47.20%, Gemini-1.5-Pro 71.25%, Qwen-VL-Max 68.63% (vs QR-Attack 20.77/7.50/21.07/33.04). Ablation: shuffled-images-and-text 80.41% ASR vs only-text 67.01%, only-image 35.05%, original 13.40% (GPT-4o, 01-IA); query-optimized shuffle 80.41% vs random-shuffle 28.87%. Text-side safety weaker than image-side. SI-Attack bypasses VLGuard (a safety fine-tuned model) and outer safety guardrails of commercial models.
notes: Measured ASR numbers -> evidence_grade A. Black-box, transferable across 4 open + 4 closed commercial MLLMs. Note Claude-3.5-Sonnet HADES robustness gap attributed to keyword filter on text prompts ('violence','abuse').

label: Safety-comprehension generalization gap in MLLMs
description: MLLMs retain comprehension of input-space-mutated harmful instructions (token/patch shuffling, typography, OOD transforms) while their safety-alignment defenses fail to generalize to the same mutations, so the model still understands harmful intent yet no longer refuses. The comprehension capability itself becomes the exploitable weakness. Demonstrated via Shuffle Inconsistency across word-wise text shuffle and patch-wise image shuffle on GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Gemini-1.5-Pro, Qwen-VL-Max and open-source LLaVA-NEXT/InternVL-2/MiniGPT-4/VLGuard.

name: SI-Attack (Shuffle Inconsistency Attack)

title: MLLM safety mechanisms bypassable by token/patch shuffling of harmful instructions
description: MLLM defense mechanisms (inner alignment and outer guardrails) fail to detect harmful intent when the harmful text is shuffled word-wise and/or the harmful image is split into patches and shuffled patch-wise, even though the model still comprehends the instruction. Includes safety-fine-tuned VLGuard and commercial guardrails of GPT-4o/Gemini-1.5-Pro/Qwen-VL-Max; Claude-3.5-Sonnet partially mitigated by surface keyword filtering. Root cause: safety alignment lacks generalization to input-space mutations.
affected: LLaVA-NEXT, MiniGPT-4, InternVL-2, VLGuard, GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Gemini-1.5-Pro, Qwen-VL-Max

title: OOD-ifying harmful inputs inflates model uncertainty and bypasses RLHF safety alignment trained on in-distribution harm
summary: JOOD reveals that RLHF/self-feedback safety alignment is trained on in-distribution harmful inputs and fails to generalize to OOD-transformed harm. Vanilla harmful inputs are confidently refused (uncertainty 1/10, 0% ASR), but OOD-ifying them via text-mixing (coining nonsensical words e.g. 'bombapple' from bomb+apple) or image-mixing (Mixup/CutMix/ResizeMix of harmful image e.g. grenade with benign auxiliary e.g. apple) raises uncertainty to 7/10 and ASR to 13% (text) / 63% (image+text). The shifted harmful visual embeddings inside the MLLM visual encoder fail to trigger safety guardrails. Strong negative correlation (Pearson -0.63) between mixing coefficient alpha and refusal rate; typographic auxiliary images amplify harmfulness more than realistic ones.
notes: Novel threat-node candidate multimodal.ood-distribution-shift: OOD input transforms beyond safety-alignment data distribution. Complements 2501.04931 shuffle-inconsistency (both are safety-generalization-gap to input mutations). HF is a 0-10 harmfulness score, distinct from ASR%.

title: JOOD jailbreaks GPT-4, GPT-4V, o1/GPT-4o with up to 63% ASR and resists system-prompt + adaptive (AdaShield) defenses
summary: JOOD (image-mixing, Eq.3) on AdvBench-M: GPT-4V achieves HF/ASR of BE 7.1/63%, Drugs 3.9/23%, Firearms 7.2/47%, Hacking 4.0/74%, Kill 2.1/4%, SocialViolence 1.1/10%, SelfHarm 0.6/23% — outperforming FigStep-Pro by +6.2 avg HF and +40% ASR in Bombs. MiniGPT-4-7B reaches Hacking 95% ASR; LLaVA-1.5-13B reaches BE 100% ASR. Text-only JOOD (Eq.1) jailbreaks GPT-4 at 13% Bombs ASR where all baselines scored 0%, and generalizes to safety-aligned GPT-4o and o1 which baselines failed to jailbreak. JOOD exclusively jailbroke 10/30 Bombs instructions baselines could not. Against system-prompt defense ASR only degraded 3% (63%->60%) vs FigStep-Pro -10%; against adaptive AdaShield defense JOOD still jailbroke >half of queries while baselines hardly succeeded.
notes: Measured ASR/HF -> grade A. Black-box, off-the-shelf transforms, defense-resistant. Jailbreaks reasoning model o1 — notable for frontier-model robustness gap.

label: OOD distribution-shift jailbreak of MLLM safety alignment
description: Safety alignment (RLHF / self-feedback) is fit to an in-distribution set of harmful inputs; transforming a harmful instruction into an out-of-distribution variant via off-the-shelf data transformations (text-mixing into coined words, image mixup/CutMix/ResizeMix with a benign auxiliary, OCR typography) shifts the harmful embedding outside the aligned distribution, inflating the model's uncertainty about malicious intent so safety guardrails do not fire while the model still answers the harmful request. Demonstrated on GPT-4, GPT-4V, o1/GPT-4o, MiniGPT-4, LLaVA-1.5. Resists system-prompt and adaptive (AdaShield) defenses.

name: JOOD (Jailbreak via Out-Of-Distribution-ifying transformations)

title: MLLM/LLM safety alignment does not generalize to OOD-transformed harmful inputs
description: Safety alignment of LLMs/MLLMs is trained on in-distribution harmful inputs and fails on out-of-distribution variants produced by simple data transformations (text word-mixing, image mixup/CutMix/ResizeMix with benign auxiliary content, typographic auxiliaries). The transformation raises model uncertainty so guardrails do not trigger, while the model still satisfies the harmful intent. Affects proprietary GPT-4/GPT-4V/o1/GPT-4o and open-source MiniGPT-4/LLaVA-1.5; survives system-prompt and AdaShield adaptive defenses.
affected: GPT-4, GPT-4V, o1, GPT-4o, MiniGPT-4-7B, LLaVA-1.5-13B

title: Vision-centric jailbreak: image as necessary scenario-construction component, not just a harmful-text trigger
summary: VisCo defines a new threat setting distinct from prior visual jailbreaks (typography/adversarial-noise) where the image only triggers unsafe behavior with vague/ambiguous intent. Here the image provides the essential content defining a realistic jailbreak scenario (e.g. for 'steal valuable items in the car', the image supplies the steps: identify car -> find valuable item -> how to steal). VisCo fabricates a deceptive multi-turn dialogue via 4 vision-focused strategies: (1) Image-Grounded Scenario Simulation (fictional narrative, e.g. crime novel), (2) Image Multi-Perspective Analysis (contrasting safety-vs-risk framing), (3) Iterative Image Interrogation (argumentative debate lowering caution), (4) Exploiting Image Hallucination (falsely attributing unsafe content to an auxiliary image to induce multimodal misinterpretation). Auxiliary images synthesized by Stable Diffusion 3.5; semantic refinement uses an uncensored Wizard-Vicuna-13B judge to obfuscate sensitive keywords by referencing in-image objects.
notes: Novel threat-node candidate multimodal.vision-centric-context-injection. Exploiting Image Hallucination strategy uniquely weaponizes multimodal misperception. Methodology framing -> grade B; ASR-specific finding below is grade A.

title: VisCo Attack reaches 85-91% ASR on GPT-4o/Gemini-2.0-Flash via fabricated multi-turn vision-centric context
summary: On MM-SafetyBench (Toxic 1-5, ASR%), VisCo vs QR-Attack(typography): GPT-4o 4.78/85.00% (vs 2.48/22.20%, +62.80pp), GPT-4o-mini 4.86/86.13% (+62.56pp), Gemini-2.0-Flash 4.88/91.07% (+60.00pp), InternVL2.5-78B 4.86/89.88% (+55.83pp). On SafeBench-Tiny vs FigStep: GPT-4o ASR 12%->76% (toxic 1.74->4.60), Gemini-2.0-Flash 54%->68%, InternVL2.5-78B 34%->84%. Ablation (GPT-4o, SafeBench-Tiny): full 50% ASR; w/o fabricated context drops to 36%, w/o refinement 42%; 4 dialogue rounds raise to 54%. A query counts as success only if any of 5 attempts scores 5 (highly harmful). Open-source Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct works as red-team assistant (68% vs 76% ASR), confirming transferability of the attack-generation pipeline.
notes: Measured ASR/toxic -> grade A. Black-box; LLM-as-attacker (Gemini-2.0-Flash-Thinking red-team assistant) + uncensored LLM-as-judge pipeline.

label: Vision-centric context-injection jailbreak of MLLMs
description: Attacker constructs a complete, realistic jailbreak scenario in which the target image is a necessary content component (supplying the harmful steps/cues) rather than a mere typographic/adversarial trigger, then injects a fabricated multi-turn deceptive dialogue history grounded in the image (scenario simulation, multi-perspective risk framing, iterative interrogation, or weaponized image hallucination) to relax the MLLM's safety constraints. Auxiliary synthesized images and uncensored-LLM-driven toxicity obfuscation further evade filters. Demonstrated on GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-2.0-Flash, InternVL2.5-78B, Qwen2.5-VL-72B, LLaVA-OV-7B.

name: VisCo (Visual Contextual) Attack

title: MLLM safety relaxed by fabricated image-grounded multi-turn context and weaponized image hallucination
description: MLLM safety alignment can be relaxed by a fabricated multi-turn dialogue history that is grounded in a target image and embeds harmful content as a contextually plausible, vision-centric scenario; the model's tendency to hallucinate/misinterpret auxiliary images is further exploited to falsely attribute unsafe content the model believes it already processed. Removing the fabricated context drops ASR from 50% to 36%, confirming context dependence. Affects GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-2.0-Flash, InternVL2.5-78B, Qwen2.5-VL-72B, LLaVA-OV-7B.
affected: GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-2.0-Flash, InternVL2.5-78B, Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct, LLaVA-OV-7B-Chat

title: Distributing jailbreak across image+suffix via iterative cross-modal interaction beats single-modal and naive multimodal attacks
summary: The paper shows MLLMs map visual features into language space, creating semantic gaps between modalities that the LLM safety checker cannot recognize, opening a larger risk space at the new-old-modality integration. Perturbing two modalities (Text&Image) jointly yields higher ASR than any single modality (e.g. MiniGPT-v2 surrogate -> LLaVA: Text&Image 78% vs Text 75% vs Image 46% ASR-G). However naive combination (GCG suffix + Visual-jailbreak image, no interaction) transfers poorly. The proposed method alternately uses one modality as supervised signal to optimize the other in the multimodal alignment space (Alg.3, iterative N rounds), distributing jailbreak information across adversarial image x' and suffix s'. The adversarial image shortens the required suffix (length 10 vs GCG's 20), lowering perplexity and detectability. Ablation: removing either modality optimization markedly drops ASR/ASR-G; the image strategy contributes more than the suffix strategy.
notes: Novel threat-node candidate multimodal.cross-modal-attack-distribution: splitting adversarial signal across modalities to evade per-modality defenses and reduce perplexity-detectability. ATLAS AML.T0043 (craft adversarial data) + AML.T0054 (jailbreak).

title: Universal adversarial image+suffix transfers across 17 MLLMs incl. InstructBLIP, Yi-VL-34B, CogVLM-17B
summary: White-box (Table II), 25-behaviors multiple-harmful test: LLaVA-7B Ours 88.0% test-ASR / 80.0% test-ASR-G (vs GCG 92.0/75.0; Visual-jailbreak 56.0/46.0); MiniGPT-v2-7B Ours 95.0/85.0 (vs GCG 88.0/77.0). Transfer-based (Tables III-IV, surrogate LLaVA-7B & MiniGPT-v2-7B): Ours reaches e.g. MiniGPT4-7B 95.0% ASR/64.0 ASR-G, InstructBLIP-7B 99.0/60.0, InstructBLIP-13B 99.0/63.0, mPLUG-Owl2-7B 77.0/73.0, CogVLM-17B 91.0/74.0, Yi-VL-6B 67.0/40.0. InstructBLIP shows notably higher ASR (weaker safety fine-tuning). Adversarial robustness increases with model size. Against larger Yi-VL-34B (Fig.5), the ensemble of LLaVA-7B+MiniGPT-7B universal samples and 20-token suffix raise ASR/ASR-G; multimodal in-context demonstrations also increase ASR for MiniCPM-v2.6 and Qwen2-VL as in-context sample count grows. ASR-G uses GPT-4 to verify the response actually fulfills the malicious instruction.
notes: Measured ASR/ASR-G across 17 MLLMs -> grade A. Universal + transferable. Multimodal in-context jailbreak (Fig.6) is an additional novel vector.

label: Cross-modal attack-information distribution jailbreak
description: Because MLLMs fuse visual features into the language space, safety risks hidden in the image modality are not recognized by the text-side safety checker, and the integration of new (image) and old (text) modalities opens a larger risk space. An attacker distributes a universal jailbreak signal across both an adversarial image and an adversarial text suffix via iterative cross-modal interaction (each modality supervises the other in the shared alignment space), which (a) beats single-modal attacks, (b) transfers across heterogeneous MLLMs, and (c) shortens the suffix to lower perplexity and evade detection. Demonstrated as universal/transferable across 17 MLLMs.

name: Multimodal Universal Jailbreak (iterative image-text interaction)

title: MLLM text-side safety checker fails to detect harm encoded in fused visual modality
description: MLLMs map visual features into the language domain via image-text alignment; the LLM's safety checker operates on the text side and cannot recognize harmful intent distributed into the image modality, leaving the new-old-modality integration space inadequately defended. A universal adversarial image paired with a short adversarial suffix, optimized by iterative cross-modal interaction, jailbreaks and transfers across many MLLMs while keeping suffix perplexity low to evade perplexity-based detection. Current defenses predominantly address single-modal risks only.
affected: LLaVA-7B/13B/34B, Yi-VL-6B/34B, MiniGPT4-7B, MiniGPT-v2-7B, InstructBLIP-7B/13B, mPLUG-Owl2-7B, MiniCPM-v2.5/v2.6, CogVLM-17B, Qwen2-VL, LLaVA-NeXT-13B

title: Cross-modal regularization synergizes image+text perturbations into a black-box universal targeted misprediction attack on LVLMs
summary: MMAS targets LVLM integrity (targeted misprediction) rather than harmful-content jailbreak. It crafts a universal, task-agnostic adversarial image (texture scale-constrained UAP via wavelet decomposition, l_inf <= 8/255, eta=16/255) and an embedding-space learnable text prompt perturbation (l_2 <= 0.5), jointly optimized in a black-box query setting (10-sample gradient approximation, 70,000 queries). The novelty is a cross-modal regularization R = ||grad_dv L . grad_dt L|| aligning the gradient directions of image and text perturbations so they reinforce rather than fight each other; ablation shows naive single-modality or unaligned combination underperforms (w/o image attack overall 0.681, w/o text 0.693, w/o joint-opt 0.793 vs full 0.872 on LLaVA/DALLE-3). Forces e.g. 'stop sign'+'proceed' -> 'go'; captioning 'a plane' -> 'a tiger eating meat'. Robust against JPEG compression, randomization, and diffusion-restoration defenses by design (maximizing disruptive impact).
notes: Novel threat-node candidate multimodal.cross-modal-synergy-perturbation: gradient-aligned synergy of image+text adversarial perturbations. Integrity/misprediction attack, distinct from jailbreak nodes. ATLAS AML.T0043 (craft adversarial data) + AML.T0015 (evade ML model). Safety-critical: autonomous driving (road-sign), content moderation evasion.

title: MMAS universal black-box attack reaches 38-50% ASR on Gemini-2.0, GPT-4o, Claude-3.5 where PGD/CroPA fail
summary: On commercial LVLMs (Table 4, SS=semantic similarity to target, ASR=attack success rate): MMAS Gemini-2.0 SS 0.576/ASR 0.413, GPT-4o SS 0.508/ASR 0.379, Claude-3.5 SS 0.645/ASR 0.496 — vastly exceeding PGD (ASR 0.013/0.006/0.024) and white-box CroPA (ASR 0.064/0.020/0.085). On open-source LVLMs (Table 1, overall semantic-similarity steering to target 'I am sorry'): LLaVA 0.883, MiniGPT-4 0.894, Flamingo 0.895, BLIP-2 0.849 (vs clean ~0.36-0.46). vs MF-Attack (Table 2, ImageNet-1k VQA ASR): MMAS mean 0.839 vs 0.646. vs CroPA (Table 3, OpenFlamingo MS-COCO ASR): MMAS universal overall 0.89 vs CroPA white-box 0.83. Transfers across datasets and across LVLM models (Table 6). More efficient than baselines: 6 min / 13.5 GB GPU vs CroPA 17 min / 31.6 GB. Scaling factor s_k=4 optimal.
notes: Measured ASR on commercial closed-source LVLMs -> grade A. Universal+transferable+defense-robust black-box attack. Note arXiv id 2605.26501 and AAAI-2026 dates are forward-dated in the PDF (^[ambiguous] re: exact publication timing) but content is self-consistent.

label: Cross-modal synergistic adversarial perturbation of LVLMs
description: An attacker jointly crafts an imperceptible universal adversarial image perturbation (texture/wavelet-constrained UAP) and an embedding-space text-prompt perturbation, and uses a cross-modal regularization term to align their gradient directions so the two perturbations synergize. The result is a black-box, universal (task-agnostic), transferable targeted-misprediction attack that steers LVLM outputs (image classification, captioning, VQA) toward an attacker-chosen target and resists input-preprocessing defenses (JPEG, randomization, diffusion restoration). Distinct from harmful-content jailbreak: it attacks model integrity, threatening safety-critical uses such as autonomous-driving road-sign interpretation and content-moderation evasion. Demonstrated on LLaVA, MiniGPT-4, Flamingo, BLIP-2, and commercial Gemini-2.0/GPT-4o/Claude-3.5.

name: MMAS (Multi-Modal Adversarial Synergy)

title: LVLMs steerable to attacker-chosen outputs by gradient-aligned image+text perturbations, robust to input preprocessing defenses
description: LVLMs are vulnerable to a universal, black-box, multi-modal adversarial attack that pairs a texture-constrained imperceptible image UAP with an embedding-space text-prompt perturbation, aligned via cross-modal regularization. The attack consistently steers classification, captioning, and VQA outputs to a target, transfers across datasets and models, and survives JPEG compression, input randomization, and diffusion-restoration defenses. Affects open-source LLaVA/MiniGPT-4/Flamingo/BLIP-2 and commercial Gemini-2.0/GPT-4o/Claude-3.5, posing risk to autonomous driving and content moderation.
affected: LLaVA, MiniGPT-4, Flamingo (OpenFlamingo), BLIP-2, Gemini-2.0, GPT-4o, Claude-3.5

title: X-Transfer: a single UAP achieving cross-data/domain/model/task 'super transferability' against CLIP via efficient surrogate scaling
summary: X-Transfer is the first attack to demonstrate super transferability — one UAP transfers across data, domains, models, and tasks simultaneously. The key technique is efficient surrogate scaling: instead of a fixed surrogate ensemble, it treats each of N candidate CLIP encoders as a multi-armed-bandit arm and uses UCB sampling to dynamically select only k surrogates per optimization step (k=4/8/16 for Base/Mid/Large search spaces of N=16/32/64), with reward = loss signal (less-fooled encoders prioritized). This cuts cost to ~k/N of standard scaling (e.g. 0.3 vs 8.0 GPU-days at k=1) while super transferability scales with N. A generic embedding-space adversarial objective keeps it agnostic to encoder architecture/embedding-dim/training objective. UCB beats random sampling (66.9%) and epsilon-greedy (69.0%) at 69.2% ASR. ViT-based and large/diverse-pretrained (MetaCLIP/DFN/Merged2B) encoders are selected most and pose the greatest UAP threat. Both non-targeted UAPs (degrade VLMs, induce hallucination) and Targeted UAPs (TUAPs, steer VLM output to attacker text e.g. 'inject a computer virus') are produced; perturbations encode discernible semantic features via CLIP concept-blending.
notes: Novel threat-node candidate multimodal.foundation-encoder-super-transfer: shared CLIP backbone as a transferable single-point-of-failure across the VLM ecosystem (supply-chain-like). ATLAS AML.T0044 (full ML model access of surrogate) + AML.T0043 (craft adversarial data) + AML.T0015 (evade ML model).

title: X-Transfer UAPs/TUAPs compromise black-box CLIP encoders and downstream large VLMs (OF-3B, LLaVA-7B, MiniGPT4, BLIP2)
summary: Zero-shot classification non-targeted ASR (Table 1, avg over 9 black-box victim CLIP encoders, eps=12/255): X-Transfer Large ImageNet 63.4%, Cars 64.6%, GTSRB 89.4%, Avg(ZS) 75.6%, MSCOCO text-retrieval TR@1 71.8%, image-retrieval IR@1 65.8% — far above best baselines (Meta-UAP/C-PGC/ETU) and the N=1 vanilla (Avg 48.4). Large VLM captioning(CIDEr)/VQA ASR (Table 2): X-Transfer Large on BLIP2 MSCOCO 64.1%, OK-VQA 53.7%, VizWiz 67.3%; OF-3B MSCOCO 53.3%; LLaVA-7B OK-VQA 31.5%; MiniGPT4 MSCOCO 28.6% — consistently best overall, despite none of these CLIP encoders or VLMs being in the surrogate search space (strict black-box). ASR scales with surrogate search-space size N; even k=1 selection achieves near-best. Adversarial training is not robust to these UAPs and does not transfer to L2/patch perturbations.
notes: Measured ASR on black-box CLIP encoders and downstream VLMs -> grade A. Real-world threat: adversaries exploit the large pool of public open-source CLIP encoders to attack deployed VLMs. X-TransferBench released as open UAP/TUAP collection.

label: Super-transferable adversarial attack on shared foundation (CLIP) encoders
description: CLIP image encoders are a shared backbone across many downstream large VLMs (LLaVA, Flamingo, BLIP2, MiniGPT-4). An adversary exploits the large public pool of open-source CLIP encoders as surrogates (selected efficiently via multi-armed-bandit/UCB scaling) to craft a single Universal Adversarial Perturbation with 'super transferability' — transferring across data, domains, models, and tasks at once — that degrades or steers (via targeted UAPs) downstream VLMs in a strict black-box setting, resisting adversarial training. A foundation-encoder single-point-of-failure / supply-chain-style risk across the VLM ecosystem, threatening safety-critical deployments (autonomous driving, content moderation).

name: X-Transfer (super-transferable UAP/TUAP via surrogate scaling)

title: Shared CLIP encoders admit super-transferable UAPs that propagate to downstream VLMs in black-box
description: Because CLIP encoders are widely reused as the vision backbone of downstream VLMs and a large pool of CLIP variants is publicly available as surrogates, a single Universal Adversarial Perturbation can be optimized (via efficient UCB-based surrogate scaling) to transfer simultaneously across data, domains, models, and tasks, degrading or steering (targeted UAP) black-box victim CLIP encoders and downstream VLMs (OF-3B, LLaVA-7B, MiniGPT4, BLIP2) that were never in the surrogate set. Adversarial training is not robust to these UAPs. Constitutes a foundation-model/supply-chain-level vulnerability of the VLM ecosystem.
affected: CLIP (ViT-L/14, ViT-B/16, ViT-B/32, RN50, RN101, SigLIP, EVA-CLIP, CLIPA, MetaCLIP, DFN, Merged2B), OpenFlamingo-3B, LLaVA-7B, MiniGPT-4, BLIP-2

title: Red teaming should target product safety specifications with realistic threat models, not abstract social biases
summary: Scale AI argues most LLM red-teaming submissions mis-prioritize: tests should elicit violations of a specific product's safety spec (defined by deployment context, tools, regulations) rather than abstract ethical principles. Risk is contextual to product and use case, so vague notions like 'financial misuse' must become testable, scenario-grounded targets with a clear task and evaluation metric (moving from keyword matching to rubric-based harm classification).
notes: Position paper; claim is normative not measured.

title: Multi-turn attacks and realistic threat models (limited-query black-box, fine-tunable white-box) should be prioritized
summary: The paper argues defenses against single-turn jailbreaks do not generalize to multi-turn ones, and single-turn attacks are easier to patch via input/output filters. Realistic black-box attacks should assume limited query access (deployers can ban users); realistic white-box attacks should assume fine-tuning capability since weight access generally suffices to remove safeguards. It also maps distinct realistic threat models for audio assistants (prosodic obfuscation, codeswitching), video generators (harm evolving across frames), and autonomous agents (expanded attack surface, MCP vulns, multi-agent collusion).
notes: Threat-model taxonomy across four product types.

title: Safeguard research must move to system level: trajectory/user monitoring, rapid response, and red-teaming the monitor
summary: The paper contends model-level refusal is insufficient and harm should be classified over entire output trajectories and across user histories, enabling system-level mitigations (detecting/banning malicious users, sybil detection, rapid patch of newly found jailbreaks). It introduces red-teaming the monitor: red teams should attempt to complete an adversarial task without being detected (a sabotage experiment), stress-testing CoT-only monitors. It also cautions against over-trusting ASR scores from non-randomized campaigns.
notes: ^[inferred] mapping of 'sabotage experiment' to frontier-detection.sabotage-evaluation.

title: AI red teaming has narrowed to model-level flaws, abandoning its sociotechnical critical-thinking origin
summary: Majumdar et al. argue that despite red teaming's military and cybersecurity heritage as a strategic critical-thinking exercise, AI red teaming has collapsed into narrow technical probing of genAI models, treated as post-build acceptance testing rather than pre-emptive critique. They note most testing remains English-only, ignores insider risk, and that red teamers experience psychological harm and lack non-technical (linguistic/legal/ethical) training. They advocate violet teaming and multifunctional teams.
notes: rainbow-team color: violet/purple teaming emphasis.

title: Two-level red teaming: macro (system) across seven lifecycle stages + micro (model)
summary: The paper proposes operationalizing AI red teaming at a macro level spanning the full development lifecycle and a micro level on the model. Macro-level red teaming applies distinct critical-thinking probes at seven stages: inception (challenge AI-solutionism/problem framing), design (interface/architecture systemic vulns), data (poisoning, representativeness, lineage), development (supply-chain/dependency risk, fine-tuning), deployment (distribution/update control points), maintenance (model drift, alert fatigue), and retirement (data retention/destruction). A dedicated blue team should co-operate throughout.
notes: Seven-stage lifecycle framework is the paper's core contribution.

title: ToolLeak: implicit tool-argument generation exfiltrates coding-agent system prompts, bypassing refusal
summary: Xie et al. discover ToolLeak: an attacker registers a malicious MCP tool whose required argument (e.g. 'note') is the agent's internal context (system prompt). During benign tool-argument generation the LLM populates the field with the system prompt without any explicit 'reveal your instructions' request, so refusal alignment is bypassed. Across five emulated backends (Claude-Sonnet-4/4.5, Grok-4, GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-pro) ToolLeak yields max valid prompt leakage and succeeds on 19/25 real agent-LLM pairs; Gemini-2.5-pro resists via output content filtering. ToolLeak attains 0.997 semantic similarity / 0.164 EED on Sonnet-4, beating Naive/Ignore/Completion/Remember/PLeak baselines.
notes: Measured results across 25 agent-LLM pairs; reference ground-truth from public system-prompt repo.

title: Two-channel prompt injection (tool description + tool return) achieves RCE on every tested coding agent-LLM pair
summary: Phase 2 introduces a two-channel prompt-injection: a lure in the tool-description channel steers tool selection, then injected procedural instructions in the higher-salience tool-return channel hijack tool-invocation, propelling the agent to run an attacker command (e.g. curl|bash). It achieves the highest attack success rate and successful RCE on all 25 agent-LLM pairs, outperforming IPI-RCE (success 0) and a single-channel RCE-1 baseline. A case study shows Claude Code (Sonnet-4.5) overriding a Haiku-4.5 guard model that flagged the command as UNSAFE. Root cause: no instruction/data separation; tool returns are treated as executable instructions. Also discloses incomplete-display vulns in Cursor/Windsurf (XML-tag content hidden in UI but processed by the model).
notes: RCE success measured on every agent-LLM pair; guard-model evasion demonstrated. ATLAS ids ^[inferred].

title: 36% of AI vendors lack a disclosure policy and only 18% mention AI risks; jailbreaking/hallucination usually out-of-scope
summary: Analyzing 264 AI vendors' VDP/BBP policies, the study finds 36% have no disclosure mechanism and just 18% explicitly address AI security. Vulnerabilities framed as security-goal violations (data access, authorization, authentication) are most consistently in-scope (>80-91%), while jailbreaking (mentioned 11 times, eligible in only 3) and hallucination (17%, eligibility ~14%) are most often excluded, justified as 'multi-turn', 'a user's own session', or 'infeasible to fully mitigate'. AI-mention policies are more complete (e.g. Safe-Harbor +48%, Service-Commitment +34%). The 'abuse risks inherent to product features' framing signals vendors treating model behavior as non-security.
notes: Measured policy-coverage statistics across 264 vendors; aligned to MIT AI Risk Taxonomy and AIID (n=320 incidents).

title: Three AI-vendor disclosure profiles (proactive/silent/restrictive); policies lag incidents and academic research
summary: The longitudinal analysis (205 AI-related policy changes across 46 vendors, 2018-2025) classifies vendors into proactive clarification (n=46: active supporters, integrationists, back-channel), silent (n=115), and restrictive (n=103). Scope-In and vulnerability-type definitions are the most frequently changed elements, indicating vendors continually adjust which product features are testable as AI matures. Alignment results show vendors address AI vulnerability disclosure later than academia and real-world incidents, highlighting a governance gap and a need for standardized reporting, safe harbors, and supply-chain relays for AI CVD/VDP.
notes: Profiles and longitudinal change counts are measured; standards mapping ^[inferred].

title: Automated red-teaming framework covers six frontier threat categories via meta-prompting + evolutionary mutation
summary: Wei et al. present an automated red-teaming framework with four modules (seed collection, meta-prompting attack generation, three-level vulnerability detection, evaluation/reporting). Category-specific meta-prompts plus an evolutionary mutation algorithm (semantic/syntactic/context/adversarial operators) generate diverse attacks across six categories: reward hacking, deceptive alignment, data exfiltration, sandbagging, inappropriate tool use, and chain-of-thought manipulation. Detection combines lexical pattern dictionaries, all-mpnet-base-v2 semantic similarity, and behavioral analysis, with weighted convex scoring.
notes: ^[ambiguous] Target GPT-OSS-20B described as 'hypothetical'; framework design solid but some reported numbers may be illustrative.

title: Reported 47 vulnerabilities (3.9x over manual) on GPT-OSS-20B; deceptive alignment most prevalent; defense cost-benefit analyzed
summary: On GPT-OSS-20B the framework reports 47 distinct vulnerabilities (21 high-severity, 12 novel) versus 12 for manual experts, a 3.9x discovery rate (5.9/hr), 6/6 category coverage, 11% false-positive rate, 89% reproducibility. Deceptive alignment yielded the most findings (11), then reward hacking (10) and inappropriate tool use (8). A defense evaluation (input filtering, output monitoring, model hardening, system-level protection, and combinations) reports per-category block rates and a cost-benefit score, with full integration (Combination B) achieving the highest block rates (~89-98%) but 82% latency and 71% compute overhead, illustrating the robustness-efficiency trade-off.
notes: ^[ambiguous] results on a stated 'hypothetical' model; treat magnitudes as reported, not independently verified.

title: Co-RedTeam: security-aware multi-agent framework reaches >60% exploit / 63.7% ASR via execution-grounded discovery+exploitation
summary: Co-RedTeam decomposes automated vulnerability red teaming into a Discovery stage (Analysis + Critique agents grounded in CWE/OWASP and code-browsing tools building evidence chains) and an Iterative Exploitation stage (Planner, Validation, Execution, Evaluation agents running in an isolated Docker env with a plan-execute-evaluate loop capped at 20 iterations). On CyBench/BountyBench/CyberGym with Gemini-3-pro it reaches 63.7% ASR on CyBench, 65.0% exploit and 20.0% detect on BountyBench, and 37.3% on CyberGym, beating OpenHands, C-Agent, VulTrail and RepoAudit. Method couples code-aware static reasoning with real execution feedback and a layered long-term memory.
notes: Results read directly from Table 1; ablation (Table 2) shows removing execution feedback collapses CyBench ASR 59.1%->17.5%.

title: Execution feedback and layered long-term memory are the load-bearing components of agentic vuln exploitation
summary: Ablations on Co-RedTeam isolate which design choices matter: removing execution feedback is the single most damaging change (CyBench 59.1%->17.5%, BountyBench exploit 60.0%->12.5%), confirming that precise validation fundamentally requires execution rather than static single-shot generation. A three-layer long-term memory (vulnerability-pattern, strategy, technical-action) drives sustained improvement; on CyberGym, warm-start evolving memory outperforms cold-start, static and no-memory, and removing memory drops CyberGym 31.5%->22.6%. Validation and critique agents primarily protect exploitation reliability and detection precision respectively.
notes: Memory evolution effect from Figure 3; ablation deltas from Table 2.

title: TEE-RedBench: LLM TEE security advisors exhibit architecturally consequential failures (attestation overclaim, boundary confusion, mitigation hallucination)
summary: TEE-RedBench red teams ChatGPT-5.2 and Claude Opus-4.6 as TEE (SGX/TrustZone) security advisors with 208 prompts across six families and a dual-track rubric (0-14) scoring accuracy, completeness, groundedness, uncertainty calibration, policy compliance, safe helpfulness and misuse resistance. It targets high-consequence failure modes: boundary confusion (wrong TCB/trust boundary), attestation overclaim (attestation 'proves' confidentiality under microarchitectural leakage), mitigation hallucination (invented patches/CVEs/config knobs), over-generalized defenses and unsafe completion. Family reliability is model-dependent: Claude is stronger on premise-setting families (architecture, attestation, threat modeling); ChatGPT scores higher on mitigations/attack-awareness but Claude's overconfident-error rate spikes on those families.
notes: Failure-mode taxonomy from Table 3; family-level rubric scores and overconfident-error rates from Table 4. ^[inferred] sector tags from confidential-computing deployment context.

title: LLM security-advisor failures transfer up to 12.02% across assistants; secure-architecture pipeline cuts prevalence 80.62%
summary: Prompt-induced failures in LLM TEE advisors are not purely idiosyncratic: a non-trivial subset of prompts that break one assistant also break the other under some paraphrase, with transferability up to 12.02% (e.g., mitigation hallucination and tool-output misinterpretation show the highest transfer, the latter being an agentic failure). This matters operationally because reusable prompt templates can propagate the same attestation/boundary mistakes across providers, limiting 'use a second model as a check' as a defense. An LLM-in-the-loop secure-architecture pipeline (policy gate -> retrieval grounding -> structured template -> verifier/checks -> human approval) reduces worst-case failure prevalence by 80.62%, though residual cross-assistant transfer remains, so guardrails reduce but do not prove correctness.
notes: Transferability values from Table 5 (Eq.4); defense-prevalence reduction from Table 6 (Eq.5). Agentic failure indicators (f_SEL, f_GRND, f_INTERP) defined in Preliminaries.

title: Structured-reasoning LLM-as-a-Judge beats encoder classifiers and safety LLMs for low-latency prompt-attack detection (F1 up to 0.871)
summary: A taxonomy-guided LLM-as-a-Judge that forces framing-stripping intent decomposition, safety-signal verification, harm assessment and mandatory self-reflection before a verdict (mapped to a 0.0-1.0 confidence score) reliably detects jailbreaks/prompt-injection under live latency. On a curated 929-sample set (770 benign incl. false-positive traps, 159 ART/PAIR adversarial) of Singapore public-service chatbot traffic, LLM judges beat encoder classifiers (PromptGuard 0.226, ProtectAI 0.355 F1), specialized safety LLMs (gpt-oss-safeguard 0.804, Qwen3Guard 0.539) and AWS Bedrock Guardrails (0.120). Best single judge gpt-5.1 F1 0.871; gemini-2.0-flash-lite-001 (deployed in production) reaches 0.844 at 1.5s. Non-thinking mode beats thinking mode; structured output beats OpenAI-Guardrails-style direct verdicts.
notes: Detector comparison from Table 2 (tau=0.5); adversarial prompts generated via PAIR with GPT-4o red-team/eval. 'content-safety' used as safety tag per sector vocab context. ^[ambiguous] safety.content-safety is a sector, not a safety.* node — primary safety tag is misuse-risk.

title: Mixture-of-Models LLM judges do not reliably beat the best single judge; gains are narrow and combination-dependent
summary: Aggregating multiple LLM judges via weighted-score Mixture-of-Models (grid-searched weights+threshold maximizing F1) yields only modest, non-guaranteed improvements for prompt-attack detection. Across 5-fold CV, MoM frequently underperforms its strongest sub-combination; larger ensembles (quads) are more likely to degrade, and gains concentrate in a few complementary pairs (e.g., gpt-5-mini + claude-haiku-4.5 +0.0239; gpt-5.1 + gpt-5-mini F1 0.8964). Weaker models can still help when they add complementary signal. Unlike traditional classifier ensembles, LLM-judge ensemble effectiveness depends on careful model selection rather than ensemble size.
notes: MoM incremental F1 deltas from Table 3.

title: RL-trained general-purpose red-team model (Qwen3-8B) generalizes to out-of-domain adversarial goals without a training-time evaluator
summary: NVIDIA trains a general-purpose red-team model via GRPO (VeRL) so it generalizes to arbitrary natural-language adversarial goals, including goals with no evaluator available at training time. Adversarial goals come from garak; a seed LLM (Qwen3-235B-A22B) generates goal examples, disguise/jailbreak methods and LLM-as-a-judge rubrics to build 36,220 diverse attack-generation input prompts. A three-tier reward (-0.2 malformed, 0.0 well-formed-but-failed, 1.0 well-formed successful) drives RL. Fine-tuned Qwen3-8B reaches 85% in-domain ASR (vs 33.89% zero-shot) and 29.35% OOD ASR (vs 20.87%), evaluated with LLM-as-a-judge rubrics in-domain and garak detectors OOD against Qwen3-8B and Gemma-3-12b-it. RL did not auto-improve attack diversity and could overfit OOD goals when seed prompts drift from the detector's target behavior.
notes: ASR figures from Section 5 / Figures 2-3. In-domain goals incl. DAN, code-adversarial (Malware Gen, Raw ANSI, Pkg-Hallucination); OOD goals evaluated with garak detectors. ^[ambiguous] content-safety is a sector tag, retained as topic-level safety descriptor.

title: Decoupling red-team training from goal-specific evaluators enables coverage of underrepresented adversarial goals (malware, exfiltration, code exploits)
summary: Prior automated red teaming optimizes against content-safety classifiers, biasing red-team models toward profanity/toxicity and leaving agentic/code-related misuse (malware generation, data exfiltration via URI variables, package-hallucination, exploit-in-tool-call) poorly covered. By using seed-generated LLM-as-a-judge rubrics rather than a fixed evaluator, the pipeline explicitly enumerates and rewards diverse adversarial goals and demonstrates that a safety-trained instruction model (not an uncensored one) can be turned into an effective red-team model. Detailed attack-generation input prompts plus diverse rubric rewards act as regularizers, avoiding the reward-hacking seen when training directly against a single garak detector.
notes: ^[inferred] linkage between evaluator-free design and code/agentic-goal coverage synthesized from Sections 2-3 and OOD goal list; reward-hacking observation stated in Section 5 and Appendix E.

title: Agentic AI red-teaming agent collapses operator workflow from weeks to hours via natural-language objectives over a 45+ attack / 450+ transform catalog
summary: Dreadnode's agent reframes AI red teaming from library-centered to operator-centered: an operator states a natural-language objective in a TUI and the agent autonomously selects from 45+ attacks (TAP, PAIR, GAP, Crescendo, Rainbow, GPTFuzzer, AutoDAN-Turbo, Persona Hijack, Echo Chamber, Reward Hacking, etc.), composes 450+ transforms (skeleton-key, DAN, role-play, low-resource translation, MCP/multi-agent/exfiltration), runs 130+ scorers, and emits findings with automatic severity classification and compliance mapping (OWASP LLM Top 10, OWASP Agentic, MITRE ATLAS, NIST AI RMF, SAIF). It is the first unified interface probing both traditional ML (SimBA/NES/ZOO/HopSkipJump adversarial examples) and generative AI (jailbreaks) plus multimodal. The five-phase lifecycle (define goal -> run -> analyze -> report -> iterate/harden) supports progressive hardening.
notes: Attack/transform/scorer counts and compliance frameworks from Section 3.2 and Table 1. ATLAS technique AML.T0054 ^[inferred] from gradient/suffix and jailbreak coverage.

title: Llama Scout case study: ~85% ASR with severity up to 1.0, most-severe finding via skeleton-key safety-researcher persona
summary: Red teaming Meta's Llama Scout from natural-language objectives (e.g., 'generate ransomware deployment guides'), the agent achieves ~85% attack success rate using Tree of Attacks with Pruning and advanced prompt transforms, with zero human-developed code. The most severe finding (score 1.0, Critical) emerges from a skeleton-key transform that tricks the model into adopting a fabricated 'safety researcher' persona, showing sophisticated social-engineering persona attacks bypass safety training. Selected adversarial findings span production-grade shellcode loaders with AMSI bypass, credential-stealing browser extensions, buffer-overflow exploits, stalking/surveillance manuals, self-harm and CBRN-adjacent (lethal gas, illicit drug manufacturing) content, spanning multiple harm categories with detailed compliance mappings.
notes: ASR, severity and skeleton-key persona from Abstract/Section 1.2 and Appendix A finding list; TAP attack named explicitly. ATLAS AML.T0054 ^[inferred].

title: DEEPTRAP discovers contextual agent vulnerabilities via reward-guided beam search over execution context
summary: DEEPTRAP formulates adversarial context manipulation in OpenClaw agents as a black-box trajectory-level optimization that injects an admissible payload into a contextual channel (memory entry, skill file, auxiliary artifact, config) while the user instruction stays benign. Method combines a multi-objective reward (risk realization J_risk, task preservation J_task, stealth J_stealth), reward-guided beam search with depth-dependent pruning, and reflection-based deep probing that conditions the proposal model on accumulated successes/failures. Demonstrates that final-response evaluation is insufficient: unsafe behavior emerges in intermediate tool calls/file writes while the user-facing task still completes.
notes: Method = reward-guided beam search + reflection deep probing; benchmark = 42 cases / 6 risk classes / 7 scenarios. ^[inferred] benchmark slug coined from paper since unnamed.

title: Six contextual vulnerability classes in agentic execution: harness hijacking, privacy leakage, unauthorized execution, supply-chain, tool abuse, encoding obfuscation
summary: DEEPTRAP enumerates six contextual risk classes for OpenClaw agents: harness hijacking (context steers agent toward attacker objectives, e.g. poisoned PLAYBOOK creating etc/cron.d/health_check), privacy leakage (most consistently activated, AGS up to 0.97), unauthorized execution, supply-chain compromise (via skills/packages/deps), tool abuse (trojan style checker embeds BLOG_API_KEY/CMS_TOKEN secrets into output), and encoding obfuscation. Across nine target models, Qwen3.5-Plus/DeepSeek-v4-Flash/Pro show high attack grading scores (AGS) with high utility grading (UGS), while Claude-Sonnet-4.6 shows lower AGS, indicating stronger resistance to contextual attacks.
notes: Results: privacy leakage most-activated; harness-hijack/encoding-obfuscation highly effective; Claude-Sonnet-4.6 most resistant. Iteration raises AGS from 0.65 to 0.75 over 5 rounds.

title: Hierarchical LLM-planner + RL-controller red teaming sustains multi-stage kill-chain attacks where standalone LLMs fail
summary: A hybrid red-teaming agent decouples strategic planning (frozen LLM emitting MITRE ATT&CK-tactic intent every 20 steps) from tactical execution (PPO RL controller acting every step over a 10-action ATT&CK-aligned space), with 4-layer kill-chain-aligned reward shaping (environment, milestone, constraint, intent-alignment) and optional Reflexion memory. Evaluated in CybORG CAGE 4 against an H-MARL Expert blue team over 500-step episodes. Standalone LLM agents (14 models, 0.6B-70B incl. Foundation-Sec-8B, DeepHat-7B, DeepSeek-R1) fail to sustain multi-stage campaigns due to long-horizon state-tracking and action-repetition limits; the hybrid architecture is needed for robust autonomous adversary emulation against AI-enabled SOAR defenders.
notes: Method = frozen LLM planner (intent every 20 steps) + PPO controller; reward shaping over 4 layers. Metrics = episode compromise rate (ECR), attack action count (AAC), avg host discovery (AHD).

title: Standalone LLM cyber agents underperform RL by ~5x reward and exhibit action-repetition loops in long-horizon ops
summary: Citing prior CAGE-4 evidence, the paper documents that all-LLM blue teams achieve mean rewards ~5x worse than all-RL teams (-2,547 vs -493) while operating at ~1/104th decision speed, struggle with precise state tracking over hundreds of sequential decisions, exhibit action-repetition loops, and cannot learn from trial-and-error within an operational context. Domain-specialized small models (Foundation-Sec-8B, CyberPal 2.0, DeepHat) narrow the gap via security fine-tuning (fine-tuning a base vs instruction-tuned model yields 2.7x larger gains), but RL-based offensive red-team agents remain under-explored (only ~8 of 160 surveyed agentic-security papers use RL). Motivates frozen-LLM-strategy + trainable-RL-tactics hybrids.
notes: Reward gap (-2,547 vs -493) and 8/160 RL stat are cited from prior work (evidence_grade B for those). Foundation-Sec-8B / DeepHat-7B are domain-specialized offensive models.

title: Multi-agent actor-critic LLM system classifies CVEs into Non-AI / AI-Supply-Chain / Adversarial-AI and maps to NIST AI 100-2e2025
summary: An actor-critic multi-agent system (CVE Classifier Agent + NISTAML Mapper Agent, each with classifier/mapper actor + critic reviewer sub-agents, GPT-4o-mini, capped at 3 loops) classifies CVEs into Non-AI, AI Supply Chain, and Adversarial AI, then maps Adversarial-AI CVEs to the NIST AI 100-2e2025 (NISTAML) adversarial-ML taxonomy (Availability/Integrity/Privacy/Misuse Violations + Supply-Chain Attacks). On a stratified validation sample, accuracy is 76.6% (Adversarial-AI recall 1.0 / precision 0.524; Non-AI precision 1.0 / recall 0.775). The pipeline operationalizes mapping unstructured CVE descriptions to a standards taxonomy via LLM judges.
notes: Method = actor-critic multi-agent (Google ADK, GPT-4o-mini). Datasets = ~128k CVEs (2021-2025), NISTAML taxonomy. Validation via Cochran stratified sample, confusion matrix.

title: Adversarial-AI share of AI CVEs grew from 0% (2021) to ~50% (2025); many NISTAML subcategories empty/under-reported
summary: Of ~128,000 CVEs (2021-2025), ~1.57% are AI-relevant: ~1.05% AI Supply Chain and ~0.52% Adversarial AI. AI Supply Chain dominated early (100% of AI CVEs in Q1 2021) but Adversarial AI's quarterly share rose steadily, exceeding supply-chain in Q2 2024 / Q1 2025 (reaching ~47.5-55%). Within Adversarial AI, Integrity Violations (NISTAML.02) and Privacy Compromises (NISTAML.03, esp. .036 Leaking Information from User) dominate; Misuse and Supply-Chain-Attacks (NISTAML.05, <3%) are lowest. Several subcategories (Clean-label/Data Poisoning .012/.013, Indirect Prompt Injection .015/.016) have zero CVEs, signalling under-research or under-reporting of adversarial-AI attack vectors.
notes: Empty subcategories = NISTAML.012/.013/.015/.016 = coverage gap signal for standards analyst. Membership-inference / model-extraction may be 'shadow CVEs' / security-by-obscurity.

title: Comiter taxonomy: AI attacks split into input attacks and poisoning attacks, exploiting inherent ML limitations not code bugs
summary: The Belfer report defines an 'AI attack' as adversarial manipulation exploiting inherent limitations of ML algorithms (not fixable code bugs), dividing attacks into input attacks (perturbing inputs at inference, e.g. tape on a stop sign making a self-driving car see a green light; imperceptible digital perturbations) and poisoning attacks (corrupting training data or model to install backdoors triggerable at the attacker's chosen time/place). It argues AI attacks expand the cyberattack surface to physical objects and data, require no traditional 'hacking' or even a computer, and cannot be solved with existing cybersecurity toolkits, constituting a distinct new vertical of vulnerability with offensive-weaponization potential.
notes: 2019 policy report (evidence_grade C = opinion/policy synthesis). Input attack = evasion/adversarial-example; poisoning attack = backdoor. Foundational framing for later AML threat taxonomies.

title: AI Security Compliance: PCI-style mandated programs across planning, implementation, and mitigation stages
summary: Comiter proposes 'AI Security Compliance' programs modeled on PCI compliance for payments, to reduce attack risk and impact by driving best-practice adoption: considering attack risks/surfaces when deploying AI, adopting IT-reforms that raise attack cost, and creating attack-response plans. Requirements span three lifecycle stages (planning, implementation, mitigation) and five most-affected sectors (content filters, military, law enforcement, commercial AI-fication of human tasks, civil society). Regulators should mandate compliance for government use and as a pre-condition for selling AI to government, mandatory for high-risk private uses and optional for low-risk uses to avoid stifling innovation. An early precursor to NIST AI RMF / EU AI Act risk-tiered governance.
notes: ^[inferred] linkage to NIST AI RMF / EU AI Act as later realizations of the risk-tiered mandate idea (report predates both).

title: AI security is an enabling requirement, not a standalone ethics principle, and can conflict with explainability/privacy
summary: Surveying AI ethics guides (Asilomar, UNESCO, Montreal, IEEE EAD, EU HLEG, AI4People), security is rarely a standalone principle but a necessary-but-not-sufficient enabler subsumed under non-maleficence and privacy. The paper argues this oversimplifies: stronger security can trade off against explainability (XAI methods increase attack susceptibility) and exploiting an AI vulnerability can be ethically justified (e.g. anti-surveillance facial-recognition evasion via adversarial accessories, or Nightshade data poisoning to protect copyright). Security viewed as a deployer obligation to those affected, vs the deployer's CIA-of-own-assets lens, can diverge across stakeholders.
standards: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI
EU HLEG Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI
notes: Nightshade = prompt-specific poisoning against text-to-image models reframed as a defensive tool. Dual-use framing: vulnerability exploitation can be ethically legitimate.

title: Searching six incident repositories yields only ~6 fully-relevant AI-vulnerability incidents, exposing cataloguing gaps
summary: Applying a four-criteria '4I' relevance scheme (Incident, Intrusion, Impact, Intelligence) to six repositories (AIAAIC ~1400, AIID ~650, AVID <50, Where in the World is AI?, CISA KEV, EuRepoC), only 6 incidents fully satisfy all criteria (~27 partial, ~8 possible). Fully-relevant cases: Tay poisoning, Facebook COVID fact-check evasion, remoteli.io bot prompt-injection hijack, TikTok suicide-video moderation evasion, Chinese tax-system facial-recognition camera-hijack ($77M fraud), and PyTorch dependency-chain compromise. AVID conflates vulnerabilities/reports with placeholder text; KEV and EuRepoC yielded zero AI-relevant hits. The small count reflects definitional ambiguity of 'AI vulnerability', inconsistent reporting, under-disclosure, and keyword-search limits, so real-world impact of AI vulns cannot yet be reliably gauged.
notes: Search Nov 2023. remoteli.io = prompt-injection-to-arbitrary-instruction; PyTorch chain = supply-chain dependency poisoning; tax-system = facial-recognition spoof for access control. KEV/EuRepoC zero AI hits = traditional-DB blind spot.

title: Ollama 'Probllama' RCE via unvalidated model-pull digest path traversal (CVE-2024-37032)
description: Ollama before 0.1.34 does not validate the format of the digest (sha256 with 64 hex digits) when getting the model path, mishandling cases such as fewer/more than 64 hex digits or an initial ../ substring. A crafted OCI manifest pulled from a rogue registry lets an attacker write arbitrary files (e.g. /etc/ld.so.preload) via the /api/pull endpoint, yielding remote code execution on the inference host.
affected: Ollama < 0.1.34 (LLM serving daemon)

title: Ollama Zip-Slip RCE via directory traversal in GGUF zip import (CVE-2024-7773)
description: Ollama 0.1.37's parseFromZipFile function in server/model.go does not check for directory-traversal sequences (../) in filenames inside an imported zip archive, allowing an attacker to write arbitrary files and achieve remote code execution.
affected: Ollama 0.1.37 (model zip import path)

title: vLLM memory corruption / RCE via unsafe prompt-embedding tensor deserialization (CVE-2025-62164)
description: In vLLM 0.10.2 to before 0.11.1 the Completions API loads user-supplied serialized prompt-embedding tensors with torch.load() without sufficient validation. Because PyTorch 2.8.0 disables sparse-tensor integrity checks by default, a maliciously crafted tensor bypasses bounds checks and triggers an out-of-bounds write during to_dense(), leading to denial-of-service and potentially RCE in the unauthenticated, network-exposed inference server.
affected: vLLM 0.10.2 to < 0.11.1 (Completions API endpoint)

title: PyTorch torch.load RCE despite weights_only=True (CVE-2025-32434)
description: PyTorch <= 2.5.1 contains a remote code execution vulnerability when loading a model with torch.load(weights_only=True). The legacy deserialization code path was not fully disabled under weights_only=True, so a crafted model file can still execute arbitrary Python during unpickling. This undermines the primary defense the ML ecosystem relied on for untrusted model loading. Patched in 2.6.0.
affected: PyTorch <= 2.5.1 (torch.load deserialization)

title: HuggingFace Transformers arbitrary code execution via pickle in load_repo_checkpoint (CVE-2024-3568)
description: huggingface/transformers allows arbitrary code execution through deserialization of untrusted data in the load_repo_checkpoint() function of TFPreTrainedModel. A malicious serialized payload embedded in a checkpoint file is unpickled during checkpoint loading, executing attacker-controlled code in the model-loading process.
affected: huggingface/transformers <= 4.38.x (load_repo_checkpoint)

title: Keras Model.load_model arbitrary code execution even with safe_mode=True (CVE-2025-1550)
description: Keras Model.load_model permits arbitrary code execution, even with safe_mode=True, through a manually constructed malicious .keras archive. The config in the archive can be crafted to invoke arbitrary callables on load, bypassing the safe-mode mitigation introduced to block Lambda-layer code execution.
affected: Keras 3.0.0 to < 3.8.0 (load_model / .keras archive)

title: TensorFlow/Keras unsafe YAML deserialization RCE in model_from_yaml (CVE-2021-37678)
description: TensorFlow and Keras can be tricked into arbitrary code execution when deserializing a Keras model from YAML, because model_from_yaml uses yaml.unsafe_load. An attacker supplying a malicious model YAML achieves code execution on load.
affected: TensorFlow < 2.6 / Keras (model_from_yaml)

title: LangChain 'LangGrinch' serialization-injection RCE / secret exfiltration (CVE-2025-68664)
description: Prior to LangChain core 0.3.81 and 1.2.5, the dumps()/dumpd() serialization functions do not escape free-form dictionaries containing 'lc' keys. Combined with the deserializer's trust of those keys, an attacker can inject a crafted object during (de)serialization to exfiltrate secrets or achieve remote code execution in LangChain-powered applications and agents.
affected: LangChain core < 0.3.81 and 1.0.0 to < 1.2.5 (dumps/dumpd)

title: LangChain JiraAPIWrapper arbitrary code execution via crafted input (CVE-2023-34540)
description: LangChain allows attackers to execute arbitrary code via crafted input passed to the JiraAPIWrapper component, which interpolates untrusted input into an evaluated expression. Part of a family of early LangChain chains/tools (LLMMathChain, APIChain) that reached eval()/exec() with model- or user-controlled content.
affected: LangChain (JiraAPIWrapper component, 2023 versions)

title: LlamaIndex arbitrary file read via path traversal in encode_image (CVE-2025-6209)
description: A path traversal vulnerability exists in run-llama/llama_index 0.12.27 to 0.12.40 in the encode_image function in generic_utils.py. By manipulating the image_path input an attacker reads arbitrary files on the server, including sensitive system files. Fixed in 0.12.41.
affected: llama_index 0.12.27 to 0.12.40 (encode_image)

title: ComfyUI-Impact-Pack path traversal to arbitrary file write / RCE (CVE-2024-21575)
description: ComfyUI-Impact-Pack is vulnerable to path traversal due to missing validation of the image.filename field in a POST request to the /upload/temp endpoint, resulting in arbitrary file writes that may, under some conditions, lead to remote code execution on the ComfyUI server.
affected: ComfyUI-Impact-Pack < 7.6.2 (/upload/temp endpoint)

title: Flowise WriteFileTool/ReadFileTool unrestricted file path leading to file R/W and RCE (CVE-2025-61913)
description: In Flowise before 3.0.8 the WriteFileTool and ReadFileTool do not restrict file path access, allowing an authenticated attacker to read and write arbitrary files on the host, potentially leading to remote command execution in the low-code LLM-agent builder.
affected: Flowise < 3.0.8 (WriteFileTool/ReadFileTool)

title: Flowise arbitrary code execution via crafted script to api/v1 (CVE-2024-31621)
description: Flowise prior to v1.8.1 allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code via a crafted script sent to the api/v1 component, an early auth/validation weakness in the agent-orchestration API surface.
affected: Flowise < 1.8.1 (api/v1 component)

title: mcp-remote OS command injection from malicious MCP server (CVE-2025-6514)
description: mcp-remote, a widely-used OAuth proxy connecting local MCP clients to remote MCP servers, is exposed to OS command injection when connecting to untrusted MCP servers: a crafted authorization_endpoint response URL is passed into the system shell, achieving remote code execution on the client. Affects 0.0.5 through 0.1.15. Demonstrates the MCP supply-chain trust problem where a malicious server compromises the client.
affected: mcp-remote 0.0.5 to 0.1.15 (MCP OAuth proxy client)

title: Serverless Framework MCP server command injection in list-projects tool (CVE-2025-69256)
description: A command injection vulnerability in the Serverless Framework built-in MCP server package (@serverless/mcp) arises from unsanitized input parameters passed to child_process.exec in the list-projects tool, enabling an attacker (via a malicious prompt/tool call) to inject arbitrary system commands on the host running the MCP server.
affected: @serverless/mcp (list-projects tool)

title: Ollama path-traversal file-existence disclosure in api/push (CVE-2024-39722)
description: Ollama before 0.1.46 exposes which files exist on the server via path traversal in the api/push route. An attacker can determine the presence of arbitrary files on the host, an information-disclosure primitive useful for chaining further attacks against the inference service.
affected: Ollama < 0.1.46 (api/push route)

title: AI-related flaws strain the CVE/CNA model: most are traditional CWEs in AI software, while prompt-injection-class flaws resist CVE assignment
summary: Empirical study of AI-related CVEs (Maugeri et al., ACM AISec '25) finds the overwhelming majority of disclosed AI vulnerabilities are conventional software weaknesses (CWE-502 unsafe deserialization, CWE-22 path traversal, CWE-78 OS command injection, CWE-94 code injection) sitting inside AI products such as LangChain, Ollama, vLLM, PyTorch, Keras, ComfyUI and MCP servers — not novel ML-specific defects. The CVE Program (MITRE as Primary CNA plus federated CNAs like GitHub, huntr.dev, JFrog, Snyk) handles these well, but model-level/behavioral flaws (prompt injection, jailbreak, training-data poisoning effects) sit awkwardly: they are often data/configuration-dependent, lack a fixed 'vulnerable version', and a 'patch' may be a probabilistic guardrail rather than a code fix, so CNAs frequently decline them. This is the reporting gap the platform tracks against continuous red teaming.
notes: CWE class distribution and product list ^[extracted] from NVD records confirmed in this cycle; the CNA-decline pattern for behavioral flaws is ^[inferred] from the OWASP-LLM debate and the cited study.

title: Whether prompt injection deserves a CVE: concrete app-level injections now get CVEs, but the architectural class does not
summary: Prompt injection is OWASP LLM01:2025 and maps to MITRE ATLAS, NIST AI RMF, EU AI Act and ISO/IEC 42001, yet its CVE status is contested. The emerging consensus in practice: a SPECIFIC, exploitable instance in a named product/version DOES warrant a CVE (e.g. indirect-injection-to-RCE chains in Microsoft Copilot, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and serialization-injection chains like LangChain CVE-2025-68664), whereas prompt injection as an ARCHITECTURAL property of LLMs — present in essentially every model with no patchable 'fixed version' — does not fit CVE/CVSS semantics.
